The learning performance in such networks with nearest neighbor heuristic can be improved upon by multiplying the individual receptive field widths by a suitable overlap factor. We present results indicat!ng optimal values for such overlap factors. We also present a new algorithm for determining receptive field centers. This method negotiates more hidden units in the regions of the input space as a function of the output and is conducive to better learning when the number of patterns (hidden units) is small.

paragraphs: This paper studies radial basis function networks whose hidden units represent receptive fields in the input space. The models combine self-organized learning with supervised learning. The authors present upper bounds for learning rates and investigate how the placement and widths of those receptive fields affect the network's ability to learn.

One change concerns receptive field widths chosen through a nearest-neighbor heuristic. The authors multiply the individual widths by an overlap factor, adjusting how much neighboring receptive fields cover the same inputs. They report improved learning performance and results indicating suitable optimal factors. This makes overlap an explicit design choice rather than simply accepting the widths produced by the original heuristic.

A second contribution is an algorithm for choosing receptive field centers using information about the desired output. It allocates more hidden units to regions according to the output relationship being learned. The reported benefit is better learning when few patterns or hidden units are available, linking representational resources to the supervised task.
summary.tldr: Adjusting receptive field overlap and using output information to place centers improves learning in radial basis function networks.

title: Algorithms for Better Representation and Faster Learning in Radial Basis Function Networks

paragraphs: This paper studies how many resources a feedforward neural network needs to approximate a class of functions. The functions satisfy a Lipschitz condition, meaning their outputs cannot change arbitrarily quickly relative to changes in their inputs. This restriction gives the analysis a defined relationship between input variation and output variation.

The authors construct a network representation based on level sets, which group inputs according to the function values they produce. They derive an upper bound on the number of network nodes needed to achieve a specified uniform approximation error. Uniform error concerns accuracy across the entire input domain, making the result a statement about the whole represented function.

The analysis also bounds the number of bits required to represent the network's weights at the desired accuracy. This distinguishes architectural size from the precision needed to store its parameters. Finally, the authors compare the representation bound with the epsilon-entropy of the function class, connecting the network's resource requirements to an information-based description of approximation complexity.
summary.tldr: A level-set construction bounds the nodes and weight-storage bits needed for neural approximation of Lipschitz functions.

title: e-Entropy and the Complexity of Feedforward Neural Networks

abstract: There exist large classes of time series, such as those with nonlinear moving average components, that are not well modeled by feedforward networks or linear models, but can be modeled by recurrent networks. We show that recurrent neural networks are a type of nonlinear autoregressive-moving average (N ARMA) model. Practical ability will be shown in the results of a competition sponsored by the Puget Sound Power and Light Company, where the recurrent networks gave the best performance on electric load forecasting.
originalAbstract: There exist large classes of time series, such as those with nonlinear moving average components, that are not well modeled by feedforward networks or linear models, but can be modeled by recurrent networks. We show that recurrent neural networks are a type of nonlinear autoregressive-moving average (N ARMA) model. Practical ability will be shown in the results of a competition sponsored by the Puget Sound Power and Light Company, where the recurrent networks gave the best performance on electric load forecasting.

paragraphs: The paper connects recurrent neural networks with nonlinear autoregressive-moving average models, abbreviated NARMA. Its motivation is that large classes of time series are poorly represented by feedforward networks or linear models. The abstract specifically identifies series containing nonlinear moving-average components as an example where recurrent networks can provide a suitable model.

The theoretical contribution is to show that recurrent neural networks belong to the NARMA model family. This gives recurrence a time-series interpretation and connects the network architecture to a recognized way of describing temporal dependence. The result helps explain why the architecture can represent dynamics that create difficulties for the other model types discussed.

The paper also reports a practical demonstration in an electric-load forecasting competition sponsored by the Puget Sound Power and Light Company. Recurrent networks achieve the best performance in that competition. The theoretical connection and forecasting result play complementary roles: one characterizes the kind of temporal model the networks implement, while the other demonstrates their usefulness on a concrete prediction task.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies recurrent networks as NARMA models and reports leading performance in an electric-load forecasting competition.

title: Recurrent Networks and NARMA Modeling

abstract: This paper reports on the performance of two methods for recognition-based segmentation of strings of on-line hand-printed capital Latin characters. The input strings consist of a time(cid:173) ordered sequence of X-Y coordinates, punctuated by pen-lifts. The methods were designed to work in "run-on mode" where there is no constraint on the spacing between characters. While both methods use a neural network recognition engine and a graph-algorithmic post-processor, their approaches to segmentation are quite differ(cid:173) ent. The first method, which we call IN SEC (for input segmen(cid:173) tation), uses a combination of heuristics to identify particular pen(cid:173) lifts as tentative segmentation points. The second method, which we call OUTSEC (for output segmentation), relies on the empiri(cid:173) cally trained recognition engine for both recognizing characters and identifying relevant segmentation points.

paragraphs: The paper examines how to separate and recognize handwritten capital Latin characters when writers are free to vary the spacing between them. Input arrives as a time-ordered stream of pen coordinates with pen-lift events. The segmentation problem is therefore to decide which parts of that recorded movement belong to individual characters.

Both proposed methods use a neural recognition engine followed by a graph-based processing stage. INSEC identifies tentative character boundaries by applying a combination of heuristics to pen lifts. This makes selected events in the input stream candidates for segmentation, which are then handled within the larger recognition process.

OUTSEC instead relies on the trained recognition engine to identify relevant segmentation points as well as recognize characters. The two approaches thus place responsibility for boundary detection in different components: explicit input heuristics in one case and learned recognition behavior in the other. Their shared goal is recognition in run-on writing, where character separation cannot depend on a required spacing convention.
summary.tldr: Two handwriting methods locate character boundaries using either pen-lift heuristics or the learned responses of a neural recognizer.

title: Recognition-based Segmentation of On-Line Hand-printed Words

TPDP does so by determining an ideal set of transition points (TPs) which specify only the control action changes necessary for optimal control. TPDP converges to an ideal TP set by using a variation of Q-Iearning to assess the mer(cid:173) its of adding, swapping and removing TPs from states throughout the state space. When applied to a race track problem, TPDP learned the optimal control policy much sooner than conventional Q-Iearning, and was able to do so using less memory.

paragraphs: Transition point dynamic programming tackles adaptive control of continuous stochastic systems with a compact policy representation. Its key idea is to store the points at which the control action needs to change. A suitable set of these transition points can describe the necessary decisions while reducing the learning and memory demands of the controller.

The algorithm uses a variation of Q-learning to evaluate changes to this set. It considers adding, swapping, and removing transition points at states throughout the state space. Learning therefore includes deciding which points deserve to be represented, as well as assessing the control behavior associated with the evolving representation.

The authors state that the method converges to an ideal transition-point set. On a race-track problem, it learns the optimal policy much sooner than conventional Q-learning and uses less memory. This result illustrates the benefit of concentrating representation on changes in control action. The reported gains concern both the time required to learn and the storage required to express the policy.
summary.tldr: Learning where control actions must change lets transition point dynamic programming solve a race-track task faster and with less memory than conventional Q-learning.

title: Transition Point Dynamic Programming

abstract: Consider the problem of learning input/output mappings through exploration, e.g. learning the kinematics or dynamics of a robotic manipulator. If actions are expensive and computation is cheap, then we should explore by selecting a trajectory through the in(cid:173) put space which gives us the most amount of information in the fewest number of steps. I discuss how results from the field of opti(cid:173) mal experiment design may be used to guide such exploration, and demonstrate its use on a simple kinematics problem.
originalAbstract: Consider the problem of learning input/output mappings through exploration, e.g. learning the kinematics or dynamics of a robotic manipulator. If actions are expensive and computation is cheap, then we should explore by selecting a trajectory through the in(cid:173) put space which gives us the most amount of information in the fewest number of steps. I discuss how results from the field of opti(cid:173) mal experiment design may be used to guide such exploration, and demonstrate its use on a simple kinematics problem.

paragraphs: This paper considers learning an input-output relationship by actively exploring it. Learning the kinematics or dynamics of a robotic manipulator provides the motivating example. In this setting, the learner influences which observations become available through the actions it chooses, so the exploration strategy is part of the learning problem.

The argument rests on an explicit resource assumption: actions are expensive while computation is cheap. Under that assumption, it makes sense to spend computation selecting an informative trajectory through the input space. The objective is to obtain as much information as possible while taking as few exploratory steps as possible.

The author discusses how optimal experiment design can guide this choice and demonstrates the approach on a simple kinematics problem. The significance is the connection between planning an experiment and planning exploration: both involve choosing observations for the information they provide. The demonstration applies that principle to learning a mapping, with the value of the approach tied to the stated imbalance between action and computation costs.
summary.tldr: Optimal experiment design guides informative exploration when collecting observations through actions is more expensive than computation.

title: Neural Network Exploration Using Optimal Experiment Design

abstract: We derive a learning algorithm for inferring an overcomplete basis by viewing it as probabilistic model of the observed data. Over(cid:173) complete bases allow for better approximation of the underlying statistical density. Using a Laplacian prior on the basis coefficients removes redundancy and leads to representations that are sparse and are a nonlinear function of the data. This can be viewed as a generalization of the technique of independent component anal(cid:173) ysis and provides a method for blind source separation of fewer mixtures than sources. We demonstrate the utility of overcom(cid:173) plete representations on natural speech and show that compared to the traditional Fourier basis the inferred representations poten(cid:173) tially have much greater coding efficiency. A traditional way to represent real-values signals is with Fourier or wavelet bases. A disadvantage of these bases, however, is that they are not specialized for any particular dataset. Principal component analysis (PCA) provides one means for finding an basis that is adapted for a dataset, but the basis vectors are restricted to be orthogonal. An extension of PCA called independent component analysis (Jutten and Herault, 1991; Comon et al., 1991; Bell and Sejnowski, 1995) allows the learning of non-orthogonal bases. All of these bases are complete in the sense that they span the input space, but they are limited in terms of how well they can approximate the dataset's statistical density. Representations that are overcomplete, i. e. more basis vectors than input variables, can provide a better representation, because the basis vectors can be specialized for Learning Nonlinear Overcomplete Representations for Efficient Coding 557 a larger variety of features present in the entire ensemble of data. A criticism of overcomplete representations is that they are redundant, i.e. a given data point may have many possible representations, but this redundancy is removed by the prior probability of the basis coefficients which specifies the probability of the alternative representations. Most of the overcomplete bases used in the literature are fixed in the sense that they are not adapted to the structure in the data. Recently Olshausen and Field (1996) presented an algorithm that allows an overcomplete basis to be learned. This algorithm relied on an approximation to the desired probabilistic objective that had several drawbacks, including tendency to breakdown in the case of low noise levels and when learning bases with higher degrees of overcompleteness. paragraphs: An overcomplete representation offers more basis vectors than there are input variables, giving a signal more possible building blocks. This flexibility lets the vectors specialize in a wider variety of patterns, but it also creates ambiguity: the same input can have multiple representations. The paper develops a probabilistic learning method that addresses both flexibility and ambiguity.

The model represents data with a linear combination of basis vectors plus additive noise. A Laplacian prior favors sparse coefficients, assigning different probabilities to alternative representations and reducing redundancy. Although reconstruction uses a linear basis, inferring the coefficients becomes a nonlinear function of the input. The authors also improve the approximation used to learn the basis, addressing weaknesses of an earlier approximation at low noise and greater overcompleteness.

The approach generalizes independent component analysis and provides a method for separating more sources than there are mixtures. On natural speech, the learned representations show potentially much greater coding efficiency than a Fourier basis. The stated advantage comes from combining data-adapted features with a probabilistic preference for economical representations.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic algorithm learns overcomplete sparse representations that offer potentially more efficient coding of natural speech.

title: Learning Nonlinear Overcomplete Representations for Efficient Coding

abstract: We employ both master equation and order parameter approaches to analyze the asymptotic dynamics of on-line learning with dif(cid:173) ferent learning rate annealing schedules. We examine the relations between the results obtained by the two approaches and obtain new results on the optimal decay coefficients and their dependence on the number of hidden nodes in a two layer architecture.
originalAbstract: We employ both master equation and order parameter approaches to analyze the asymptotic dynamics of on-line learning with dif(cid:173) ferent learning rate annealing schedules. We examine the relations between the results obtained by the two approaches and obtain new results on the optimal decay coefficients and their dependence on the number of hidden nodes in a two layer architecture.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the learning rate should decrease during online learning. Such an annealing schedule determines how update sizes change as learning proceeds. The authors focus on asymptotic dynamics, examining the behavior of the learning process in its long-run regime under different schedules.

They analyze the problem using two theoretical approaches: a master-equation approach and an order-parameter approach. They then examine how the results from the two descriptions relate to one another. This comparison connects two ways of studying the same learning dynamics, rather than treating their conclusions as unrelated prescriptions.

The analysis produces new results for optimal decay coefficients and how those coefficients depend on the number of hidden nodes in a two-layer architecture. The implication is that the best coefficient in a learning-rate decay schedule is tied to network structure in the studied setting. The contribution is a theoretical account of that dependence, grounded in a comparison of the two analytical methods.
summary.tldr: Two theoretical analyses connect optimal learning-rate decay coefficients to the number of hidden nodes in a two-layer network.

title: Two Approaches to Optimal Annealing

abstract: A goal of statistical language modeling is to learn the joint probability function of sequences of words. This is intrinsically difficult because of the curse of dimensionality: we propose to fight it with its own weapons. In the proposed approach one learns simultaneously (1) a distributed rep(cid:173) resentation for each word (i.e. a similarity between words) along with (2) the probability function for word sequences, expressed with these repre(cid:173) sentations. Generalization is obtained because a sequence of words that has never been seen before gets high probability if it is made of words that are similar to words forming an already seen sentence. We report on experiments using neural networks for the probability function, showing on two text corpora that the proposed approach very significantly im(cid:173) proves on a state-of-the-art trigram model.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the difficulty of assigning probabilities to sequences of words when the number of possible sequences is enormous. Observed sentences cover only a small portion of that space. The proposed approach addresses this problem by learning representations of words together with a probability model that uses those representations.

Each word receives a distributed representation that expresses similarities to other words. These similarities are learned alongside the sequence probabilities, so the representation and the language model develop together. This creates a route for generalization: an unseen sequence can receive high probability when its words resemble those in a sequence the model has encountered.

The authors implement the probability function with neural networks and evaluate the approach on two text corpora. They report a very significant improvement over a state-of-the-art trigram model. The central contribution is a way to share what is learned across related word sequences, using learned word similarity to address the dimensionality problem in language modeling.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning word representations and sequence probabilities enables generalization to unseen sentences and substantially improves on a trigram model in two corpora.

title: A Neural Probabilistic Language Model

abstract: Neurons in area V4 have relatively large receptive fields (RFs), so multi(cid:173) ple visual features are simultaneously "seen" by these cells. Recordings from single V 4 neurons suggest that simultaneously presented stimuli compete to set the output firing rate, and that attention acts to isolate individual features by biasing the competition in favor of the attended object. We propose that both stimulus competition and attentional bias(cid:173) ing arise from the spatial segregation of afferent synapses onto different regions of the excitable dendritic tree of V 4 neurons. The pattern of feed(cid:173) forward, stimulus-driven inputs follows from a Hebbian rule: excitatory afferents with similar RFs tend to group together on the dendritic tree, avoiding randomly located inhibitory inputs with similar RFs. The same principle guides the formation of inputs that mediate attentional mod(cid:173) ulation. Using both biophysically detailed compartmental models and simplified models of computation in single neurons, we demonstrate that such an architecture could account for the response properties and atten(cid:173) tional modulation of V 4 neurons. Our results suggest an important role for nonlinear dendritic conductances in extrastriate cortical processing.

paragraphs: A neuron in visual area V4 can receive information about several features within its receptive field. Recordings suggest that simultaneously presented stimuli compete to determine its firing rate, and that attention shifts this competition toward an attended object. The paper asks whether the organization of inputs within a single neuron could explain both effects.

The proposed architecture separates incoming synapses across different regions of an excitable dendritic tree. Under a Hebbian organizing rule, excitatory inputs with similar receptive fields cluster together while avoiding randomly positioned inhibitory inputs with similar receptive fields. The same organizing principle applies to inputs carrying attentional modulation.

The authors examine this architecture using both detailed biophysical compartment models and simpler models of single-neuron computation. Their results show that the arrangement could account for V4 response properties and attentional effects. This supports nonlinear dendritic activity as a possible contributor to visual processing beyond primary visual cortex; it does not establish that this architecture is the biological cause.
summary.tldr: Models suggest that spatially organized dendritic inputs could explain stimulus competition and attentional biasing in V4 neurons.

title: Dendritic Compartmentalization Could Underlie Competition and Attentional Biasing of Simultaneous Visual Stimuli

abstract: Address-event representation (AER), originally proposed as a means to communicate sparse neural events between neuromorphic chips, has proven efﬁcient in implementing large-scale networks with arbitrary, conﬁgurable synaptic connectivity. In this work, we further extend the functionality of AER to implement arbitrary, conﬁgurable synaptic plas- ticity in the address domain. As proof of concept, we implement a bi- ologically inspired form of spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) based on relative timing of events in an AER framework. Experimen- tal results from an analog VLSI integrate-and-ﬁre network demonstrate address domain learning in a task that requires neurons to group corre- lated inputs.
originalAbstract: Address-event representation (AER), originally proposed as a means to communicate sparse neural events between neuromorphic chips, has proven efﬁcient in implementing large-scale networks with arbitrary, conﬁgurable synaptic connectivity. In this work, we further extend the functionality of AER to implement arbitrary, conﬁgurable synaptic plas- ticity in the address domain. As proof of concept, we implement a bi- ologically inspired form of spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) based on relative timing of events in an AER framework. Experimen- tal results from an analog VLSI integrate-and-ﬁre network demonstrate address domain learning in a task that requires neurons to group corre- lated inputs.

paragraphs: Address-event representation provides a way to communicate sparse neural events between neuromorphic chips. It also supports large networks whose synaptic connections can be configured. This paper extends that framework so the address domain can control synaptic plasticity as well, adding configurable changes in connection strength to its existing connectivity capabilities.

As a proof of concept, the authors implement a biologically inspired spike timing-dependent plasticity rule. Learning depends on the relative timing of events represented in the AER system. This connects the event-based communication framework to a learning mechanism, allowing temporal relationships among neural events to influence how the network's synapses change.

Experiments use an analog VLSI network of integrate-and-fire neurons on a task requiring neurons to group correlated inputs. The results demonstrate learning in the address domain for that task. The contribution is thus both an extension of the AER framework toward configurable plasticity and a hardware demonstration showing that a timing-based learning rule can operate within it.
summary.tldr: An address-event framework gains configurable synaptic learning, demonstrated with spike timing-dependent plasticity in analog neural hardware.

title: Spike Timing-Dependent Plasticity in the Address Domain

abstract: We present a probabilistic approach to learning a Gaussian Process classifier in the presence of unlabeled data. Our approach involves a "null category noise model" (NCNM) inspired by ordered cate- gorical noise models. The noise model reflects an assumption that the data density is lower between the class-conditional densities. We illustrate our approach on a toy problem and present compar- ative results for the semi-supervised classification of handwritten digits.
originalAbstract: We present a probabilistic approach to learning a Gaussian Process classifier in the presence of unlabeled data. Our approach involves a "null category noise model" (NCNM) inspired by ordered cate- gorical noise models. The noise model reflects an assumption that the data density is lower between the class-conditional densities. We illustrate our approach on a toy problem and present compar- ative results for the semi-supervised classification of handwritten digits.

paragraphs: This paper extends Gaussian-process classification to a setting containing both labeled and unlabeled examples. The aim is to let observations without known categories contribute to learning within a probabilistic framework. Doing so requires an assumption linking the distribution of input data to the separation between classes, since unlabeled examples do not directly reveal their categories.

The authors express that link through a null category noise model, inspired by ordered categorical noise models. It reflects the assumption that the regions between class-conditional densities contain less data. In plain terms, the method treats relatively sparse regions between class-associated concentrations as informative about how those classes should be separated.

The paper illustrates the approach on a toy problem and presents comparative results for semi-supervised handwritten-digit classification. These examples put the probabilistic formulation into use without the abstract claiming a particular margin of improvement. The contribution is the noise model's role in connecting unlabeled observations with classification, and its interpretation depends on the stated low-density-between-classes assumption.
summary.tldr: A null category noise model lets Gaussian-process classification use unlabeled data under a low-density-between-classes assumption.

title: Semi-supervised Learning via Gaussian Processes

abstract: We present a theoretical study on the discriminative clustering framework, recently proposed for simultaneous subspace selection via linear discriminant analysis (LDA) and clustering. Empirical results have shown its favorable performance in comparison with several other popular clustering algorithms. However, the inherent relationship between subspace selection and clustering in this framework is not well understood, due to the iterative nature of the algorithm. We show in this paper that this iterative subspace selection and clustering is equivalent to kernel K-means with a specific kernel Gram matrix. This provides significant and new insights into the nature of this subspace selection procedure. Based on this equivalence relationship, we propose the Discriminative K-means (DisKmeans) algorithm for simultaneous LDA subspace selection and clustering, as well as an automatic parameter estimation procedure. We also present the nonlinear extension of DisKmeans using kernels. We show that the learning of the kernel matrix over a convex set of pre-specified kernel matrices can be incorporated into the clustering formulation. The connection between DisKmeans and several other clustering algorithms is also analyzed. The presented theories and algorithms are evaluated through experiments on a collection of benchmark data sets.

Earlier empirical results favored this framework, but its iterative procedure made the relationship between these two operations difficult to understand. This paper addresses that theoretical question by showing an equivalence to kernel K-means with a particular kernel Gram matrix.

The equivalence gives a different mathematical description of the joint procedure: subspace selection and clustering can be understood through a kernel-based clustering formulation. Building on this connection, the authors introduce Discriminative K-means, or DisKmeans, together with an automatic parameter-estimation procedure. The result turns the theoretical relationship into an algorithm for performing both tasks.

The paper also develops a nonlinear kernel extension and shows how learning a kernel matrix within a convex set of specified candidates can enter the clustering formulation. It analyzes relationships with other clustering methods and evaluates the theories and algorithms on benchmark datasets. The central contribution is a unified explanation and algorithmic development of a framework whose favorable empirical behavior had previously been better understood than its internal relationships.
summary.tldr: An equivalence with kernel K-means explains joint discriminant subspace selection and clustering and motivates the DisKmeans algorithm.

title: Discriminative K-means for Clustering

abstract: Polysemy is a problem for methods that exploit image search engines to build object category models. Existing unsupervised approaches do not take word sense into consideration. We propose a new method that uses a dictionary to learn models of visual word sense from a large collection of unlabeled web data. The use of LDA to discover a latent sense space makes the model robust despite the very limited nature of dictionary definitions. The definitions are used to learn a distribution in the latent space that best represents a sense. The algorithm then uses the text surrounding image links to retrieve images with high probability of a particular dictionary sense. An object classifier is trained on the resulting sense-specific images. We evaluate our method on a dataset obtained by searching the web for polysemous words. Category classification experiments show that our dictionary-based approach outperforms baseline methods.

paragraphs: A word with multiple meanings can return images belonging to different visual categories. This creates a problem for systems that learn object-category models from image-search results. The paper introduces a method that uses dictionary meanings to organize unlabeled web data into sense-specific image collections before training an object classifier.

The method uses latent Dirichlet allocation to discover a latent sense space. Dictionary definitions then help learn a distribution in that space representing each sense. This intermediate representation makes the model robust despite the limited information in definitions. Text surrounding image links is used to identify images with high probability of belonging to a particular dictionary sense.

The retrieved sense-specific images supply the data for training an object classifier. Evaluation uses a dataset collected by searching the web for words with multiple meanings, and classification experiments show better performance than the baseline methods considered. The result supports using dictionary-guided textual interpretation to improve visual training data: resolving meaning during image selection helps the subsequent classifier learn the intended category.
summary.tldr: Dictionary-guided latent sense models select meaning-specific web images and improve object classification over the tested baselines.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Visual Sense Models for Polysemous Words

abstract: Probabilistic programming languages allow modelers to specify a stochastic process using syntax that resembles modern programming languages. Because the program is in machine-readable format, a variety of techniques from compiler design and program analysis can be used to examine the structure of the distribution represented by the probabilistic program. We show how nonstandard interpretations of probabilistic programs can be used to craft efficient inference algorithms: information about the structure of a distribution (such as gradients or dependencies) is generated as a monad-like side computation while executing the program. These interpretations can be easily coded using special-purpose objects and operator overloading. We implement two examples of nonstandard interpretations in two different languages, and use them as building blocks to construct inference algorithms: automatic differentiation, which enables gradient based methods, and provenance tracking, which enables efficient construction of global proposals.

paragraphs: A probabilistic program describes a stochastic process in executable, machine-readable form. This paper uses that program structure to obtain information useful for inference. The key idea is to run the program with an alternative interpretation that carries out an additional computation alongside its ordinary operations.

These side computations collect information such as gradients or dependencies within the represented distribution. The authors describe their organization as monad-like and implement them using special-purpose objects and operator overloading. This provides a way to obtain useful structural information through execution itself, drawing on ideas from compiler design and program analysis.

The paper implements two examples across two programming languages. Automatic differentiation supplies gradients for gradient-based inference, while provenance tracking records dependencies that support efficient construction of global proposals. These examples demonstrate how different interpretations can become reusable building blocks for inference algorithms. The broader contribution is a connection between the executable form of a model and the computations needed to reason about it.
summary.tldr: Alternative executions of probabilistic programs collect gradients and dependencies that help construct efficient inference algorithms.

title: Nonstandard Interpretations of Probabilistic Programs for Efficient Inference

abstract: Graphical models are a very useful tool to describe and understand natural phenomena, from gene expression to climate change and social interactions. The topological structure of these graphs/networks is a fundamental part of the analysis, and in many cases the main goal of the study. However, little work has been done on incorporating prior topological knowledge onto the estimation of the underlying graphical models from sample data. In this work we propose extensions to the basic joint regression model for network estimation, which explicitly incorporate graph-topological constraints into the corresponding optimization approach. The first proposed extension includes an eigenvector centrality constraint, thereby promoting this important prior topological property. The second developed extension promotes the formation of certain motifs, triangle-shaped ones in particular, which are known to exist for example in genetic regulatory networks. The presentation of the underlying formulations, which serve as examples of the introduction of topological constraints in network estimation, is complemented with examples in diverse datasets demonstrating the importance of incorporating such critical prior knowledge.

paragraphs: When estimating a network from observations, its overall structure can be as important as its individual connections. This paper studies how prior knowledge about that structure can enter the estimation process. It extends a joint-regression approach so that graph topology becomes an explicit part of the optimization.

The first extension introduces an eigenvector-centrality constraint, promoting a desired pattern of node importance within the network. The second encourages particular small connection patterns, especially triangles. Such motifs are known to occur in settings including genetic regulatory networks, making them a concrete example of structural knowledge that an estimator can use.

The two formulations illustrate different ways to express prior information about a graph: through a centrality property and through recurring local patterns. Examples across diverse datasets demonstrate the importance of incorporating this knowledge. The contribution is a way to shape network estimation using stated structural expectations, allowing those expectations to influence the graph that is inferred from sample data.
summary.tldr: Network-estimation extensions incorporate prior topology through eigenvector-centrality constraints and encouragement of motifs such as triangles.

title: Topology Constraints in Graphical Models

abstract: Although many variants of stochastic gradient descent have been proposed for large-scale convex optimization, most of them require projecting the solution at {\it each} iteration to ensure that the obtained solution stays within the feasible domain. For complex domains (e.g., positive semidefinite cone), the projection step can be computationally expensive, making stochastic gradient descent unattractive for large-scale optimization problems. We address this limitation by developing a novel stochastic gradient descent algorithm that does not need intermediate projections. Instead, only one projection at the last iteration is needed to obtain a feasible solution in the given domain. Our theoretical analysis shows that with a high probability, the proposed algorithms achieve an $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence rate for general convex optimization, and an $O(\ln T/T)$ rate for strongly convex optimization under mild conditions about the domain and the objective function.

For complex domains (e.g., positive semidefinite cone), the projection step can be computationally expensive, making stochastic gradient descent unattractive for large-scale optimization problems. We address this limitation by developing a novel stochastic gradient descent algorithm that does not need intermediate projections. Instead, only one projection at the last iteration is needed to obtain a feasible solution in the given domain. Our theoretical analysis shows that with a high probability, the proposed algorithms achieve an $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence rate for general convex optimization, and an $O(\ln T/T)$ rate for strongly convex optimization under mild conditions about the domain and the objective function.

paragraphs: Constrained stochastic gradient descent commonly projects each updated solution back into the feasible domain. For complicated domains, such as the positive semidefinite cone, this projection can be expensive enough to undermine the method's appeal for large problems. The paper targets that repeated computational cost while still requiring a feasible final answer.

The authors develop stochastic gradient algorithms that avoid intermediate projections and perform just one projection at the last iteration. This changes when feasibility is enforced: the final projection supplies a solution in the permitted domain without paying for that operation at every step. The computational motivation is strongest when projection itself is costly.

The theoretical analysis gives high-probability convergence rates under mild conditions on the domain and objective. For general convex optimization, the rate is O(1/sqrt(T)); for strongly convex optimization, it is O(ln(T)/T). These guarantees show that eliminating repeated projections can coexist with controlled convergence under the stated conditions. The result is a principled way to reduce projection work while retaining both final feasibility and quantitative optimization guarantees.
summary.tldr: Stochastic gradient algorithms use only a final projection while retaining high-probability convergence guarantees under conditions on the objective and domain.

title: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Only One Projection

abstract: Causal inference uses observational data to infer the causal structure of the data generating system. We study a class of restricted Structural Equation Models for time series that we call Time Series Models with Independent Noise (TiMINo). These models require independent residual time series, whereas traditional methods like Granger causality exploit the variance of residuals. This work contains two main contributions: (1) Theoretical: By restricting the model class (e.g. to additive noise) we provide more general identifiability results than existing ones. The results cover lagged and instantaneous effects that can be nonlinear and unfaithful, and non-instantaneous feedbacks between the time series. (2) Practical: If there are no feedback loops between time series, we propose an algorithm based on non-linear independence tests of time series. When the data are causally insufficient, or the data generating process does not satisfy the model assumptions, this algorithm may still give partial results, but mostly avoids incorrect answers. The Structural Equation Model point of view allows us to extend both the theoretical and the algorithmic part to situations in which the time series have been measured with different time delays (as may happen for fMRI data, for example). TiMINo outperforms existing methods on artificial and real data. Code is provided.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer causal relationships from observational time series. Its TiMINo models require the residual time series—the parts left unexplained by the model—to be independent. This differs from traditional Granger-style methods, which use residual variance to assess predictive relationships.

Restricting the structural equations, for example to additive-noise models, enables broader identifiability results. The theory covers nonlinear effects, both immediate and delayed relationships, certain unfaithful cases, and feedback that operates through time rather than instantaneously. These results establish conditions under which causal structure can be distinguished from observational data.

The practical algorithm has a narrower scope: it assumes no feedback loops between time series and uses nonlinear independence tests. When relevant causes are missing or model assumptions fail, it may return partial results and mostly avoids incorrect answers; this is not a guarantee of correctness under misspecification. The framework also accommodates different measurement delays across series. Experiments on artificial and real data report better performance than existing methods, supporting the usefulness of the independence-based approach.
summary.tldr: TiMINo uses independent residual time series and restricted structural equations to identify causal relationships under stated model conditions.

title: Causal Inference on Time Series using Restricted Structural Equation Models

abstract: Modern visual recognition systems are often limited in their ability to scale to large numbers of object categories. This limitation is in part due to the increasing difficulty of acquiring sufficient training data in the form of labeled images as the number of object categories grows. One remedy is to leverage data from other sources -- such as text data -- both to train visual models and to constrain their predictions. In this paper we present a new deep visual-semantic embedding model trained to identify visual objects using both labeled image data as well as semantic information gleaned from unannotated text. We demonstrate that this model matches state-of-the-art performance on the 1000-class ImageNet object recognition challenge while making more semantically reasonable errors, and also show that the semantic information can be exploited to make predictions about tens of thousands of image labels not observed during training. Semantic knowledge improves such zero-shot predictions by up to 65%, achieving hit rates of up to 10% across thousands of novel labels never seen by the visual model.

In this paper we present a new deep visual-semantic embedding model trained to identify visual objects using both labeled image data as well as semantic information gleaned from unannotated text. paragraphs: Recognizing more object categories usually requires labeled images for more categories, making training data a bottleneck. DeViSE addresses this by combining labeled image examples with semantic information learned from unannotated text. The model uses both visual evidence and knowledge about the meanings of labels when identifying objects.

On the 1,000-class ImageNet recognition challenge, the model matches the state-of-the-art performance described in the paper while making errors that are more reasonable in semantic terms. This means the contribution concerns the character of mistakes as well as overall recognition performance. Information from language helps constrain the model's predictions through relationships between object labels.

The same semantic information enables predictions involving tens of thousands of labels absent from visual training. In these zero-shot settings, semantic knowledge improves predictions by up to 65%, with hit rates reaching 10% across thousands of novel labels. These are reported upper-end results, not uniform gains across every unseen category. The findings show how text can extend the reach of a visual model beyond its labeled image categories.
summary.tldr: DeViSE combines images and text-derived semantics to recognize familiar objects and predict labels unseen during visual training.

title: DeViSE: A Deep Visual-Semantic Embedding Model

abstract: Several authors have recently developed risk-sensitive policy gradient methods that augment the standard expected cost minimization problem with a measure of variability in cost. These studies have focused on specific risk-measures, such as the variance or conditional value at risk (CVaR). In this work, we extend the policy gradient method to the whole class of coherent risk measures, which is widely accepted in finance and operations research, among other fields. We consider both static and time-consistent dynamic risk measures. For static risk measures, our approach is in the spirit of policy gradient algorithms and combines a standard sampling approach with convex programming. For dynamic risk measures, our approach is actor-critic style and involves explicit approximation of value function. Most importantly, our contribution presents a unified approach to risk-sensitive reinforcement learning that generalizes and extends previous results.

For static risk measures, our approach is in the spirit of policy gradient algorithms and combines a standard sampling approach with convex programming. paragraphs: This paper develops policy-gradient methods for reinforcement learning objectives that account for risk in costs. Earlier work considered particular measures such as variance or conditional value at risk. The authors extend the approach to the full class of coherent risk measures, providing a common framework for this broader family of objectives.

The framework covers both static risk measures and time-consistent dynamic ones. For the static case, the proposed method combines standard sampling with convex programming in the spirit of policy-gradient algorithms. This provides a way to incorporate the selected risk measure into policy optimization through sampled information and an optimization problem.

For dynamic risk measures, the method takes an actor-critic form and explicitly approximates the value function. The distinction between static and dynamic formulations matters because they require different algorithmic treatment within the same overall approach. The main stated contribution is this unification: risk-sensitive policy optimization can be developed across coherent risk measures while extending previous results beyond the specific measures they addressed.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies policy-gradient methods for coherent risk measures, covering static objectives and time-consistent dynamic risk.

title: Policy Gradient for Coherent Risk Measures

abstract: Deep neural networks currently demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in several domains.At the same time, models of this class are very demanding in terms of computational resources. In particular, a large amount of memory is required by commonly used fully-connected layers, making it hard to use the models on low-end devices and stopping the further increase of the model size. In this paper we convert the dense weight matrices of the fully-connected layers to the Tensor Train format such that the number of parameters is reduced by a huge factor and at the same time the expressive power of the layer is preserved.In particular, for the Very Deep VGG networks we report the compression factor of the dense weight matrix of a fully-connected layer up to 200000 times leading to the compression factor of the whole network up to 7 times.
originalAbstract: Deep neural networks currently demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in several domains.At the same time, models of this class are very demanding in terms of computational resources. In particular, a large amount of memory is required by commonly used fully-connected layers, making it hard to use the models on low-end devices and stopping the further increase of the model size. In this paper we convert the dense weight matrices of the fully-connected layers to the Tensor Train format such that the number of parameters is reduced by a huge factor and at the same time the expressive power of the layer is preserved.In particular, for the Very Deep VGG networks we report the compression factor of the dense weight matrix of a fully-connected layer up to 200000 times leading to the compression factor of the whole network up to 7 times.

paragraphs: Fully connected layers can account for a large memory burden in deep neural networks. Their dense weight matrices make models harder to deploy on devices with limited resources and constrain further growth in model size. This paper addresses that burden by changing how the layer’s weights are represented.

The authors convert dense matrices into Tensor Train format, greatly reducing the number of stored parameters while preserving the layer’s expressive power as stated in the abstract. The approach targets the representation of the fully connected transformation, linking compact parameter storage to the function that the layer needs to perform.

For Very Deep VGG networks, the authors report compression of a fully connected layer’s dense weight matrix by up to 200,000 times. The reported compression of the entire network reaches up to seven times. These are distinct scopes of compression: a dramatic reduction in one matrix translates into a smaller reduction across the full model. The results demonstrate the memory-saving potential of tensor representations for parameter-heavy neural-network layers.
summary.tldr: Tensor Train representations dramatically compress fully connected weights, with reported whole-network VGG compression reaching seven times.

title: Tensorizing Neural Networks

abstract: We propose a mechanism for purchasing information from a sequence of participants.The participants may simply hold data points they wish to sell, or may have more sophisticated information; either way, they are incentivized to participate as long as they believe their data points are representative or their information will improve the mechanism's future prediction on a test set.The mechanism, which draws on the principles of prediction markets, has a bounded budget and minimizes generalization error for Bregman divergence loss functions.We then show how to modify this mechanism to preserve the privacy of participants' information: At any given time, the current prices and predictions of the mechanism reveal almost no information about any one participant, yet in total over all participants, information is accurately aggregated.

paragraphs: The paper treats information collection as a market in which participants arrive in sequence and can sell what they know. Their contributions may be individual data points or more sophisticated information. The mechanism draws on prediction-market principles to connect participation with improving future predictions on a test set.

The participation incentive is conditional on participants’ beliefs. They are motivated to contribute when they believe their data are representative or their information will improve predictions. The mechanism operates with a bounded budget and minimizes generalization error for Bregman divergence losses. This connects the economic problem of eliciting information with a specified family of prediction objectives.

The authors also modify the mechanism to protect participants’ information. At any given time, its current prices and predictions reveal almost no information about any single participant, while the combined information remains accurately aggregated. The result links useful collective prediction with limited individual disclosure. Its privacy statement concerns what the current market outputs reveal, rather than claiming that the mechanism exposes no information whatsoever.
summary.tldr: A bounded-budget prediction market elicits useful information and can be modified to limit what its outputs reveal about individual participants.

title: A Market Framework for Eliciting Private Data

abstract: An iterative regularization path with structural sparsity is proposed in this paper based on variable splitting and the Linearized Bregman Iteration, hence called \emph{Split LBI}. Despite its simplicity, Split LBI outperforms the popular generalized Lasso in both theory and experiments. A theory of path consistency is presented that equipped with a proper early stopping, Split LBI may achieve model selection consistency under a family of Irrepresentable Conditions which can be weaker than the necessary and sufficient condition for generalized Lasso. Furthermore, some $\ell_2$ error bounds are also given at the minimax optimal rates. The utility and benefit of the algorithm are illustrated by applications on both traditional image denoising and a novel example on partial order ranking.

Despite its simplicity, Split LBI outperforms the popular generalized Lasso in both theory and experiments. A theory of path consistency is presented that equipped with a proper early stopping, Split LBI may achieve model selection consistency under a family of Irrepresentable Conditions which can be weaker than the necessary and sufficient condition for generalized Lasso. Furthermore, some $\ell_2$ error bounds are also given at the minimax optimal rates. The utility and benefit of the algorithm are illustrated by applications on both traditional image denoising and a novel example on partial order ranking.

paragraphs: Structural sparsity seeks solutions whose selected components follow an underlying structure. This paper introduces Split LBI, an iterative regularization method combining variable splitting with Linearized Bregman Iteration. Its sequence of iterates forms a regularization path, making the point at which the procedure stops part of how the model is selected.

The theory shows that, with appropriate early stopping, Split LBI may consistently identify the model under a family of irrepresentable conditions. These conditions can be weaker than the necessary and sufficient condition for generalized Lasso. The paper also provides some squared-distance error bounds at minimax-optimal rates, supporting the quality of estimation as well as selection.

Applications to image denoising and partial-order ranking illustrate the method's utility. The authors report advantages over generalized Lasso in both theory and experiments. The theoretical advantage is specifically conditional on the stated requirements, including suitable stopping, while the experiments demonstrate benefits in the applications studied. Together, they motivate an iterative route to structured sparse estimation.
summary.tldr: Split LBI combines variable splitting and iterative regularization, with conditional model-selection guarantees and reported advantages over generalized Lasso.

title: Split LBI: An Iterative Regularization Path with Structural Sparsity

abstract: We introduce a new machine learning approach for image segmentation that uses a neural network to model the conditional energy of a segmentation given an image. Our approach, combinatorial energy learning for image segmentation (CELIS) places a particular emphasis on modeling the inherent combinatorial nature of dense image segmentation problems. We propose efficient algorithms for learning deep neural networks to model the energy function, and for local optimization of this energy in the space of supervoxel agglomerations. We extensively evaluate our method on a publicly available 3-D microscopy dataset with 25 billion voxels of ground truth data. On an 11 billion voxel test set, we find that our method improves volumetric reconstruction accuracy by more than 20% as compared to two state-of-the-art baseline methods: graph-based segmentation of the output of a 3-D convolutional neural network trained to predict boundaries, as well as a random forest classifier trained to agglomerate supervoxels that were generated by a 3-D convolutional neural network.
originalAbstract: We introduce a new machine learning approach for image segmentation that uses a neural network to model the conditional energy of a segmentation given an image. Our approach, combinatorial energy learning for image segmentation (CELIS) places a particular emphasis on modeling the inherent combinatorial nature of dense image segmentation problems. We propose efficient algorithms for learning deep neural networks to model the energy function, and for local optimization of this energy in the space of supervoxel agglomerations. We extensively evaluate our method on a publicly available 3-D microscopy dataset with 25 billion voxels of ground truth data. On an 11 billion voxel test set, we find that our method improves volumetric reconstruction accuracy by more than 20% as compared to two state-of-the-art baseline methods: graph-based segmentation of the output of a 3-D convolutional neural network trained to predict boundaries, as well as a random forest classifier trained to agglomerate supervoxels that were generated by a 3-D convolutional neural network.

paragraphs: Dense image segmentation involves deciding how many small image elements should be grouped into coherent regions. These decisions interact, making the problem combinatorial. CELIS addresses that structure by using a neural network to assign an energy to a proposed segmentation conditioned on the image.

The paper provides efficient algorithms both for learning this energy function and for locally optimizing it. The search operates over agglomerations of supervoxels, meaning combinations of small three-dimensional image regions. This connects a learned assessment of the segmentation with a procedure for changing its grouping, so the model directly addresses the space of possible region combinations.

Evaluation uses a public three-dimensional microscopy dataset containing 25 billion voxels of ground truth. On an 11 billion voxel test set, CELIS improves volumetric reconstruction accuracy by more than 20% over two state-of-the-art baselines. Those baselines use CNN boundary predictions with graph-based segmentation, or a random forest to merge CNN-generated supervoxels. The result supports the value of learned combinatorial energies for this reconstruction setting.
summary.tldr: CELIS learns segmentation energies and locally optimizes supervoxel groupings, improving reconstruction accuracy on a large microscopy test set.

title: Combinatorial Energy Learning for Image Segmentation

abstract: Graphical models with latent count variables arise in a number of fields. Standard exact inference techniques such as variable elimination and belief propagation do not apply to these models because the latent variables have countably infinite support. As a result, approximations such as truncation or MCMC are employed. We present the first exact inference algorithms for a class of models with latent count variables by developing a novel representation of countably infinite factors as probability generating functions, and then performing variable elimination with generating functions. Our approach is exact, runs in pseudo-polynomial time, and is much faster than existing approximate techniques. It leads to better parameter estimates for problems in population ecology by avoiding error introduced by approximate likelihood computations.
originalAbstract: Graphical models with latent count variables arise in a number of fields. Standard exact inference techniques such as variable elimination and belief propagation do not apply to these models because the latent variables have countably infinite support. As a result, approximations such as truncation or MCMC are employed. We present the first exact inference algorithms for a class of models with latent count variables by developing a novel representation of countably infinite factors as probability generating functions, and then performing variable elimination with generating functions. Our approach is exact, runs in pseudo-polynomial time, and is much faster than existing approximate techniques. It leads to better parameter estimates for problems in population ecology by avoiding error introduced by approximate likelihood computations.

paragraphs: Hidden count variables can take any nonnegative integer value, giving them infinitely many possible states. That creates a difficulty for standard exact inference methods in graphical models. Common alternatives truncate the range of counts or use sampling approximations, but those choices introduce approximation into the calculations used to learn and reason about the model.

This paper represents factors over countably infinite states with probability generating functions. It then performs variable elimination directly with those functions. The representation makes exact inference possible for the class of latent-count models considered, without replacing the infinite state space with a finite cutoff.

The authors describe the resulting algorithms as exact and pseudo-polynomial in running time, and report that they are much faster than existing approximate techniques. In population-ecology problems, avoiding approximate likelihood calculations leads to better parameter estimates. The significance is therefore both computational and statistical: the representation supports efficient exact calculations whose improved accuracy carries through to the inferred model parameters.
summary.tldr: Probability generating functions enable fast exact inference for a class of latent-count models and improve parameter estimation in population ecology.

title: Probabilistic Inference with Generating Functions for Poisson Latent Variable Models

abstract: We consider robust optimization problems, where the goal is to optimize in the worst case over a class of objective functions. We develop a reduction from robust improper optimization to stochastic optimization: given an oracle that returns $\alpha$-approximate solutions for distributions over objectives, we compute a distribution over solutions that is $\alpha$-approximate in the worst case. We show that derandomizing this solution is NP-hard in general, but can be done for a broad class of statistical learning tasks. We apply our results to robust neural network training and submodular optimization. We evaluate our approach experimentally on corrupted character classification and robust influence maximization in networks.
originalAbstract: We consider robust optimization problems, where the goal is to optimize in the worst case over a class of objective functions. We develop a reduction from robust improper optimization to stochastic optimization: given an oracle that returns $\alpha$-approximate solutions for distributions over objectives, we compute a distribution over solutions that is $\alpha$-approximate in the worst case. We show that derandomizing this solution is NP-hard in general, but can be done for a broad class of statistical learning tasks. We apply our results to robust neural network training and submodular optimization. We evaluate our approach experimentally on corrupted character classification and robust influence maximization in networks.

paragraphs: Robust optimization seeks a solution that performs well against the worst objective in a specified collection. For nonconvex problems, finding such a solution can be difficult. This paper connects the robust problem to stochastic optimization, where an optimization procedure instead handles a distribution over objectives.

The reduction assumes access to an oracle that returns α-approximate solutions for distributions over objectives. Using that oracle, the method constructs a distribution over solutions with an α-approximation guarantee in the worst case. The form of the output matters: the robust guarantee is obtained for a randomized choice among solutions, which is why the paper describes the optimization as improper.

Turning that distribution into a deterministic solution is NP-hard in general, although the authors show it can be done for a broad class of statistical learning tasks. They apply the framework to robust neural network training and submodular optimization, with experiments on corrupted character classification and robust influence maximization. The contribution separates the attainable randomized guarantee from the additional difficulty of derandomization.
summary.tldr: A reduction turns approximate stochastic optimization into worst-case robust optimization over distributions of solutions, while characterizing the difficulty of derandomization.

title: Robust Optimization for Non-Convex Objectives

abstract: The \emph{Cheap Gradient Principle}~\citep{Griewank:2008:EDP:1455489} --- the computational cost of computing a $d$-dimensional vector of partial derivatives of a scalar function is nearly the same (often within a factor of $5$) as that of simply computing the scalar function itself --- is of central importance in optimization; it allows us to quickly obtain (high-dimensional) gradients of scalar loss functions which are subsequently used in black box gradient-based optimization procedures. The current state of affairs is markedly different with regards to computing sub-derivatives: widely used ML libraries, including TensorFlow and PyTorch, do \emph{not} correctly compute (generalized) sub-derivatives even on simple differentiable examples. This work considers the question: is there a \emph{Cheap Sub-gradient Principle}? Our main result shows that, under certain restrictions on our library of non-smooth functions (standard in non-linear programming), provably correct generalized sub-derivatives can be computed at a computational cost that is within a (dimension-free) factor of $6$ of the cost of computing the scalar function itself.

paragraphs: Automatic differentiation is valuable because computing all partial derivatives of a scalar function can cost only a small multiple of evaluating the function itself. This paper asks whether a similar principle holds for generalized sub-derivatives, which extend differentiation to nonsmooth settings. It also identifies correctness failures in the automatic sub-differentiation behavior of the machine-learning libraries discussed.

The authors establish a cheap sub-gradient principle under restrictions on the library of nonsmooth functions. They describe these restrictions as standard in nonlinear programming. Within this qualified setting, generalized sub-derivatives can be computed with a proof of correctness, rather than relying solely on rules that appear reasonable for individual operations.

The computational cost is at most six times the cost of evaluating the scalar function, with no dependence of that factor on the input dimension. This makes the result relevant to high-dimensional optimization. Its scope remains conditional on the stated function-library restrictions: the theorem supports efficient, correct sub-differentiation for qualified programs, rather than arbitrary nonsmooth code.
summary.tldr: Under stated restrictions, correct generalized sub-derivatives cost at most six times a function evaluation, independent of dimension.

title: Provably Correct Automatic Sub-Differentiation for Qualified Programs

abstract: Deep generative models have achieved remarkable success in various data domains, including images, time series, and natural languages. There remain, however, substantial challenges for combinatorial structures, including graphs. One of the key challenges lies in the difficulty of ensuring semantic validity in context. For example, in molecular graphs, the number of bonding-electron pairs must not exceed the valence of an atom; whereas in protein interaction networks, two proteins may be connected only when they belong to the same or correlated gene ontology terms. These constraints are not easy to be incorporated into a generative model. In this work, we propose a regularization framework for variational autoencoders as a step toward semantic validity. We focus on the matrix representation of graphs and formulate penalty terms that regularize the output distribution of the decoder to encourage the satisfaction of validity constraints. Experimental results confirm a much higher likelihood of sampling valid graphs in our approach, compared with others reported in the literature.

paragraphs: A generated graph can have the right mathematical form while violating rules of its application. A molecular graph, for example, must respect constraints on how many bonds an atom can support. In protein interaction networks, connections may need to agree with relationships between gene ontology terms. This paper addresses the difficulty of building such semantic requirements into graph generation.

The proposed approach adds regularization to a variational autoencoder. Working with matrix representations of graphs, the authors formulate penalties on the decoder's output distribution. Those penalties encourage the model to place more probability on graphs that satisfy the relevant validity constraints.

Experiments show a substantially higher probability of sampling valid graphs than approaches reported in the literature. The distinction between encouragement and enforcement matters: the method improves the likelihood of validity rather than establishing that every generated graph is valid. Its contribution is a framework for making domain constraints influence the generative distribution during learning.
summary.tldr: Penalties on a graph autoencoder's output distribution make semantically valid graphs more likely to be generated.

title: Constrained Generation of Semantically Valid Graphs via Regularizing Variational Autoencoders

abstract: The loss functions of deep neural networks are complex and their geometric properties are not well understood. We show that the optima of these complex loss functions are in fact connected by simple curves, over which training and test accuracy are nearly constant. We introduce a training procedure to discover these high-accuracy pathways between modes. Inspired by this new geometric insight, we also propose a new ensembling method entitled Fast Geometric Ensembling (FGE). Using FGE we can train high-performing ensembles in the time required to train a single model. We achieve improved performance compared to the recent state-of-the-art Snapshot Ensembles, on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet.

paragraphs: The paper investigates the geometry of neural network loss functions by studying connections between trained solutions. It shows simple curves connecting optima along which training and test accuracy remain nearly constant. This reveals that movement between good solutions need not entail a substantial loss of predictive performance along the discovered path.

The authors introduce a training procedure for finding these high-accuracy connections. The contribution is therefore more than an observation about loss geometry: it includes a way to construct pathways between modes. These paths provide a concrete means of exploring relationships between solutions within the network's parameter space.

Inspired by that geometry, the paper proposes Fast Geometric Ensembling. The method trains high-performing ensembles within the time required to train a single model, according to the abstract. It improves on Snapshot Ensembles on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. The practical finding connects loss-surface structure to a way of obtaining ensemble benefits with a substantially constrained training budget.
summary.tldr: High-accuracy curves connecting neural network solutions inspire an ensembling method that fits within a single model's training time.

title: Loss Surfaces, Mode Connectivity, and Fast Ensembling of DNNs

abstract: We draw attention to an important, yet largely overlooked aspect of evaluating fairness for automated decision making systems---namely risk and welfare considerations. Our proposed family of measures corresponds to the long-established formulations of cardinal social welfare in economics, and is justified by the Rawlsian conception of fairness behind a veil of ignorance. The convex formulation of our welfare-based measures of fairness allows us to integrate them as a constraint into any convex loss minimization pipeline. Our empirical analysis reveals interesting trade-offs between our proposal and (a) prediction accuracy, (b) group discrimination, and (c) Dwork et al's notion of individual fairness. Furthermore and perhaps most importantly, our work provides both heuristic justification and empirical evidence suggesting that a lower-bound on our measures often leads to bounded inequality in algorithmic outcomes; hence presenting the first computationally feasible mechanism for bounding individual-level inequality.

Its proposed family of measures comes from cardinal social welfare in economics. The motivation uses the idea of a veil of ignorance: assessing a decision system without knowing which person's position one will occupy.

The measures have a convex formulation, allowing them to become constraints in a convex loss minimization pipeline. This connects the fairness proposal to a tractable learning procedure. Rather than leaving welfare as an external evaluation criterion, the formulation makes it something the training process can explicitly take into account.

Empirical analysis explores trade-offs with prediction accuracy, group discrimination, and an existing notion of individual fairness. The authors also offer heuristic reasoning and empirical evidence that imposing a lower bound on their welfare measures often bounds inequality in individual outcomes. That last relationship is suggestive and qualified, rather than an unconditional guarantee that welfare constraints always control inequality.
summary.tldr: Welfare-based fairness constraints offer a tractable way to consider risk and may also help bound inequality in individual outcomes.

title: Fairness Behind a Veil of Ignorance: A Welfare Analysis for Automated Decision Making

abstract: Search-based methods for hard combinatorial optimization are often guided by heuristics. Tuning heuristics in various conditions and situations is often time-consuming. In this paper, we propose NeuRewriter that learns a policy to pick heuristics and rewrite the local components of the current solution to iteratively improve it until convergence. The policy factorizes into a region-picking and a rule-picking component, each parameterized by a neural network trained with actor-critic methods in reinforcement learning. NeuRewriter captures the general structure of combinatorial problems and shows strong performance in three versatile tasks: expression simplification, online job scheduling and vehicle routing problems. NeuRewriter outperforms the expression simplification component in Z3; outperforms DeepRM and Google OR-tools in online job scheduling; and outperforms recent neural baselines and Google OR-tools in vehicle routing problems.
