paragraphs: Submodular functions are useful for assigning value to sets when diversity and coverage matter, including data selection and summarization. Learning such functions can be difficult when the available model family is too restrictive. This paper introduces FlexSubNet, a neural family covering both monotone and non-monotone submodular functions.

Given observed sets and their values, the method recursively applies a concave function to modular functions. It learns the concave function through an expressive neural network implementing differentiable quadrature, avoiding restriction to a narrow predefined family. The authors also develop a characterization of monotone alpha-submodular functions, an approximate form of submodularity, and build a corresponding neural model.

The framework extends to supervision consisting of a larger candidate set and a high-value subset. For this setting, the authors develop a greedy sampler whose behavior is invariant to input ordering, using the learned set functions to support subset selection. Experiments on synthetic and real data outperform several baselines. The contribution connects more flexible set-value estimation with a method for learning which subsets to choose.
summary.tldr: FlexSubNet learns expressive submodular set functions and uses them to support differentiable subset selection.

title: Neural Estimation of Submodular Functions with Applications to Differentiable Subset Selection

abstract: We revisit the problem of learning mixtures of spherical Gaussians. Given samples from a mixture $\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mathcal{N}(\mu_j, I_d)$, the goal is to estimate the means $\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_k \in \mathbb{R}^d$ up to a small error. The hardness of this learning problem can be measured by the \emph{separation} $\Delta$ defined as the minimum distance between all pairs of means. Regev and Vijayaraghavan (2017) showed that with $\Delta = \Omega(\sqrt{\log k})$ separation, the means can be learned using $\mathrm{poly}(k, d)$ samples, whereas super-polynomially many samples are required if $\Delta = o(\sqrt{\log k})$ and $d = \Omega(\log k)$. This leaves open the low-dimensional regime where $d = o(\log k)$. In this work, we give an algorithm that efficiently learns the means in $d = O(\log k/\log\log k)$ dimensions under separation $d/\sqrt{\log k}$ (modulo doubly logarithmic factors). This separation is strictly smaller than $\sqrt{\log k}$, and is also shown to be necessary. Along with the results of Regev and Vijayaraghavan (2017), our work almost pins down the critical separation threshold at which efficient parameter learning becomes possible for spherical Gaussian mixtures. More generally, our algorithm runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(k)\cdot f(d, \Delta, \epsilon)$, and is thus fixed-parameter tractable in parameters $d$, $\Delta$ and $\epsilon$. Our approach is based on estimating the Fourier transform of the mixture at carefully chosen frequencies, and both the algorithm and its analysis are simple and elementary. Our positive results can be easily extended to learning mixtures of non-Gaussian distributions, under a mild condition on the Fourier spectrum of the distribution.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover the centers of overlapping Gaussian distributions from samples of their mixture. Its setting uses equally weighted spherical Gaussians with identity covariance. A central question is how far apart their centers must be for accurate recovery to be computationally and statistically feasible.

The authors develop an algorithm that estimates the mixture’s Fourier transform at carefully selected frequencies. In dimensions up to order log(k)/log log(k), it efficiently learns the centers with separation roughly d/√log(k), allowing doubly logarithmic factors. This improves on the larger separation threshold associated with the previously understood higher-dimensional regime.

The paper also establishes necessity of the stated separation scale, helping nearly identify the threshold for efficient learning when combined with earlier results. More generally, runtime is polynomial in the number of components with additional dependence on dimension, separation, and accuracy. The approach also extends to non-Gaussian mixtures when their Fourier spectra satisfy a stated mild condition.
summary.tldr: Carefully chosen Fourier measurements enable efficient Gaussian-mixture learning at smaller separation scales in low dimensions.

title: A Fourier Approach to Mixture Learning

abstract: Via an overparameterized linear model with Gaussian features, we provide conditions for good generalization for multiclass classification of minimum-norm interpolating solutions in an asymptotic setting where both the number of underlying features and the number of classes scale with the number of training points. The survival/contamination analysis framework for understanding the behavior of overparameterized learning problems is adapted to this setting, revealing that multiclass classification qualitatively behaves like binary classification in that, as long as there are not too many classes (made precise in the paper), it is possible to generalize well even in settings where regression tasks would not generalize. Besides various technical challenges, it turns out that the key difference from the binary classification setting is that there are relatively fewer training examples of each class in the multiclass setting as the number of classes increases, making the multiclass problem ``harder'' than the binary one.

paragraphs: This paper investigates when a linear classifier with many parameters can generalize despite fitting its training data exactly. It focuses on minimum-norm interpolating solutions: among solutions that fit the training examples, these have the smallest parameter norm. The analysis assumes Gaussian features and an asymptotic setting where both the feature count and the number of classes grow with the training sample size.

The authors adapt a survival-and-contamination analysis framework to multiclass classification. They derive conditions under which the classifier generalizes well, showing a qualitative similarity to binary classification. Provided the number of classes is not too large under the paper's conditions, good classification can remain possible in settings where regression would fail to generalize.

The growing number of classes introduces a particular difficulty: each class has relatively fewer training examples. This helps explain why the multiclass problem is harder than the binary case within the analyzed setting. The findings therefore extend an account of successful overparameterized classification while identifying class growth as an important constraint on that success.
summary.tldr: Under Gaussian-feature assumptions, minimum-norm multiclass classifiers can generalize where regression fails if the number of classes grows slowly enough.

title: Generalization for multiclass classification with overparameterized linear models

abstract: A good metric, which promises a reliable comparison between solutions, is essential for any well-defined task. Unlike most vision tasks that have per-sample ground-truth, image synthesis tasks target generating unseen data and hence are usually evaluated through a distributional distance between one set of real samples and another set of generated samples. This study presents an empirical investigation into the evaluation of synthesis performance, with generative adversarial networks (GANs) as a representative of generative models. In particular, we make in-depth analyses of various factors, including how to represent a data point in the representation space, how to calculate a fair distance using selected samples, and how many instances to use from each set. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple datasets and settings reveal several important findings. Firstly, a group of models that include both CNN-based and ViT-based architectures serve as reliable and robust feature extractors for measurement evaluation. Secondly, Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) provides a better comparison across various extractors and hierarchical layers in one model. Finally, CKA is more sample-efficient and enjoys better agreement with human judgment in characterizing the similarity between two internal data correlations. These findings contribute to the development of a new measurement system, which enables a consistent and reliable re-evaluation of current state-of-the-art generative models.

paragraphs: Generated images usually lack a single correct reference image, so evaluation often compares collections of real and generated samples. This paper investigates how those comparisons depend on measurement choices, using generative adversarial networks as a representative case. It examines image representations, distance calculations, and the number of samples used.

Experiments across multiple datasets and settings identify a group of convolutional and vision-transformer models that provide reliable, robust feature representations for evaluation. The study also finds that Centered Kernel Alignment, or CKA, supports better comparisons across feature extractors and across layers within a model. This matters because the representation used to measure similarity is itself part of the evaluation procedure.

CKA is additionally more sample-efficient and agrees better with human judgments when characterizing similarity between the internal correlations of two datasets. The authors combine these findings into a new measurement system and use it to re-evaluate leading generative models. The contribution concerns the reliability of evaluation, showing how representation and comparison choices can support more consistent assessments of synthesis performance.
summary.tldr: The study develops a more consistent image-synthesis evaluation system using robust feature extractors and Centered Kernel Alignment.

title: Revisiting the Evaluation of Image Synthesis with GANs

abstract: Inverse protein folding is challenging due to its inherent one-to-many mapping characteristic, where numerous possible amino acid sequences can fold into a single, identical protein backbone. This task involves not only identifying viable sequences but also representing the sheer diversity of potential solutions. However, existing discriminative models, such as transformer-based auto-regressive models, struggle to encapsulate the diverse range of plausible solutions. In contrast, diffusion probabilistic models, as an emerging genre of generative approaches, offer the potential to generate a diverse set of sequence candidates for determined protein backbones. We propose a novel graph denoising diffusion model for inverse protein folding, where a given protein backbone guides the diffusion process on the corresponding amino acid residue types. The model infers the joint distribution of amino acids conditioned on the nodes' physiochemical properties and local environment. Moreover, we utilize amino acid replacement matrices for the diffusion forward process, encoding the biologically-meaningful prior knowledge of amino acids from their spatial and sequential neighbors as well as themselves, which reduces the sampling space of the generative process. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance over a set of popular baseline methods in sequence recovery and exhibits great potential in generating diverse protein sequences for a determined protein backbone structure.

paragraphs: Inverse protein folding seeks amino acid sequences compatible with a specified protein backbone. Many sequences can correspond to the same backbone, so the task involves representing multiple plausible answers as well as recovering a viable sequence. The paper explores diffusion modeling as a way to address this one-to-many relationship.

Its graph denoising diffusion model uses the given backbone to guide generation of amino acid residue types. It models their joint distribution using the nodes’ physicochemical properties and local environments. The forward diffusion process also uses amino acid replacement matrices to incorporate biological prior knowledge about residues and their spatial and sequential neighbors, reducing the space the generative process must explore.

The authors report state-of-the-art sequence recovery relative to the popular baselines they evaluate. They also describe strong potential for generating diverse sequences for a fixed backbone. These are related but distinct findings: the recovery result establishes performance on that measured objective, while the diversity finding supports the broader motivation for modeling multiple possible sequence solutions.
summary.tldr: A backbone-guided graph diffusion model improves reported sequence recovery and shows potential for generating diverse compatible protein sequences.

title: Graph Denoising Diffusion for Inverse Protein Folding

abstract: Neural SDEs are continuous-time generative models for sequential data. State-of-the-art performance for irregular time series generation has been previously obtained by training these models adversarially as GANs. However, as typical for GAN architectures, training is notoriously unstable, often suffers from mode collapse, and requires specialised techniques such as weight clipping and gradient penalty to mitigate these issues. In this paper, we introduce a novel class of scoring rules on pathspace based on signature kernels and use them as objective for training Neural SDEs non-adversarially. By showing strict properness of such kernel scores and consistency of the corresponding estimators, we provide existence and uniqueness guarantees for the minimiser. With this formulation, evaluating the generator-discriminator pair amounts to solving a system of linear path-dependent PDEs which allows for memory-efficient adjoint-based backpropagation. Moreover, because the proposed kernel scores are well-defined for paths with values in infinite dimensional spaces of functions, our framework can be easily extended to generate spatiotemporal data. Our procedure significantly outperforms alternative ways of training Neural SDEs on a variety of tasks including the simulation of rough volatility models, the conditional probabilistic forecasts of real-world forex pairs where the conditioning variable is an observed past trajectory, and the mesh-free generation of limit order book dynamics.

Adversarial training has produced strong results for irregular time series, but can be unstable and suffer from mode collapse. This paper replaces adversarial training with scoring rules defined over entire paths using signature kernels, giving the generator a non-adversarial learning objective.

The authors establish strict properness of the scores and consistency of their estimators, providing existence and uniqueness guarantees for the minimizer. They also connect evaluation to a system of linear, path-dependent partial differential equations. This formulation permits memory-efficient backpropagation using adjoint methods. Because the scores also apply to paths whose values are functions, the framework extends to spatiotemporal generation.

Experiments report substantially better performance than alternative neural-SDE training approaches across several tasks. These include rough-volatility simulation, probabilistic forecasts of foreign-exchange pairs conditioned on past trajectories, and mesh-free generation of limit-order-book dynamics. The work combines a theoretically justified distributional objective with a computational formulation suited to learning from complex sequential data.
summary.tldr: Signature-kernel scoring rules enable theoretically grounded, non-adversarial neural-SDE training with improved results on sequential generation tasks.

title: Non-adversarial training of Neural SDEs with signature kernel scores

abstract: Existing automatic evaluation on text-to-image synthesis can only provide an image-text matching score, without considering the object-level compositionality, which results in poor correlation with human judgments. In this work, we propose LLMScore, a new framework that offers evaluation scores with multi-granularity compositionality. LLMScore leverages the large language models (LLMs) to evaluate text-to-image models. Initially, it transforms the image into image-level and object-level visual descriptions. Then an evaluation instruction is fed into the LLMs to measure the alignment between the synthesized image and the text, ultimately generating a score accompanied by a rationale. Our substantial analysis reveals the highest correlation of LLMScore with human judgments on a wide range of datasets (Attribute Binding Contrast, Concept Conjunction, MSCOCO, DrawBench, PaintSkills). Notably, our LLMScore achieves Kendall's tau correlation with human evaluations that is 58.8% and 31.2% higher than the commonly-used text-image matching metrics CLIP and BLIP, respectively.

LLMScore addresses this by evaluating alignment at multiple levels of detail and producing a rationale alongside the score.

It then supplies an evaluation instruction to a large language model, which uses these descriptions to assess alignment with the original text. This creates a language-based evaluation process that explicitly includes both broad image content and more detailed composition.

These are improvements in agreement with human evaluations, rather than improvements to the generated images themselves. The contribution is an evaluation framework that combines a numerical assessment with an accompanying explanation.
summary.tldr: LLMScore uses scene and object descriptions to generate image-text alignment scores and rationales that correlate more closely with human judgments in evaluations.

title: LLMScore: Unveiling the Power of Large Language Models in Text-to-Image Synthesis Evaluation

abstract: Minimally-invasive surgery (MIS) and robot-assisted minimally invasive (RAMIS) surgery offer well-documented benefits to patients such as reduced post-operative pain and shorter hospital stays.However, the automation of MIS and RAMIS through the use of AI has been slow due to difficulties in data acquisition and curation, partially caused by the ethical considerations of training, testing and deploying AI models in medical environments.We introduce \texttt{SARAMIS}, the first large-scale dataset of anatomically derived 3D rendering assets of the human abdominal anatomy.Using previously existing, open-source CT datasets of the human anatomy, we derive novel 3D meshes, tetrahedral volumes, textures and diffuse maps for over 104 different anatomical targets in the human body, representing the largest, open-source dataset of 3D rendering assets for synthetic simulation of vision tasks in MIS+RAMIS, increasing the availability of openly available 3D meshes in the literature by three orders of magnitude.We supplement our dataset with a series of GPU-enabled rendering environments, which can be used to generate datasets for realistic MIS/RAMIS tasks.Finally, we present an example of the use of \texttt{SARAMIS} assets for an autonomous navigation task in colonoscopy from CT abdomen-pelvis scans for the first time in the literature.\texttt{SARAMIS} is publically made available at https://github.com/NMontanaBrown/saramis/, with assets released under a CC-BY-NC-SA license.

paragraphs: Developing AI for minimally invasive and robot-assisted surgery is constrained by the difficulty of collecting and curating medical data. Ethical considerations also complicate training and testing in clinical environments. SARAMIS addresses this bottleneck by providing anatomical assets that researchers can use to create simulated visual data.

The authors derive 3D meshes, tetrahedral volumes, textures, and diffuse maps from existing open-source CT datasets. The collection covers more than 104 anatomical targets and focuses on human abdominal anatomy. They describe it as the largest open-source collection of rendering assets for these surgical simulation tasks, expanding the available supply of 3D meshes by three orders of magnitude.

GPU-enabled rendering environments accompany the assets so researchers can generate datasets for relevant vision tasks. The paper demonstrates an autonomous colonoscopy-navigation example using assets derived from abdomen-pelvis CT scans. This establishes an example use of the simulation resource; the central contribution is the reusable anatomical collection and rendering infrastructure. The assets are publicly released under a CC-BY-NC-SA license.
summary.tldr: SARAMIS supplies a large collection of CT-derived anatomical assets and GPU rendering environments for simulating surgical vision tasks.

title: SARAMIS: Simulation Assets for Robotic Assisted and Minimally Invasive Surgery

abstract: We study the problem of computing pairwise statistics, i.e., ones of the form $\binom{n}{2}^{-1} \sum_{i \ne j} f(x_i, x_j)$, where $x_i$ denotes the input to the $i$th user, with differential privacy (DP) in the local model. This formulation captures important metrics such as Kendall's $\tau$ coefficient, Area Under Curve, Gini's mean difference, Gini's entropy, etc. We give several novel and generic algorithms for the problem, leveraging techniques from DP algorithms for linear queries.

This formulation captures important metrics such as Kendall's $\tau$ coefficient, Area Under Curve, Gini's mean difference, Gini's entropy, etc. We give several novel and generic algorithms for the problem, leveraging techniques from DP algorithms for linear queries.

paragraphs: This paper studies statistics built by applying a function to pairs of users' inputs and aggregating the results. Such quantities depend on relationships between observations, so the computational target extends beyond a summary of separate individual contributions. The authors investigate how to calculate these pairwise summaries under differential privacy in the local model.

The formulation covers several familiar measures, including Kendall's tau, Area Under Curve, Gini's mean difference, and Gini's entropy. Treating them as instances of a shared pairwise problem allows the work to address a family of statistics together. The particular function applied to each pair determines which quantity the computation estimates.

The authors contribute several new generic algorithms, drawing on techniques developed for differentially private linear queries. The methodological contribution is this connection between tools for linear queries and the problem of private pairwise computation. It provides algorithmic approaches that apply across the stated formulation, making the work relevant to multiple statistical quantities under the same local privacy setting.
summary.tldr: The paper develops generic locally differentially private algorithms for pairwise statistics using techniques from private linear-query computation.

title: On Computing Pairwise Statistics with Local Differential Privacy

abstract: Recent 4D shape representations model continuous temporal evolution of implicit shapes by (1) learning query flows without leveraging shape and articulation priors or (2) decoding shape occupancies separately for each time value. Thus, they do not effectively capture implicit correspondences between articulated shapes or regularize jittery temporal deformations. In this work, we present FourierHandFlow, which is a spatio-temporally continuous representation for human hands that combines a 3D occupancy field with articulation-aware query flows represented as Fourier series. Given an input RGB sequence, we aim to learn a fixed number of Fourier coefficients for each query flow to guarantee smooth and continuous temporal shape dynamics. To effectively model spatio-temporal deformations of articulated hands, we compose our 4D representation based on two types of Fourier query flow: (1) pose flow that models query dynamics influenced by hand articulation changes via implicit linear blend skinning and (2) shape flow that models query-wise displacement flow. In the experiments, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on video-based 4D reconstruction while being computationally more efficient than the existing 3D/4D implicit shape representations. We additionally show our results on motion inter- and extrapolation and texture transfer using the learned correspondences of implicit shapes. To the best of our knowledge, FourierHandFlow is the first neural 4D continuous hand representation learned from RGB videos. The code will be publicly accessible.

paragraphs: FourierHandFlow represents the three-dimensional shape of a human hand continuously through time using RGB video. The paper targets weaknesses in existing implicit shape representations: they can miss correspondences between articulated shapes or produce jittery temporal changes. Its approach combines a spatial occupancy field with flows that describe how queries move as the hand changes.

Each query flow is represented by a fixed collection of Fourier coefficients, providing smooth, continuous temporal dynamics. The representation separates two kinds of change. Pose flow captures motion associated with articulation through implicit linear blend skinning, while shape flow captures displacement at individual query locations. This structure brings articulation information into the temporal representation.

The authors also demonstrate motion interpolation, extrapolation, and texture transfer using learned shape correspondences. These applications show how a continuous representation can support relationships across time as well as reconstruction of individual hand shapes.
summary.tldr: FourierHandFlow combines articulation-aware Fourier flows with an occupancy field to reconstruct smoothly changing hand shapes from RGB video.

title: FourierHandFlow: Neural 4D Hand Representation Using Fourier Query Flow

abstract: Online pricing has been the focus of extensive research in recent years, particularly in the context of selling an item to sequentially arriving users. However, what if a provider wants to maximize revenue by selling multiple items to multiple users in each round? This presents a complex problem, as the provider must intelligently offer the items to those users who value them the most without exceeding their highest acceptable prices. In this study, we tackle this challenge by designing online algorithms that can efficiently offer and price items while learning user valuations from accept/reject feedback. We focus on three user valuation models (fixed valuations, random experiences, and random valuations) and provide algorithms with nearly-optimal revenue regret guarantees. In particular, for any market setting with $N$ users, $M$ items, and load $L$ (which roughly corresponds to the maximum number of simultaneous allocations possible), our algorithms achieve regret of order $O(NM\log\log(LT))$ under fixed valuations model, $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{NMLT})$ under random experiences model and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{NMLT})$ under random valuations model in $T$ rounds.

paragraphs: This paper studies a seller who can offer multiple items to multiple users in each round. The seller must decide both who receives an offer and what price to charge, while initially lacking users’ valuations. Learning comes from whether each offer is accepted or rejected, linking revenue generation to information gathering.

The authors design online algorithms for three valuation models: fixed valuations, random experiences, and random valuations. Their guarantees depend on the number of users N, the number of items M, the number of rounds T, and market load L. Load roughly measures how many allocations can happen simultaneously, so the analysis explicitly accounts for the market’s allocation capacity.

Under fixed valuations, revenue regret has order O(NM log log(LT)). For both random models, the bound is of order square root of NMLT, up to logarithmic factors. The authors characterize these guarantees as nearly optimal. The results show how offering and pricing decisions can be coordinated while learning from limited feedback, with different rates reflecting the different valuation models.
summary.tldr: Online offering and pricing algorithms learn valuations from accept/reject feedback with nearly optimal revenue regret across three multi-user, multi-item market models.

title: Online Pricing for Multi-User Multi-Item Markets

abstract: Efficiently selecting an appropriate spike stream data length to extract precise information is the key to the spike vision tasks. To address this issue, we propose a dynamic timing representation for spike streams. Based on multi-layers architecture, it applies dilated convolutions on temporal dimension to extract features on multi-temporal scales with few parameters. And we design layer attention to dynamically fuse these features. Moreover, we propose an unsupervised learning method for optical flow estimation in a spike-based manner to break the dependence on labeled data. In addition, to verify the robustness, we also build a spike-based synthetic validation dataset for extreme scenarios in autonomous driving, denoted as SSES dataset. It consists of various corner cases. Experiments show that our method can predict optical flow from spike streams in different high-speed scenes, including real scenes. For instance, our method achieves $15\%$ and $19\%$ error reduction on PHM dataset compared to the best spike-based work, SCFlow, in $\Delta t=10$ and $\Delta t=20$ respectively, using the same settings as in previous works. The source code and dataset are available at \href{https://github.com/Bosserhead/USFlow}{https://github.com/Bosserhead/USFlow}.

paragraphs: This paper estimates optical flow from spike-camera streams while addressing how much temporal data to use. Selecting an appropriate stream length is important for extracting precise information. The proposed dynamic timing representation captures several temporal scales, giving the model access to features describing different spans of the spike sequence.

A multilayer architecture uses dilated convolutions along time to obtain these features with few parameters. Layer attention then combines them dynamically. The authors pair this representation with an unsupervised, spike-based learning method for optical flow, removing dependence on labeled training data. They also construct SSES, a synthetic validation dataset containing extreme autonomous-driving scenarios and corner cases.

Experiments demonstrate optical-flow prediction in multiple high-speed settings, including real scenes. On PHM, the method reduces error relative to SCFlow by 15% at Δt = 10 and 19% at Δt = 20 under the same settings used in prior work. These results support combining adaptive temporal features with unsupervised learning for the evaluated spike-stream motion-estimation tasks.
summary.tldr: Dynamic temporal features and unsupervised learning improve spike-camera optical-flow estimation across evaluated high-speed scenes.

title: Unsupervised Optical Flow Estimation with Dynamic Timing Representation for Spike Camera

abstract: Learning continuous-time point processes is essential to many discrete event forecasting tasks. However, integration poses a major challenge, particularly for spatiotemporal point processes (STPPs), as it involves calculating the likelihood through triple integrals over space and time. Existing methods for integrating STPP either assume a parametric form of the intensity function, which lacks flexibility; or approximating the intensity with Monte Carlo sampling, which introduces numerical errors. Recent work by Omi et al. proposes a dual network approach for efficient integration of flexible intensity function. However, their method only focuses on the 1D temporal point process. In this paper, we introduce a novel paradigm: `Auto-STPP` (Automatic Integration for Spatiotemporal Neural Point Processes) that extends the dual network approach to 3D STPP. While previous work provides a foundation, its direct extension overly restricts the intensity function and leads to computational challenges. In response, we introduce a decomposable parametrization for the integral network using ProdNet. This approach, leveraging the product of simplified univariate graphs, effectively sidesteps the computational complexities inherent in multivariate computational graphs. We prove the consistency of `Auto-STPP` and validate it on synthetic data and benchmark real-world datasets. `Auto-STPP` shows a significant advantage in recovering complex intensity functions from irregular spatiotemporal events, particularly when the intensity is sharply localized. Our code is open-source at https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/AutoSTPP.

paragraphs: Spatiotemporal point processes describe discrete events occurring across space and time. Learning them requires integrating an event-intensity function over those dimensions, which can be computationally difficult. Existing approaches either restrict the function’s mathematical form or approximate the integral through random sampling, introducing numerical error.

Auto-STPP extends a dual-network integration approach from time alone to three-dimensional space-time modeling. A straightforward extension would impose excessive restrictions on the intensity and create difficult computations. The authors instead use ProdNet to express the integral network through products of simpler functions of individual variables. This decomposition makes the multivariate integration problem more manageable while supporting flexible intensity functions.

The paper proves consistency of Auto-STPP and evaluates it using synthetic and real-world benchmark data. Its reported advantage is recovering complex event-intensity patterns from irregular observations, especially when activity is concentrated sharply in particular regions of space and time. The contribution links a computational strategy for integration with improved recovery of the underlying event patterns in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Auto-STPP uses a decomposed integral network to learn flexible spatiotemporal event intensities with consistency guarantees.

title: Automatic Integration for Spatiotemporal Neural Point Processes

abstract: Model-free reinforcement learning algorithms have exhibited great potential in solving single-task sequential decision-making problems with high-dimensional observations and long horizons, but are known to be hard to generalize across tasks. Model-based RL, on the other hand, learns task-agnostic models of the world that naturally enables transfer across different reward functions, but struggles to scale to complex environments due to the compounding error. To get the best of both worlds, we propose a self-supervised reinforcement learning method that enables the transfer of behaviors across tasks with different rewards, while circumventing the challenges of model-based RL. In particular, we show self-supervised pre-training of model-free reinforcement learning with a number of random features as rewards allows implicit modeling of long-horizon environment dynamics. Then, planning techniques like model-predictive control using these implicit models enable fast adaptation to problems with new reward functions. Our method is self-supervised in that it can be trained on offline datasets without reward labels, but can then be quickly deployed on new tasks. We validate that our proposed method enables transfer across tasks on a variety of manipulation and locomotion domains in simulation, opening the door to generalist decision-making agents.

paragraphs: Model-free reinforcement learning can solve demanding individual tasks but often transfers poorly when rewards change. Learning an environment model makes transfer more natural, yet errors in that model can accumulate over long predictions. This paper proposes self-supervised pretraining that combines transferable information about dynamics with model-free learning.

The method uses a collection of random features as reward signals during pretraining. Learning to predict and pursue these signals implicitly models long-horizon environment dynamics. Planning methods such as model-predictive control can then use those implicit models to adapt quickly to a new reward function. The approach learns reusable information without requiring task-reward labels in its offline training data.

The authors validate transfer across simulated manipulation and locomotion domains. These experiments support the possibility of training behaviors before the eventual reward is specified and adapting them when a new task arrives. The key idea is that model-free pretraining can encode useful long-term dynamics indirectly, providing a basis for planning across tasks without relying on the conventional explicit model-learning route.
summary.tldr: Random-feature rewards enable self-supervised model-free pretraining that implicitly captures dynamics and supports fast transfer to new reward functions.

title: Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning that Transfers using Random Features

abstract: Despite rapid progress in Visual question answering (\textit{VQA}), existing datasets and models mainly focus on testing reasoning in 2D. However, it is important that VQA models also understand the 3D structure of visual scenes, for example to support tasks like navigation or manipulation. This includes an understanding of the 3D object pose, their parts and occlusions. In this work, we introduce the task of 3D-aware VQA, which focuses on challenging questions that require a compositional reasoning over the 3D structure of visual scenes. We address 3D-aware VQA from both the dataset and the model perspective. First, we introduce Super-CLEVR-3D, a compositional reasoning dataset that contains questions about object parts, their 3D poses, and occlusions. Second, we propose PO3D-VQA, a 3D-aware VQA model that marries two powerful ideas: probabilistic neural symbolic program execution for reasoning and deep neural networks with 3D generative representations of objects for robust visual recognition. Our experimental results show our model PO3D-VQA outperforms existing methods significantly, but we still observe a significant performance gap compared to 2D VQA benchmarks, indicating that 3D-aware VQA remains an important open research area.

paragraphs: Answering questions about an image can require understanding how objects occupy three-dimensional space. An object’s orientation, the arrangement of its parts, and which objects hide others all matter. This paper introduces 3D-aware visual question answering to test that understanding, extending the emphasis of existing datasets and models beyond reasoning mainly about two-dimensional scenes.

The contribution combines a dataset with a model. Super-CLEVR-3D asks questions about parts, poses, and occlusions that require combining multiple pieces of spatial information. PO3D-VQA pairs neural networks using three-dimensional generative object representations with probabilistic neural-symbolic program execution. The recognition component supplies structured visual information, while the reasoning component uses it to work through the question.

In the reported experiments, PO3D-VQA substantially outperforms existing methods. However, performance still falls well short of that on two-dimensional VQA benchmarks. The results therefore show both the value of explicitly representing three-dimensional structure and the remaining difficulty of reasoning about it. The task exposes capabilities relevant to navigation and manipulation without establishing that those broader applications are solved.
summary.tldr: A new dataset and model improve question answering about three-dimensional scenes while revealing substantial remaining challenges.

title: 3D-Aware Visual Question Answering about Parts, Poses and Occlusions

abstract: We consider a non-convex constrained optimization problem, where the objective function is weakly convex and the constraint function is either convex or weakly convex. To solve this problem, we consider the classical switching subgradient method, which is an intuitive and easily implementable first-order method whose oracle complexity was only known for convex problems. This paper provides the first analysis on the oracle complexity of the switching subgradient method for finding a nearly stationary point of non-convex problems. Our results are derived separately for convex and weakly convex constraints. Compared to existing approaches, especially the double-loop methods, the switching gradient method can be applied to non-smooth problems and achieves the same complexity using only a single loop, which saves the effort on tuning the number of inner iterations.

To solve this problem, we consider the classical switching subgradient method, which is an intuitive and easily implementable first-order method whose oracle complexity was only known for convex problems. This paper provides the first analysis on the oracle complexity of the switching subgradient method for finding a nearly stationary point of non-convex problems. Our results are derived separately for convex and weakly convex constraints. Compared to existing approaches, especially the double-loop methods, the switching gradient method can be applied to non-smooth problems and achieves the same complexity using only a single loop, which saves the effort on tuning the number of inner iterations.

paragraphs: The switching subgradient method is an intuitive first-order approach to constrained optimization, but its oracle complexity had been understood only for convex problems. This paper analyzes objectives that are weakly convex, with constraints that may be either convex or weakly convex.

The authors derive separate results for the two constraint settings, targeting a nearly stationary point. The method can handle nonsmooth problems while retaining a single-loop implementation, avoiding the need to choose and tune an inner-iteration count as in double-loop alternatives.

The resulting complexity matches existing approaches in the studied settings. The abstract does not state the exact oracle bounds or report experiments. The theoretical target is approximate stationarity in a nonconvex constrained problem, not a global optimum. The contribution makes a simple established algorithm more broadly justified without removing the assumptions that define the weakly convex problem class.
summary.tldr: A single-loop switching subgradient method gains complexity guarantees for weakly convex constrained problems.

title: Oracle Complexity of Single-Loop Switching Subgradient Methods for Non-Smooth Weakly Convex Functional Constrained Optimization

abstract: Diffusion model based language-guided image editing has achieved great success recently. However, existing state-of-the-art diffusion models struggle with rendering correct text and text style during generation. To tackle this problem, we propose a universal self-supervised text editing diffusion model (DiffUTE), which aims to replace or modify words in the source image with another one while maintaining its realistic appearance. Specifically, we build our model on a diffusion model and carefully modify the network structure to enable the model for drawing multilingual characters with the help of glyph and position information. Moreover, we design a self-supervised learning framework to leverage large amounts of web data to improve the representation ability of the model. Experimental results show that our method achieves an impressive performance and enables controllable editing on in-the-wild images with high fidelity. Our code will be avaliable in \url{https://github.com/chenhaoxing/DiffUTE}.

paragraphs: Changing words inside an image requires more than generating plausible visual content. The replacement must have the correct characters and a suitable visual style while fitting the source image. DiffUTE addresses this problem with a diffusion model designed to replace or modify image text while maintaining a realistic appearance.

The authors modify the network structure to incorporate glyph and position information. These inputs supply guidance about character shapes and where the text belongs, supporting the rendering of multilingual characters. They also develop a self-supervised training framework that uses large amounts of web data to strengthen the model’s representations. The approach therefore combines explicit information about the desired text with learning from abundant visual examples.

Experiments report strong performance on controllable text editing in images encountered outside controlled settings, with high visual fidelity. The significance is that text is treated as content whose spelling, placement, and appearance must be coordinated during image editing. The findings support DiffUTE’s usefulness for these edits, including multilingual characters, without establishing that every language or image style is handled equally well.
summary.tldr: DiffUTE uses glyph and position guidance with self-supervised diffusion training to edit text inside images while preserving realistic appearance.

title: DiffUTE: Universal Text Editing Diffusion Model

abstract: While deep reinforcement learning (RL) has been demonstrated effective in solving complex control tasks, sample efficiency remains a key challenge due to the large amounts of data required for remarkable performance. Existing research explores the application of representation learning for data-efficient RL, e.g., learning predictive representations by predicting long-term future states. However, many existing methods do not fully exploit the structural information inherent in sequential state signals, which can potentially improve the quality of long-term decision-making but is difficult to discern in the time domain. To tackle this problem, we propose State Sequences Prediction via Fourier Transform (SPF), a novel method that exploits the frequency domain of state sequences to extract the underlying patterns in time series data for learning expressive representations efficiently. Specifically, we theoretically analyze the existence of structural information in state sequences, which is closely related to policy performance and signal regularity, and then propose to predict the Fourier transform of infinite-step future state sequences to extract such information. One of the appealing features of SPF is that it is simple to implement while not requiring storage of infinite-step future states as prediction targets. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms several state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of both sample efficiency and performance.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning often needs large amounts of experience to learn effective control. Predicting future states can help an agent learn useful representations, but this paper argues that existing methods do not fully exploit the structure of state sequences. Some of that structure is difficult to recognize directly in the time domain.

State Sequences Prediction via Fourier Transform, or SPF, learns representations by predicting the Fourier transform of infinite-step future state sequences. The authors theoretically analyze structural information related to policy performance and signal regularity, motivating this frequency-domain prediction task. Although the target concerns an infinite future sequence, the method does not require storing that sequence as training data.

Experiments show SPF outperforming several leading algorithms in both sample efficiency and overall performance. The authors also describe it as simple to implement. Its contribution is to change what a predictive representation is trained to capture: frequency-domain structure provides information about long-term state evolution that can support better learning and decisions with fewer samples in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: SPF predicts future state sequences in the frequency domain to learn representations that improve reinforcement learning efficiency and performance.

title: State Sequences Prediction via Fourier Transform for Representation Learning

abstract: Interpretability methods are valuable only if their explanations faithfully describe the explained model. In this work, we consider neural networks whose predictions are invariant under a specific symmetry group. This includes popular architectures, ranging from convolutional to graph neural networks. Any explanation that faithfully explains this type of model needs to be in agreement with this invariance property. We formalize this intuition through the notion of explanation invariance and equivariance by leveraging the formalism from geometric deep learning. Through this rigorous formalism, we derive (1) two metrics to measure the robustness of any interpretability method with respect to the model symmetry group; (2) theoretical robustness guarantees for some popular interpretability methods and (3) a systematic approach to increase the invariance of any interpretability method with respect to a symmetry group. By empirically measuring our metrics for explanations of models associated with various modalities and symmetry groups, we derive a set of 5 guidelines to allow users and developers of interpretability methods to produce robust explanations.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether explanations respect the symmetries of the models they describe. Its setting is neural networks whose predictions stay unchanged under a specified group of transformations. If an explanation faithfully represents such a model, its behavior under those transformations should agree with the model’s invariance.

The authors formalize this requirement using explanation invariance and equivariance, drawing on geometric deep learning. Invariance concerns explanations remaining unchanged, while equivariance concerns their changing consistently with a transformation. This framework yields two metrics for measuring explanation robustness relative to the model’s symmetry group, along with theoretical guarantees for some popular interpretability methods.

The paper also develops a systematic way to increase an interpretability method’s invariance with respect to a symmetry group. Experiments apply the metrics across models associated with different modalities and symmetries, leading to five guidelines for producing robust explanations. The contribution makes symmetry agreement a concrete, testable aspect of explanation quality for the class of invariant models under consideration.
summary.tldr: The paper turns agreement with model symmetries into measurable explanation-robustness criteria, theoretical guarantees, and a method for improving invariance.

title: Evaluating the Robustness of Interpretability Methods through Explanation Invariance and Equivariance

abstract: When deploying machine learning solutions, they must satisfy multiple requirements beyond accuracy, such as fairness, robustness, or safety. These requirements are imposed during training either implicitly, using penalties, or explicitly, using constrained optimization methods based on Lagrangian duality. Either way, specifying requirements is hindered by the presence of compromises and limited prior knowledge about the data. Furthermore, their impact on performance can often only be evaluated by actually solving the learning problem. This paper presents a constrained learning approach that adapts the requirements while simultaneously solving the learning task. To do so, it relaxes the learning constraints in a way that contemplates how much they affect the task at hand by balancing the performance gains obtained from the relaxation against a user-defined cost of that relaxation. We call this approach resilient constrained learning after the term used to describe ecological systems that adapt to disruptions by modifying their operation. We show conditions under which this balance can be achieved and introduce a practical algorithm to compute it, for which we derive approximation and generalization guarantees. We showcase the advantages of this resilient learning method in image classification tasks involving multiple potential invariances and in federated learning under distribution shift.

paragraphs: Machine-learning systems may need to satisfy fairness, robustness, or safety requirements alongside predictive accuracy. Choosing the strength of those requirements is difficult because their effects and trade-offs may become clear only during training. Resilient constrained learning addresses this problem by adapting requirements while solving the learning task.

The approach allows constraints to be relaxed, but assigns a user-defined cost to that relaxation. Training balances the performance gained by loosening a requirement against the cost of doing so. This makes the compromise part of the learning problem itself, with the user's cost specification expressing how much relaxation is acceptable relative to task improvement.

The paper gives conditions under which this balance can be achieved and presents a practical algorithm with approximation and generalization guarantees. Applications include image classification with multiple possible invariances and federated learning under distribution shift. These examples demonstrate the advantages of adapting constraints when their interaction with the task is difficult to assess in advance.
summary.tldr: Resilient constrained learning adapts training requirements by balancing the performance benefits of relaxation against user-defined costs.

title: Resilient Constrained Learning

abstract: Flexible sensors are promising for ubiquitous sensing of human status due to their flexibility and easy integration as wearable systems. However, on-body displacement of sensors is inevitable since the device cannot be firmly worn at a fixed position across different sessions. This displacement issue causes complicated patterns and significant challenges to subsequent machine learning algorithms. Our work proposes a novel self-adaptive motion tracking network to address this challenge. Our network consists of three novel components: i) a light-weight learnable Affine Transformation layer whose parameters can be tuned to efficiently adapt to unknown displacements; ii) a Fourier-encoded LSTM network for better pattern identification; iii) a novel sequence discrepancy loss equipped with auxiliary regressors for unsupervised tuning of Affine Transformation parameters.

paragraphs: Flexible wearable sensors can support human motion tracking, but their position on the body can change between sessions. Because a device cannot always be worn at exactly the same location, the resulting signals develop complicated variations. This paper proposes a self-adaptive tracking network designed to address those unknown sensor displacements.

The network combines three components with distinct roles. A lightweight learnable affine transformation layer provides adjustable parameters for adapting to displacement. A Fourier-encoded long short-term memory network handles the task of identifying patterns in the sensor sequences. Together, these components separate a tunable signal transformation from the sequence-modeling part of the tracking system.

The third component is a sequence discrepancy loss supported by auxiliary regressors. It enables unsupervised tuning of the affine transformation parameters, giving the system a way to adjust its adaptation layer without supervised tuning for the new displacement. The contribution is this coordinated architecture: a compact adjustable transformation, a temporal pattern-recognition network, and an objective for adaptation all address the practical problem of changing sensor placement.
summary.tldr: A motion-tracking network combines an adaptable affine layer, Fourier-encoded sequence modeling, and unsupervised tuning to address wearable-sensor displacement.

title: Self-Adaptive Motion Tracking against On-body Displacement of Flexible Sensors

abstract: We consider the problem of inferring latent stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with a time and memory cost that scales independently with the amount of data, the total length of the time series, and the stiffness of the approximate differential equations. This is in stark contrast to typical methods for inferring latent differential equations which, despite their constant memory cost, have a time complexity that is heavily dependent on the stiffness of the approximate differential equation. We achieve this computational advancement by removing the need to solve differential equations when approximating gradients using a novel amortization strategy coupled with a recently derived reparametrization of expectations under linear SDEs. We show that, in practice, this allows us to achieve similar performance to methods based on adjoint sensitivities with more than an order of magnitude fewer evaluations of the model in training.

We achieve this computational advancement by removing the need to solve differential equations when approximating gradients using a novel amortization strategy coupled with a recently derived reparametrization of expectations under linear SDEs. paragraphs: Latent stochastic differential equations describe hidden dynamics that include randomness. Learning these dynamics can be computationally expensive because training typically requires differential-equation calculations. The paper targets inference whose time and memory costs scale independently of the amount of data, the total time-series length, and the stiffness of the approximate equations.

The central change concerns how training gradients are approximated. The authors combine a new amortization strategy with a recently derived way to reparametrize expectations under linear stochastic differential equations. Together, these remove the need to solve differential equations during gradient approximation. This matters because methods with constant memory usage can still spend considerable computation handling stiff equations.

In practice, the proposed approach achieves performance similar to methods using adjoint sensitivities while requiring more than an order of magnitude fewer model evaluations during training. That finding supports the computational value of changing the inference procedure itself. The stated empirical gain concerns model evaluations, alongside comparable performance, rather than a separately quantified reduction in elapsed training time.
summary.tldr: A new gradient approximation strategy makes latent-SDE inference cheaper while retaining performance comparable to adjoint-based methods.

title: Amortized Reparametrization: Efficient and Scalable Variational Inference for Latent SDEs

abstract: In this paper, we address the challenge of speech enhancement in real-world recordings, which often contain various forms of distortion, such as background noise, reverberation, and microphone artifacts.We revisit the use of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for speech enhancement and theoretically show that GANs are naturally inclined to seek the point of maximum density within the conditional clean speech distribution, which, as we argue, is essential for speech enhancement task.We study various feature extractors for perceptual loss to facilitate the stability of adversarial training, developing a methodology for probing the structure of the feature space.This leads us to integrate WavLM-based perceptual loss into MS-STFT adversarial training pipeline, creating an effective and stable training procedure for the speech enhancement model.The resulting speech enhancement model, which we refer to as FINALLY, builds upon the HiFi++ architecture, augmented with a WavLM encoder and a novel training pipeline.Empirical results on various datasets confirm our model's ability to produce clear, high-quality speech at 48 kHz, achieving state-of-the-art performance in the field of speech enhancement. Demo page: https://samsunglabs.github.io/FINALLY-page/

Demo page: https://samsunglabs.github.io/FINALLY-page/

paragraphs: FINALLY targets speech recordings degraded by background noise, reverberation, and microphone artifacts. The paper revisits generative adversarial networks for restoring clear speech. Its theoretical analysis argues that these networks tend toward the highest-density point in the clean-speech distribution conditioned on the recording, a behavior the authors consider valuable for enhancement.

The work also studies how perceptual losses can stabilize adversarial training. Such losses compare representations of audio, making the choice of feature extractor consequential. The authors develop a way to probe feature-space structure and use the results to select a WavLM-based perceptual loss. They combine it with an adversarial training pipeline based on multi-scale short-time Fourier transforms.

The resulting model extends the HiFi++ architecture with a WavLM encoder and the new training procedure. Across several datasets, the authors report high-quality speech at 48 kHz and state-of-the-art enhancement performance. The contribution connects a theoretical motivation for adversarial learning with a concrete representation and training design that works well in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: FINALLY combines adversarial training and WavLM-based perceptual guidance to achieve reported state-of-the-art speech enhancement at 48 kHz.

title: FINALLY: fast and universal speech enhancement with studio-like quality

abstract: *Boundaries* are the timestamps at which a class in a time series changes. Recently, representation-based boundary detection has gained popularity, but its emphasis on consecutive distance difference backfires, especially when the changes are gradual. In this paper, we propose a boundary detection method, **RECURVE**, based on a novel change metric, the ***curvature*** of a representation trajectory, to accommodate both gradual and abrupt changes. Here, a sequence of representations in the representation space is interpreted as a trajectory, and a curvature at each timestamp can be computed. Using the theory of random walk, we formally show that the mean curvature is lower near boundaries than at other points. Extensive experiments using diverse real-world time-series datasets confirm the superiority of RECURVE over state-of-the-art methods.

In this paper, we propose a boundary detection method, **RECURVE**, based on a novel change metric, the ***curvature*** of a representation trajectory, to accommodate both gradual and abrupt changes. Here, a sequence of representations in the representation space is interpreted as a trajectory, and a curvature at each timestamp can be computed. paragraphs: Boundary detection identifies the times when a time series changes from one class to another. Methods based on learned representations often look for differences in the distances between consecutive representations. That emphasis can become unreliable when a transition happens gradually, because the relevant change unfolds over a sequence rather than appearing as a sharp local difference.

RECURVE treats the sequence of representations as a trajectory through representation space. It computes the curvature of that trajectory at each timestamp and uses curvature as its change metric. This shifts attention from the size of consecutive movements to the trajectory's bending behavior, providing a way to accommodate both gradual and abrupt class transitions.

Using random-walk theory, the authors formally establish that mean curvature is lower near boundaries than at other points. This theoretical result supplies the basis for the proposed detection signal. Experiments across diverse real-world time-series datasets show RECURVE outperforming the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support trajectory curvature as a useful source of boundary information beyond consecutive-distance differences.
summary.tldr: RECURVE detects time-series class boundaries using representation-trajectory curvature, accommodating both gradual and abrupt transitions.

title: Exploiting Representation Curvature for Boundary Detection in Time Series

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViT) is known for its scalability. In this work, we target to scale down a ViT to fit in an environment with dynamic-changing resource constraints. We observe that smaller ViTs are intrinsically the sub-networks of a larger ViT with different widths. Thus, we propose a general framework, named Scala, to enable a single network to represent multiple smaller ViTs with flexible inference capability, which aligns with the inherent design of ViT to vary from widths. Concretely, Scala activates several subnets during training, introduces Isolated Activation to disentangle the smallest sub-network from other subnets, and leverages Scale Coordination to ensure each sub-network receives simplified, steady, and accurate learning objectives. Comprehensive empirical validations on different tasks demonstrate that with only one-shot training, Scala learns slimmable representation without modifying the original ViT structure and matches the performance of Separate Training. Compared with the prior art, Scala achieves an average improvement of 1.6% on ImageNet-1K with fewer parameters.

paragraphs: A vision model may need to operate under resource limits that change over time. Scala addresses this by training one vision transformer to contain multiple usable subnetworks of different widths. Its starting observation is that narrower vision transformers can be represented as subnetworks within a wider one, providing a natural way to vary inference size.

During training, Scala activates several subnetworks. Isolated Activation separates the smallest subnetwork from the others, while Scale Coordination supplies each subnetwork with learning objectives intended to be simpler, steadier, and accurate. These mechanisms support training multiple widths together without changing the original vision transformer structure.

Across different evaluated tasks, a single training run produces slimmable representations that match the performance of separately trained networks. Relative to prior work, Scala reports an average improvement of 1.6% on ImageNet-1K while using fewer parameters. The findings indicate that flexible inference capacity can be learned jointly, allowing a trained network to offer multiple operating sizes as available resources change.
summary.tldr: Scala trains one vision transformer with multiple usable widths, enabling inference that adapts to changing resource budgets.

title: Slicing Vision Transformer for Flexible Inference

abstract: Visual Grounding aims to localize the referring object in an image given a natural language expression. Recent advancements in DETR-based visual grounding methods have attracted considerable attention, as they directly predict the coordinates of the target object without relying on additional efforts, such as pre-generated proposal candidates or pre-defined anchor boxes. However, existing research primarily focuses on designing stronger multi-modal decoder, which typically generates learnable queries by random initialization or by using linguistic embeddings. This vanilla query generation approach inevitably increases the learning difficulty for the model, as it does not involve any target-related information at the beginning of decoding. Furthermore, they only use the deepest image feature during the query learning process, overlooking the importance of features from other levels. To address these issues, we propose a novel approach, called RefFormer. It consists of the query adaption module that can be seamlessly integrated into CLIP and generate the referential query to provide the prior context for decoder, along with a task-specific decoder. By incorporating the referential query into the decoder, we can effectively mitigate the learning difficulty of the decoder, and accurately concentrate on the target object. Additionally, our proposed query adaption module can also act as an adapter, preserving the rich knowledge within CLIP without the need to tune the parameters of the backbone network. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed method, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches on five visual grounding benchmarks.

paragraphs: Visual grounding locates the object in an image described by a natural-language expression. DETR-based approaches predict object coordinates directly, but their decoder queries often begin with random values or linguistic embeddings that lack target-related context. Existing query learning also relies on the deepest image features, overlooking other feature levels.

RefFormer addresses these issues with a query adaptation module integrated into CLIP and a decoder designed for the grounding task. The module generates a referential query that supplies relevant context at the start of decoding. This gives the decoder information to guide its attention toward the referred object and reduces the difficulty of learning that focus.

The query module also serves as an adapter, allowing the method to retain CLIP's learned knowledge without updating the backbone's parameters. Experiments report effectiveness and efficiency, with performance exceeding leading approaches on five grounding benchmarks. The central contribution is to improve the information used to initiate object localization, alongside the decoder that turns that information into a prediction.
summary.tldr: RefFormer supplies target-related referential queries to a grounding decoder, improving object localization while keeping the CLIP backbone frozen.

title: Referencing Where to Focus: Improving Visual Grounding with Referential Query

abstract: Unexpected stimuli induce "error" or "surprise" signals in the brain. The theory of predictive coding promises to explain these observations in terms of Bayesian inference by suggesting that the cortex implements variational inference in a probabilistic graphical model. However, when applied to machine learning tasks, this family of algorithms has yet to perform on par with other variational approaches in high-dimensional, structured inference problems. To address this, we introduce a novel predictive coding algorithm for structured generative models, that we call divide-and-conquer predictive coding (DCPC); it differs from other formulations of predictive coding, as it respects the correlation structure of the generative model and provably performs maximum-likelihood updates of model parameters, all without sacrificing biological plausibility. Empirically, DCPC achieves better numerical performance than competing algorithms and provides accurate inference in a number of problems not previously addressed with predictive coding. We provide an open implementation of DCPC in Pyro on Github.

However, when applied to machine learning tasks, this family of algorithms has yet to perform on par with other variational approaches in high-dimensional, structured inference problems. To address this, we introduce a novel predictive coding algorithm for structured generative models, that we call divide-and-conquer predictive coding (DCPC); it differs from other formulations of predictive coding, as it respects the correlation structure of the generative model and provably performs maximum-likelihood updates of model parameters, all without sacrificing biological plausibility. paragraphs: Predictive coding connects the brain's responses to unexpected events with probabilistic inference. In this account, neural processing estimates hidden causes within a generative model. However, existing predictive coding algorithms have struggled to match other variational methods on machine learning problems with many variables and structured relationships.

Divide-and-conquer predictive coding, or DCPC, addresses this gap by respecting the correlation structure of the generative model. Relationships between variables are therefore part of the inference procedure. The authors also prove that the algorithm performs maximum-likelihood updates of model parameters, connecting its learning rule to a standard statistical objective while retaining the biological plausibility they seek.

The reported experiments show better numerical performance than competing algorithms and accurate inference on several problems previously unaddressed by predictive coding. These findings matter because they extend the practical reach of the approach beyond an explanation of surprise signals. DCPC provides both a structured inference algorithm and a theoretical account of how its model parameters are updated.
summary.tldr: DCPC respects correlations in structured generative models, improving predictive coding inference while providing proven maximum-likelihood parameter updates.

title: Divide-and-Conquer Predictive Coding: a structured Bayesian inference algorithm

abstract: Structure-based drug design (SBDD), which aims to generate 3D ligand molecules binding to target proteins, is a fundamental task in drug discovery. Existing SBDD methods typically treat protein as rigid and neglect protein structural change when binding with ligand molecules, leading to a big gap with real-world scenarios and inferior generation qualities (e.g., many steric clashes). To bridge the gap, we propose FlexSBDD, a deep generative model capable of accurately modeling the flexible protein-ligand complex structure for ligand molecule generation. FlexSBDD adopts an efficient flow matching framework and leverages E(3)-equivariant network with scalar-vector dual representation to model dynamic structural changes. Moreover, novel data augmentation schemes based on structure relaxation/sidechain repacking are adopted to boost performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlexSBDD achieves state-of-the-art performance in generating high-affinity molecules and effectively modeling the protein's conformation change to increase favorable protein-ligand interactions (e.g., Hydrogen bonds) and decrease steric clashes.
originalAbstract: Structure-based drug design (SBDD), which aims to generate 3D ligand molecules binding to target proteins, is a fundamental task in drug discovery. Existing SBDD methods typically treat protein as rigid and neglect protein structural change when binding with ligand molecules, leading to a big gap with real-world scenarios and inferior generation qualities (e.g., many steric clashes). To bridge the gap, we propose FlexSBDD, a deep generative model capable of accurately modeling the flexible protein-ligand complex structure for ligand molecule generation. FlexSBDD adopts an efficient flow matching framework and leverages E(3)-equivariant network with scalar-vector dual representation to model dynamic structural changes. Moreover, novel data augmentation schemes based on structure relaxation/sidechain repacking are adopted to boost performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlexSBDD achieves state-of-the-art performance in generating high-affinity molecules and effectively modeling the protein's conformation change to increase favorable protein-ligand interactions (e.g., Hydrogen bonds) and decrease steric clashes.

paragraphs: Structure-based drug design generates three-dimensional ligand molecules intended to bind a target protein. Treating that protein as fixed overlooks structural changes that occur during binding. The paper argues that this mismatch can reduce generation quality, including producing steric clashes where the generated structures overlap unfavorably.

FlexSBDD models the protein-ligand complex as flexible during ligand generation. It uses flow matching together with an E(3)-equivariant network and paired scalar and vector representations to capture structural changes. The geometric design supports modeling spatial relationships consistently, while data augmentation based on structure relaxation and sidechain repacking supplies additional structural variation during training.

The reported experiments show state-of-the-art performance in generating high-affinity molecules and effective modeling of protein conformational changes. Those changes are associated with more favorable interactions, including hydrogen bonds, and fewer steric clashes. The contribution is to make protein adjustment part of the generation problem itself, so the proposed ligand and the protein's possible response are considered together when constructing the complex.
summary.tldr: FlexSBDD jointly models ligand generation and protein flexibility to improve binding interactions and reduce structural clashes.

title: FlexSBDD: Structure-Based Drug Design with Flexible Protein Modeling

abstract: Pre-trained foundation models, particularly large language models, have achieved remarkable success and led to massive fine-tuned variants. These models are commonly fine-tuned locally and then uploaded by users to cloud platforms such as HuggingFace for secure storage. However, the huge model number and their billion-level parameters impose heavy storage overhead for cloud with limited resources. Our empirical and theoretical analysis reveals that most fine-tuned models in cloud have a small difference (delta) from their pre-trained models. To this end, we propose a novel lossless compression scheme FM-Delta specifically for storing massive fine-tuned models in cloud. FM-Delta maps fine-tuned and pre-trained model parameters into integers with the same bits, and entropy codes their integer delta. In this way, cloud only needs to store one uncompressed pre-trained model and other compressed fine-tuned models. Extensive experiments have demonstrated that FM-Delta efficiently reduces cloud storage consumption for massive fine-tuned models by an average of around 50% with only negligible additional time in most end-to-end cases. For example, on up to 10 fine-tuned models in the GPT-NeoX-20B family, FM-Delta reduces the original storage requirement from 423GB to 205GB, significantly saving cloud storage costs.

paragraphs: FM-Delta targets the storage burden created by keeping many fine-tuned versions of large foundation models. Storing every version independently repeats much of the information already present in its pretrained parent. The authors' empirical and theoretical analysis finds that most fine-tuned models in the cloud differ only slightly from their pretrained versions, motivating compression based on those differences.

The method maps pretrained and fine-tuned parameter values into integers with the same bits, then entropy-codes the differences between those integers.
