summary.tldr: DeepFund evaluates language models on live investment tasks using post-pretraining market data, exposing practical weaknesses obscured by potentially leaky back-tests.

title: Time Travel is Cheating: Going Live with DeepFund for Real-Time Fund Investment Benchmarking

abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of achieving high-quality and fast image generation that aligns with complex human preferences. While recent advancements in diffusion models and distillation have enabled rapid generation, the effective integration of reward feedback for improved abilities like controllability and preference alignment remains a key open problem. Existing reward-guided post-training approaches targeting accelerated few-step generation often deem diffusion distillation losses indispensable. However, in this paper, we identify an interesting yet fundamental paradigm shift: as conditions become more specific, well-designed reward functions emerge as the primary driving force in training strong, few-step image generative models. Motivated by this insight, we introduce Reward-Instruct, a novel and surprisingly simple reward-centric approach for converting pre-trained base diffusion models into reward-enhanced few-step generators. Unlike existing methods, Reward-Instruct does not rely on expensive yet tricky diffusion distillation losses. Instead, it iteratively updates the few-step generator's parameters by directly sampling from a reward-tilted parameter distribution. Such a training approach entirely bypasses the need for expensive diffusion distillation losses, making it favorable to scale in high image resolutions. Despite its simplicity, Reward-Instruct yields surprisingly strong performance. Our extensive experiments on text-to-image generation have demonstrated that Reward-Instruct achieves state-of-the-art results in visual quality and quantitative metrics compared to distillation-reliant methods, while also exhibiting greater robustness to the choice of reward function.

title: Reward-Instruct: A Reward-Centric Approach to Fast Photo-Realistic Image Generation

abstract: In-Context Reinforcement Learning (ICRL) enables agents to learn automatically and on-the-fly from their interactive experiences. However, a major challenge in scaling up ICRL is the lack of scalable task collections. To address this, we propose the procedurally generated tabular Markov Decision Processes, named AnyMDP. Through a carefully designed randomization process, AnyMDP is capable of generating high-quality tasks on a large scale while maintaining relatively low structural biases. To facilitate efficient meta-training at scale, we further introduce decoupled policy distillation and induce prior information in the ICRL framework. Our results demonstrate that, with a sufficiently large scale of AnyMDP tasks, the proposed model can generalize to tasks that were not considered in the training set through versatile in-context learning paradigms. The scalable task set provided by AnyMDP also enables a more thorough empirical investigation of the relationship between data distribution and ICRL performance. We further show that the generalization of ICRL potentially comes at the cost of increased task diversity and longer adaptation periods. This finding carries critical implications for scaling robust ICRL capabilities, highlighting the necessity of diverse and extensive task design, and prioritizing asymptotic performance over few-shot adaptation.

paragraphs: In-context reinforcement learning aims to let agents adapt from their ongoing interactions. Scaling this capability requires a large supply of training tasks, which is difficult to assemble. The paper introduces AnyMDP, a procedural generator of tabular Markov decision processes, to create tasks at scale through carefully designed randomization while maintaining relatively low structural bias.

The authors also introduce decoupled policy distillation and incorporate prior information to make large-scale meta-training more efficient. The generated task supply also enables broader empirical study of how the training distribution affects adaptation.

This qualifies the benefit: broader capability need not mean reaching good behavior after only a few interactions. The authors consequently emphasize extensive, diverse task design and performance after sustained adaptation when scaling robust in-context reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: AnyMDP supplies scalable randomized training tasks for in-context reinforcement learning, with generalization potentially requiring more diversity and longer adaptation.

title: Towards Large-Scale In-Context Reinforcement Learning by Meta-Training in Randomized Worlds

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an effective approach for fine-tuning large language models (LLMs), particularly to enhance their reasoning capabilities. However, RL fine-tuning remains highly resource-intensive, and existing work has largely overlooked the problem of data efficiency. In this paper, we propose two techniques to improve data efficiency in LLM RL fine-tuning: difficulty-targeted online data selection and rollout replay. We introduce the notion of adaptive difficulty to guide online data selection, prioritizing questions of moderate difficulty that are more likely to yield informative learning signals. To estimate adaptive difficulty efficiently, we develop an attention-based framework that requires rollouts for only a small reference set of questions. The adaptive difficulty of the remaining questions is then estimated based on their similarity to this set. To further reduce rollout cost, we introduce a rollout replay mechanism inspired by experience replay in traditional RL. This technique reuses recent rollouts, lowering per-step computation while maintaining stable updates. Experiments across 6 LLM-dataset combinations show that our method reduces RL fine-tuning time by 23% to 62% while reaching the same level of performance as the original GRPO algorithm. Our code repository is available at https://github.com/ASTRAL-Group/data-efficient-llm-rl/.

paragraphs: Reinforcement fine-tuning can improve language-model reasoning, but generating training responses consumes substantial resources. This paper addresses that cost through two complementary changes: choosing questions that provide useful learning signals and reusing recently generated rollouts. Both changes target how efficiently the training process uses its data.

For question selection, the authors define adaptive difficulty and prioritize moderately difficult questions. An attention-based estimator uses rollouts from a small reference set, then estimates other questions’ difficulty through their similarity to that set. This avoids requiring fresh rollouts for every candidate question simply to decide which ones are useful for training.

The rollout replay mechanism reuses recent rollouts to reduce computation per step while maintaining stable updates. Across six combinations of language models and datasets, the combined approach reduces fine-tuning time by 23% to 62% while reaching the same performance level as the original GRPO algorithm. These results show that selecting informative questions and extracting more use from existing rollouts can substantially reduce training time in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Difficulty-aware question selection and recent-rollout replay reduce RL fine-tuning time by 23%–62% while matching GRPO performance in six tested combinations.

title: Improving Data Efficiency for LLM Reinforcement Fine-tuning Through Difficulty-targeted Online Data Selection and Rollout Replay

abstract: Efficient detection of multiple object instances is one of the fundamental challenges in computer vision. For certain object categories, even the best automatic systems are yet unable to produce high-quality detection results, and fully manual annotation would be an expensive process. How can detection algorithms interplay with human expert annotators? To make the best use of scarce (human) labeling resources, one needs to decide when to invoke the expert, such that the best possible performance can be achieved while requiring a minimum amount of supervision. In this paper, we propose a principled approach to active object detection, and show that for a rich class of base detectors algorithms, one can derive a natural sequential decision problem for deciding when to invoke expert supervision. We further show that the objective function satisfies adaptive submodularity, which allows us to derive strong performance guarantees for our algorithm. We demonstrate the proposed algorithm on three real-world tasks, including a problem for biodiversity monitoring from micro UAVs in the Sumatra rain forest. Our results show that active detection not only outperforms its passive counterpart; for certain tasks, it also works significantly better than straightforward application of existing active learning techniques. To the best of our knowledge, our approach is the first to rigorously address the active detection problem from both empirical and theoretical perspectives.

They show that its objective satisfies adaptive submodularity, a mathematical property that supports performance guarantees for their algorithm. Active detection outperforms its passive counterpart in the reported results. On certain tasks, it also substantially outperforms straightforward applications of existing active learning methods, supporting the value of a decision procedure designed specifically for detection.
summary.tldr: A sequential approach to requesting expert supervision gives active object detection theoretical guarantees and strong results on three real-world tasks.

title: Active Detection via Adaptive Submodularity

abstract: Different real-world applications of multi-label classification often demand different evaluation criteria. We formalize this demand with a general setup, cost-sensitive multi-label classification (CSMLC), which takes the evaluation criteria into account during learning. Nevertheless, most existing algorithms can only focus on optimizing a few specific evaluation criteria, and cannot systematically deal with different ones. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm, called condensed filter tree (CFT), for optimizing any criteria in CSMLC. CFT is derived from reducing CSMLC to the famous filter tree algorithm for cost-sensitive multi-class classification via constructing the label powerset. We successfully cope with the difficulty of having exponentially many extended-classes within the powerset for representation, training and prediction by carefully designing the tree structure and focusing on the key nodes. Experimental results across many real-world datasets validate that CFT is competitive with special purpose algorithms on special criteria and reaches better performance on general criteria.

paragraphs: Multi-label classification assigns a set of labels to an example, and different applications judge those sets using different criteria. This paper formalizes a learning setup that incorporates the chosen evaluation criterion as a cost. Its aim is to support varied criteria systematically, instead of requiring a separate specialized algorithm for each one.

The proposed condensed filter tree converts the problem into cost-sensitive multiclass classification. It does so through the label powerset, where possible combinations of labels become classes. This creates an immediate computational challenge because the number of combinations grows exponentially. The method addresses representation, training, and prediction through a carefully designed tree that concentrates on key nodes.

Experiments across many real-world datasets find that the method is competitive with specialized algorithms on their particular criteria and performs better on general criteria. These results support the practical value of a common framework for differing application objectives. The stated contribution is an algorithm for optimizing arbitrary criteria within the cost-sensitive setup, supported by those empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: Condensed filter trees make cost-sensitive multi-label learning practical across varied evaluation criteria by organizing the exponentially large label powerset.

title: Condensed Filter Tree for Cost-Sensitive Multi-Label Classification

abstract: Mutual information is a very popular measure for comparing clusterings. Previous work has shown that it is beneficial to make an adjustment for chance to this measure, by subtracting an expected value and normalizing via an upper bound. This yields the constant baseline property that enhances intuitiveness. In this paper, we argue that a further type of statistical adjustment for the mutual information is also beneficial - an adjustment to correct selection bias. This type of adjustment is useful when carrying out many clustering comparisons, to select one or more preferred clusterings. It reduces the tendency for the mutual information to choose clustering solutions i) with more clusters, or ii) induced on fewer data points, when compared to a reference one. We term our new adjusted measure the *standardized mutual information*. It requires computation of the variance of mutual information under a hypergeometric model of randomness, which is technically challenging. We derive an analytical formula for this variance and analyze its complexity. We then experimentally assess how our new measure can address selection bias and also increase interpretability. We recommend using the standardized mutual information when making multiple clustering comparisons in situations where the number of records is small compared to the number of clusters considered.

paragraphs: Mutual information measures agreement between clusterings, but chance can create apparent agreement. Earlier adjustments subtract the expected value and normalize against an upper bound, establishing a constant baseline. This paper argues that choosing among many candidate clusterings creates an additional concern: selection bias.

The proposed standardized mutual information reduces the tendency to prefer candidates with more clusters or fewer data points when comparing them with a reference clustering. It requires the variance of mutual information under a hypergeometric randomness model. The authors derive an analytical formula for this technically challenging quantity and analyze the computational complexity of obtaining it.

Experiments examine how standardization addresses selection bias and improves interpretability. The authors specifically recommend the measure for multiple clustering comparisons when the number of records is small relative to the number of clusters being considered. The contribution distinguishes correcting an average chance baseline from accounting for variability when selecting among alternatives, showing why the latter can matter for interpreting a high agreement score.
summary.tldr: Standardized mutual information uses chance variability to reduce selection bias when comparing many clusterings, especially with few records relative to clusters.

title: Standardized Mutual Information for Clustering Comparisons: One Step Further in Adjustment for Chance

abstract: In the Graph Inference problem, one seeks to recover the edges of an unknown graph from the observations of cascades propagating over this graph. In this paper, we approach this problem from the sparse recovery perspective. We introduce a general model of cascades, including the voter model and the independent cascade model, for which we provide the first algorithm which recovers the graph’s edges with high probability and O(s log m) measurements where s is the maximum degree of the graph and m is the number of nodes. Furthermore, we show that our algorithm also recovers the edge weights (the parameters of the diffusion process) and is robust in the context of approximate sparsity. Finally we prove an almost matching lower bound of Ω(s \log m/s) and validate our approach empirically on synthetic graphs.

In this paper, we approach this problem from the sparse recovery perspective. We introduce a general model of cascades, including the voter model and the independent cascade model, for which we provide the first algorithm which recovers the graph’s edges with high probability and O(s log m) measurements where s is the maximum degree of the graph and m is the number of nodes. Furthermore, we show that our algorithm also recovers the edge weights (the parameters of the diffusion process) and is robust in the context of approximate sparsity. Finally we prove an almost matching lower bound of Ω(s \log m/s) and validate our approach empirically on synthetic graphs.

paragraphs: Graph inference asks whether the connections of an unknown network can be recovered by observing cascades that spread across it. This paper treats that task as sparse recovery. The relevant structural quantity is the maximum number of neighbors of a node, allowing the analysis to express recovery requirements in terms of graph sparsity.

The authors introduce a general cascade model that includes both the voter model and the independent cascade model. For this setting, their algorithm recovers graph edges with high probability using O(s log m) measurements, where s is the maximum degree and m is the number of nodes. It also recovers edge weights governing diffusion and remains robust under approximate sparsity.

An almost matching lower bound shows that the measurement requirement is close to a fundamental limit in the analyzed setting. Experiments on synthetic graphs validate the approach empirically. Together, these results address both which connections exist and how strongly diffusion operates along them, with recovery stated probabilistically rather than as an unconditional guarantee.
summary.tldr: A sparse-recovery approach infers graph edges and diffusion weights from cascades with near-optimal measurement requirements.

title: Inferring Graphs from Cascades: A Sparse Recovery Framework

abstract: We formalize and study the multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem in a generalized stochastic setting, in which rewards are not assumed to be numerical. Instead, rewards are measured on a qualitative scale that allows for comparison but invalidates arithmetic operations such as averaging. Correspondingly, instead of characterizing an arm in terms of the mean of the underlying distribution, we opt for using a quantile of that distribution as a representative value. We address the problem of quantile-based online learning both for the case of a finite (pure exploration) and infinite time horizon (cumulative regret minimization). For both cases, we propose suitable algorithms and analyze their properties. These properties are also illustrated by means of first experimental studies.

paragraphs: Multi-armed bandit problems involve learning which choices produce desirable outcomes through repeated interaction. This paper considers a setting where outcomes can be ordered but are not numerical. Such qualitative rewards support comparisons, yet arithmetic operations such as averaging have no valid meaning, so the usual mean-based description of a choice is unavailable.

The authors use a quantile of each choice's reward distribution as its representative value. A quantile identifies a position within an ordered distribution, allowing the learning objective to respect the qualitative reward scale. This changes how choices are assessed while retaining the central challenge of learning about uncertain outcomes through experience.

The paper develops algorithms for two settings: a finite horizon devoted to pure exploration and an infinite horizon focused on cumulative regret minimization. It analyzes their properties and provides initial experiments illustrating them. The contribution is a formal framework and associated methods for online learning when reward order is meaningful but numerical averages are not.
summary.tldr: Quantile-based bandit algorithms enable online learning from rewards that can be ranked but cannot meaningfully be averaged.

title: Qualitative Multi-Armed Bandits: A Quantile-Based Approach

abstract: We derive a new discrepancy statistic for measuring differences between two probability distributions based on combining Stein’s identity and the reproducing kernel Hilbert space theory. We apply our result to test how well a probabilistic model fits a set of observations, and derive a new class of powerful goodness-of-fit tests that are widely applicable for complex and high dimensional distributions, even for those with computationally intractable normalization constants. Both theoretical and empirical properties of our methods are studied thoroughly.
originalAbstract: We derive a new discrepancy statistic for measuring differences between two probability distributions based on combining Stein’s identity and the reproducing kernel Hilbert space theory. We apply our result to test how well a probabilistic model fits a set of observations, and derive a new class of powerful goodness-of-fit tests that are widely applicable for complex and high dimensional distributions, even for those with computationally intractable normalization constants. Both theoretical and empirical properties of our methods are studied thoroughly.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to check whether a probabilistic model fits observed data. It develops a discrepancy statistic: a quantity designed to measure differences between two probability distributions. Such a quantity provides the basis for testing whether the distribution described by a model is consistent with the observations available.

The construction combines Stein’s identity with reproducing kernel Hilbert space theory. These two mathematical ingredients yield a new way to measure distributional mismatch and, from it, a family of goodness-of-fit tests. A central attraction is that the tests apply even when a model’s normalization constant is computationally intractable, a setting explicitly included in the paper’s scope.

The authors describe the resulting tests as powerful and broadly applicable to complex, high-dimensional distributions. They investigate both theoretical properties and empirical behavior. The practical significance is that difficulty evaluating a normalization constant need not prevent model checking with this approach. The contribution connects a mathematical discrepancy to a concrete statistical task: assessing how well a proposed probabilistic model accounts for data.
summary.tldr: Combining Stein’s identity with kernel methods yields goodness-of-fit tests that also handle models with intractable normalization constants.

title: A Kernelized Stein Discrepancy for Goodness-of-fit Tests

abstract: Parameter inference in mechanistic models of coupled differential equations is a topical and challenging problem. We propose a new method based on kernel ridge regression and gradient matching, and an objective function that simultaneously encourages goodness of fit and penalises inconsistencies with the differential equations. Fast minimisation is achieved by exploiting partial convexity inherent in this function, and setting up an iterative algorithm in the vein of the EM algorithm. An evaluation of the proposed method on various benchmark data suggests that it compares favourably with state-of-the-art alternatives.

Fast minimisation is achieved by exploiting partial convexity inherent in this function, and setting up an iterative algorithm in the vein of the EM algorithm. An evaluation of the proposed method on various benchmark data suggests that it compares favourably with state-of-the-art alternatives.

paragraphs: Mechanistic models built from coupled differential equations describe how interacting quantities change over time. Inferring their parameters requires reconciling observed data with the dynamics specified by those equations. This paper proposes a method for that task that combines kernel ridge regression with gradient matching, connecting fitted trajectories to the rates of change required by the model.

Its objective has two complementary roles: it rewards a good fit to observations and penalizes disagreement with the differential equations. This makes consistency with the proposed mechanism part of the fitting process. The method therefore considers both how well a trajectory follows the data and how well its changes agree with the equations.

For fast optimization, the authors exploit partial convexity within the objective and construct an iterative procedure resembling the EM algorithm. Partial convexity supplies useful structure without implying that the entire inference problem is convex. Evaluations on several benchmark datasets suggest favorable comparisons with state-of-the-art alternatives, supporting the method as a promising approach to efficient parameter inference.
summary.tldr: An iterative gradient-matching method fits nonlinear dynamical models by balancing agreement with observations against consistency with differential equations.

title: Fast Parameter Inference in Nonlinear Dynamical Systems using Iterative Gradient Matching

abstract: We introduce a new algorithm named WGAN, an alternative to traditional GAN training. In this new model, we show that we can improve the stability of learning, get rid of problems like mode collapse, and provide meaningful learning curves useful for debugging and hyperparameter searches. Furthermore, we show that the corresponding optimization problem is sound, and provide extensive theoretical work highlighting the deep connections to different distances between distributions.
originalAbstract: We introduce a new algorithm named WGAN, an alternative to traditional GAN training. In this new model, we show that we can improve the stability of learning, get rid of problems like mode collapse, and provide meaningful learning curves useful for debugging and hyperparameter searches. Furthermore, we show that the corresponding optimization problem is sound, and provide extensive theoretical work highlighting the deep connections to different distances between distributions.

paragraphs: Wasserstein GAN, or WGAN, is introduced as an alternative approach to training generative adversarial networks. The paper connects the behavior of the training process to the choice of distance between probability distributions. Its theoretical work examines those connections and establishes the soundness of the corresponding optimization problem.

The authors show that the approach can improve training stability and eliminate problems such as mode collapse. They also report meaningful learning curves, making the training signal useful for debugging and choosing hyperparameters. These are related practical benefits: a more interpretable account of training progress can help users assess and adjust the learning process.

The paper's significance lies in bringing mathematical foundations and training behavior together. The distribution-distance analysis explains the motivation for a different optimization formulation, while the stated findings describe improvements it can deliver in practice. The claims describe capabilities of the proposed approach; they do not establish that every possible WGAN training run must be stable or free of collapse.
summary.tldr: WGAN connects GAN training to distribution distances to improve stability, address mode collapse, and provide useful learning curves.

title: Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: Undirected graphical models are applied in genomics, protein structure prediction, and neuroscience to identify sparse interactions that underlie discrete data. Although Bayesian methods for inference would be favorable in these contexts, they are rarely used because they require doubly intractable Monte Carlo sampling. Here, we develop a framework for scalable Bayesian inference of discrete undirected models based on two new methods. The first is Persistent VI, an algorithm for variational inference of discrete undirected models that avoids doubly intractable MCMC and approximations of the partition function. The second is Fadeout, a reparameterization approach for variational inference under sparsity-inducing priors that captures a posteriori correlations between parameters and hyperparameters with noncentered parameterizations. We find that, together, these methods for variational inference substantially improve learning of sparse undirected graphical models in simulated and real problems from physics and biology.

paragraphs: Sparse undirected graphical models describe interactions underlying discrete observations in areas such as biology and neuroscience. Bayesian inference is appealing for these problems, but doubly intractable Monte Carlo sampling makes it difficult to use. The paper develops a scalable variational framework through two complementary methods that address inference and sparsity.

Persistent VI handles discrete undirected models while avoiding doubly intractable MCMC and approximations of the partition function. Fadeout addresses variational inference with sparsity-inducing priors. It uses noncentered parameterizations to capture posterior correlations between model parameters and hyperparameters, preserving relationships relevant to learning which interactions are present.

Together, the methods substantially improve learning of sparse undirected graphical models in simulated and real problems from physics and biology. The two components tackle different parts of the challenge: performing inference in an undirected model and representing uncertainty under sparsity-promoting priors. Their combined empirical results support the framework as a practical route to Bayesian learning in settings where the usual sampling requirements have discouraged its use.
summary.tldr: Persistent VI and Fadeout combine scalable inference with sparsity-aware parameterization to improve Bayesian learning of undirected graphical models.

title: Variational Inference for Sparse and Undirected Models

abstract: Asynchronous parallel stochastic gradient optimization has been playing a pivotal role to solve large-scale machine learning problems in big data applications. Zeroth-order (derivative-free) methods estimate the gradient only by two function evaluations, thus have been applied to solve the problems where the explicit gradient calculations are computationally expensive or infeasible. Recently, the first asynchronous parallel stochastic zeroth-order algorithm (AsySZO) was proposed. However, its convergence rate is O(1/SQRT{T}) for the smooth, possibly non-convex learning problems, which is significantly slower than O(1/T) the best convergence rate of (asynchronous) stochastic gradient algorithm. To fill this gap, in this paper, we first point out the fundamental reason leading to the slow convergence rate of AsySZO, and then propose a new asynchronous stochastic zerothorder algorithm (AsySZO+). We provide a faster convergence rate O(1/bT) (b is the mini-batch size) for AsySZO+ by the rigorous theoretical analysis, which is a significant improvement over O(1/SQRT{T}). The experimental results on the application of ensemble learning confirm that our AsySZO+ has a faster convergence rate than the existing (asynchronous) stochastic zeroth-order algorithms.

paragraphs: Some learning problems make explicit gradient calculations too costly or unavailable. Zeroth-order methods address this by estimating a gradient from function evaluations. This paper focuses on asynchronous parallel versions for shared-memory machines, where the aim is to combine derivative-free optimization with parallel computation for large learning problems.

The authors examine why the earlier AsySZO algorithm has a convergence rate of O(1/√T) for smooth, potentially nonconvex problems. They then propose AsySZO+, with a theoretical rate of O(1/(bT)), where b is the mini-batch size. This improves the stated dependence on the iteration count and explicitly incorporates the contribution of mini-batching into the bound.

Experiments on ensemble learning support the theoretical motivation: AsySZO+ converges faster than the existing asynchronous and other stochastic zeroth-order algorithms considered. The significance is that avoiding explicit derivatives need not entail the slower rate of the earlier method in the analyzed setting. The claimed improvement concerns convergence behavior, with the experimental evidence supplied by the ensemble-learning application.
summary.tldr: AsySZO+ improves the analyzed convergence rate of asynchronous derivative-free optimization and converges faster in ensemble-learning experiments.

title: Faster Derivative-Free Stochastic Algorithm for Shared Memory Machines

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel reinforcement-learning algorithm consisting in a stochastic variance-reduced version of policy gradient for solving Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) methods have proven to be very successful in supervised learning. However, their adaptation to policy gradient is not straightforward and needs to account for I) a non-concave objective function; II) approximations in the full gradient computation; and III) a non-stationary sampling process. The result is SVRPG, a stochastic variance-reduced policy gradient algorithm that leverages on importance weights to preserve the unbiasedness of the gradient estimate. Under standard assumptions on the MDP, we provide convergence guarantees for SVRPG with a convergence rate that is linear under increasing batch sizes. Finally, we suggest practical variants of SVRPG, and we empirically evaluate them on continuous MDPs.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods learn a decision-making policy from sampled experience. This paper introduces SVRPG, which adapts stochastic variance reduction to policy gradient learning in Markov decision processes. The aim is to bring a successful optimization idea from supervised learning into a setting where the sampling process changes as the policy changes.

That adaptation must address three difficulties: the objective is nonconcave, full gradients can only be approximated, and the data distribution is nonstationary. SVRPG uses importance weights to preserve an unbiased gradient estimate despite the sampling issue. This makes the changing relationship between the policy and its collected experience part of the algorithm’s design.

Under standard assumptions on the Markov decision process, the authors establish convergence guarantees, including a linear convergence rate when batch sizes increase. The increasing-batch condition is part of that rate claim. They also propose practical variants and evaluate them empirically on continuous decision processes, connecting the theoretical algorithm to implementations suited to policy learning.
summary.tldr: SVRPG adapts variance reduction to policy learning with importance weighting and proves conditional convergence guarantees.

title: Stochastic Variance-Reduced Policy Gradient

abstract: We study the policy evaluation problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning. In this problem, a group of agents works cooperatively to evaluate the value function for the global discounted accumulative reward problem, which is composed of local rewards observed by the agents. Over a series of time steps, the agents act, get rewarded, update their local estimate of the value function, then communicate with their neighbors. The local update at each agent can be interpreted as a distributed consensus-based variant of the popular temporal difference learning algorithm TD(0). While distributed reinforcement learning algorithms have been presented in the literature, almost nothing is known about their convergence rate. Our main contribution is providing a finite-time analysis for the convergence of the distributed TD(0) algorithm. We do this when the communication network between the agents is time-varying in general. We obtain an explicit upper bound on the rate of convergence of this algorithm as a function of the network topology and the discount factor. Our results mirror what we would expect from using distributed stochastic gradient descent for solving convex optimization problems.

paragraphs: The paper studies how cooperating agents can evaluate a policy when each agent observes only its own local rewards. Their shared target is a value function describing the global discounted accumulation of rewards. The focus is policy evaluation: estimating the value of behavior through learning and communication across the group.

Each agent acts, receives a reward, updates its local value estimate, and exchanges information with neighboring agents. With linear function approximation, this becomes a distributed version of TD(0) that combines temporal-difference updates with a process for bringing local estimates into agreement. The communication network is allowed to change over time, so the analysis addresses an evolving pattern of information exchange.

The main contribution is a finite-time convergence analysis, giving an explicit upper bound that depends on network topology and the discount factor. Such a bound describes progress over a limited number of updates, beyond eventual convergence alone. The results resemble the behavior expected from distributed stochastic gradient descent for convex optimization, providing a theoretical account of this distributed learning procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds finite-time convergence of distributed TD(0), explicitly accounting for changing communication networks and reward discounting.

title: Finite-Time Analysis of Distributed TD(0) with Linear Function Approximation on Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: He et al. (2018) have called into question the utility of pre-training by showing that training from scratch can often yield similar performance to pre-training. We show that although pre-training may not improve performance on traditional classification metrics, it improves model robustness and uncertainty estimates. Through extensive experiments on label corruption, class imbalance, adversarial examples, out-of-distribution detection, and confidence calibration, we demonstrate large gains from pre-training and complementary effects with task-specific methods. We show approximately a 10% absolute improvement over the previous state-of-the-art in adversarial robustness. In some cases, using pre-training without task-specific methods also surpasses the state-of-the-art, highlighting the need for pre-training when evaluating future methods on robustness and uncertainty tasks.

paragraphs: Pretraining may appear unnecessary when a model trained from scratch achieves similar classification performance. This paper asks whether that comparison overlooks other benefits. It evaluates robustness and uncertainty estimation, examining aspects of model behavior that ordinary classification metrics may fail to capture even when their reported scores are similar.

The experiments cover corrupted labels, class imbalance, adversarial examples, detection of out-of-distribution inputs, and confidence calibration. Across this investigation, the authors demonstrate large gains from pretraining and find that those gains can complement methods designed specifically for the task. This makes pretraining relevant to both resistance to difficult conditions and the quality of a model’s uncertainty estimates.

The paper reports approximately a ten-percentage-point absolute improvement over the previous state of the art in adversarial robustness. In some cases, pretraining alone also surpasses prior state-of-the-art methods. These findings support including pretraining when evaluating robustness and uncertainty techniques, since differences in pretraining can materially affect the comparison even when conventional classification performance changes little.
summary.tldr: Experiments show that pretraining can substantially improve robustness and uncertainty estimates even when standard classification metrics reveal little benefit.

title: Using Pre-Training Can Improve Model Robustness and Uncertainty

abstract: We study the interplay between surrogate methods for structured prediction and techniques from multitask learning designed to leverage relationships between surrogate outputs. We propose an efficient algorithm based on trace norm regularization which, differently from previous methods, does not require explicit knowledge of the coding/decoding functions of the surrogate framework. As a result, our algorithm can be applied to the broad class of problems in which the surrogate space is large or even infinite dimensional. We study excess risk bounds for trace norm regularized structured prediction proving the consistency and learning rates for our estimator. We also identify relevant regimes in which our approach can enjoy better generalization performance than previous methods. Numerical experiments on ranking problems indicate that enforcing low-rank relations among surrogate outputs may indeed provide a significant advantage in practice.

paragraphs: Structured prediction uses surrogate learning problems to make complex output prediction manageable. This paper studies how relationships among those surrogate outputs can improve learning. It connects the surrogate approach with multitask learning, where related prediction tasks can share structure instead of being treated as independent.

The proposed algorithm uses trace norm regularization to encourage low-rank relationships among the surrogate outputs. Unlike previous methods, it does not require explicit knowledge of the surrogate framework's coding and decoding functions. That makes the algorithm applicable when the surrogate space is very large or even infinite dimensional, extending the range of problems where this shared-structure approach can be used.

The authors establish excess-risk bounds, consistency, and learning rates, and identify regimes where generalization can improve over previous methods. Ranking experiments indicate that enforcing low-rank relationships can also provide a significant practical advantage. The theoretical benefit is conditional on the identified regimes, while the experiments supply evidence that the proposed relationships can matter in actual structured-prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: Trace norm regularization exploits shared structure among surrogate outputs, with consistency guarantees and practical benefits in ranking experiments.

title: Leveraging Low-Rank Relations Between Surrogate Tasks in Structured Prediction

abstract: The issue of disagreements amongst human experts is a ubiquitous one in both machine learning and medicine. In medicine, this often corresponds to doctor disagreements on a patient diagnosis. In this work, we show that machine learning models can be successfully trained to give uncertainty scores to data instances that result in high expert disagreements. In particular, they can identify patient cases that would benefit most from a medical second opinion. Our central methodological finding is that Direct Uncertainty Prediction (DUP), training a model to predict an uncertainty score directly from the raw patient features, works better than Uncertainty Via Classification, the two step process of training a classifier and postprocessing the output distribution to give an uncertainty score. We show this both with a theoretical result, and on extensive evaluations on a large scale medical imaging application.

paragraphs: Doctors can disagree about a diagnosis, making some patient cases especially useful candidates for a second opinion. This paper asks whether machine learning can recognize cases likely to produce that disagreement. Its target is an uncertainty score associated with disagreement among experts, giving the prediction a specific meaning tied to human judgments.

The proposed method, Direct Uncertainty Prediction, learns that score directly from raw patient features. The comparison approach first trains a classifier and then converts its output distribution into an uncertainty estimate. These approaches use different learning targets: one explicitly learns to predict uncertainty, while the other obtains uncertainty through a model trained for classification.

The authors find that direct prediction works better, supporting the comparison with a theoretical result and extensive evaluations in a large medical imaging application. They also show that models can identify cases that would benefit most from another medical opinion. The finding makes the training objective central: when the desired output concerns expert disagreement, directly learning that quantity can be more effective than deriving it from classification outputs.
summary.tldr: Learning uncertainty directly from patient features better identifies expert disagreement than deriving uncertainty from a classifier in the paper's analysis and evaluations.

title: Direct Uncertainty Prediction for Medical Second Opinions

abstract: We identify a trade-off between robustness and accuracy that serves as a guiding principle in the design of defenses against adversarial examples. Although this problem has been widely studied empirically, much remains unknown concerning the theory underlying this trade-off. In this work, we decompose the prediction error for adversarial examples (robust error) as the sum of the natural (classification) error and boundary error, and provide a differentiable upper bound using the theory of classification-calibrated loss, which is shown to be the tightest possible upper bound uniform over all probability distributions and measurable predictors. Inspired by our theoretical analysis, we also design a new defense method, TRADES, to trade adversarial robustness off against accuracy. Our proposed algorithm performs well experimentally in real-world datasets. The methodology is the foundation of our entry to the NeurIPS 2018 Adversarial Vision Challenge in which we won the 1st place out of 2,000 submissions, surpassing the runner-up approach by 11.41% in terms of mean L_2 perturbation distance.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical account of the tradeoff between ordinary classification accuracy and resistance to adversarial examples. It separates robust prediction error into natural classification error and boundary error. This decomposition makes the relationship between the two objectives explicit and provides a basis for designing a defense.

Using classification-calibrated loss theory, the authors derive a differentiable upper bound on robust error. They show that it is the tightest bound of its kind uniformly over all probability distributions and measurable predictors. That uniform tightness is a property of the theoretical bound, giving the subsequent algorithm a principled target for balancing accuracy and robustness.

Its methodology also underpinned the authors' winning entry in the stated adversarial vision challenge, exceeding the runner-up by 11.41% in mean L2 perturbation distance. The contribution connects an error decomposition, a sharp bound, and an empirically effective training method.
summary.tldr: TRADES uses a tight theoretical bound on robust error to guide the balance between adversarial robustness and classification accuracy.

title: Theoretically Principled Trade-off between Robustness and Accuracy

abstract: Obtaining theoretical guarantees for neural networks training appears to be a hard problem in a general case. Recent research has been focused on studying this problem in the limit of infinite width and two different theories have been developed: a mean-field (MF) and a constant kernel (NTK) limit theories. We propose a general framework that provides a link between these seemingly distinct theories. Our framework out of the box gives rise to a discrete-time MF limit which was not previously explored in the literature. We prove a convergence theorem for it, and show that it provides a more reasonable approximation for finite-width nets compared to the NTK limit if learning rates are not very small. Also, our framework suggests a limit model that coincides neither with the MF limit nor with the NTK one. We show that for networks with more than two hidden layers RMSProp training has a non-trivial discrete-time MF limit but GD training does not have one. Overall, our framework demonstrates that both MF and NTK limits have considerable limitations in approximating finite-sized neural nets, indicating the need for designing more accurate infinite-width approximations for them.

paragraphs: Infinite-width limits simplify neural-network training enough to make theoretical analysis more tractable. Two major descriptions are mean-field theory and the constant-kernel, or NTK, limit. This paper introduces a framework linking them and uses it to examine how well such limits represent finite networks.

The framework produces a discrete-time mean-field limit with a convergence theorem. The authors show that this limit gives a more reasonable approximation than NTK when learning rates are not very small. It also suggests another limiting model that is distinct from both mean-field and NTK descriptions, expanding the range of possible theoretical approximations.

The analysis further shows that the optimizer matters: for networks with more than two hidden layers, RMSProp has a nontrivial discrete-time mean-field limit, whereas gradient descent does not. Overall, the results identify considerable limitations in both familiar limits as approximations to finite networks. They motivate more accurate limiting descriptions that account for the training conditions rather than treating infinite width as a single universal approximation.
summary.tldr: A unified framework links mean-field and NTK limits while showing how learning rates, depth, and optimizers affect their relevance to finite networks.

title: Towards a General Theory of Infinite-Width Limits of Neural Classifiers

abstract: When using large-batch training to speed up stochastic gradient descent, learning rates must adapt to new batch sizes in order to maximize speed-ups and preserve model quality. Re-tuning learning rates is resource intensive, while fixed scaling rules often degrade model quality. We propose AdaScale SGD, an algorithm that reliably adapts learning rates to large-batch training. By continually adapting to the gradient’s variance, AdaScale automatically achieves speed-ups for a wide range of batch sizes. We formally describe this quality with AdaScale’s convergence bound, which maintains final objective values, even as batch sizes grow large and the number of iterations decreases. In empirical comparisons, AdaScale trains well beyond the batch size limits of popular “linear learning rate scaling” rules. This includes large-batch training with no model degradation for machine translation, image classification, object detection, and speech recognition tasks. AdaScale’s qualitative behavior is similar to that of "warm-up" heuristics, but unlike warm-up, this behavior emerges naturally from a principled mechanism. The algorithm introduces negligible computational overhead and no new hyperparameters, making AdaScale an attractive choice for large-scale training in practice.

paragraphs: Larger training batches can speed up stochastic gradient descent, but the learning rate must change appropriately to preserve model quality. Repeatedly tuning it consumes resources, while fixed scaling rules can stop working at large batch sizes. AdaScale addresses this problem by adapting the learning rate throughout training.

The adaptation responds to gradient variance, tying the learning rate to the variability in the optimization signal. The authors provide a convergence bound that maintains final objective values as batch sizes increase and the number of iterations decreases. This gives a theoretical account of the method's ability to obtain speedups across a wide range of batch sizes.

Empirically, AdaScale supports batch sizes beyond the limits observed for popular linear scaling rules, without model degradation in the reported translation, classification, detection, and speech tasks. Its behavior resembles learning-rate warm-up, but emerges from the variance-based mechanism. Negligible computational overhead and no additional hyperparameters make the method a practical way to reduce the tuning burden of distributed training.
summary.tldr: AdaScale adapts learning rates to gradient variance, enabling larger training batches with little overhead and no new hyperparameters.

title: AdaScale SGD: A User-Friendly Algorithm for Distributed Training

abstract: Model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) formulates meta-learning as a bilevel optimization problem, where the inner level solves each subtask based on a shared prior, while the outer level searches for the optimal shared prior by optimizing its aggregated performance over all the subtasks. Despite its empirical success, MAML remains less understood in theory, especially in terms of its global optimality, due to the nonconvexity of the meta-objective (the outer-level objective). To bridge such a gap between theory and practice, we characterize the optimality gap of the stationary points attained by MAML for both reinforcement learning and supervised learning, where the inner-level and outer-level problems are solved via first-order optimization methods. In particular, our characterization connects the optimality gap of such stationary points with (i) the functional geometry of inner-level objectives and (ii) the representation power of function approximators, including linear models and neural networks. To the best of our knowledge, our analysis establishes the global optimality of MAML with nonconvex meta-objectives for the first time.

paragraphs: Model-agnostic meta-learning, or MAML, learns a shared prior that supports adaptation across tasks. Its inner optimization adapts to each task, while its outer optimization improves the shared prior using performance across tasks. The outer objective is nonconvex, making it difficult to understand whether points reached by optimization are globally good solutions.

This paper characterizes the optimality gap of stationary points attained by MAML in both supervised learning and reinforcement learning. The analysis considers first-order optimization at both levels. It connects the gap from global optimality to two ingredients: the functional geometry of the individual task objectives and the representational capacity of the function approximators, including linear models and neural networks.

The authors report an analysis establishing global optimality for MAML with nonconvex meta-objectives. Its explanatory value comes from linking optimization quality to task structure and model expressiveness. The result should be understood through that characterization: it concerns the analyzed setting and its structural properties, rather than asserting that every practical MAML run necessarily finds a global optimum.
summary.tldr: The paper links MAML's stationary-point optimality to task geometry and model expressiveness, establishing global-optimality results for nonconvex meta-objectives.

title: On the Global Optimality of Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) in real-world safety-critical target settings like urban driving is hazardous, imperiling the RL agent, other agents, and the environment. To overcome this difficulty, we propose a "safety-critical adaptation" task setting: an agent first trains in non-safety-critical "source" environments such as in a simulator, before it adapts to the target environment where failures carry heavy costs. We propose a solution approach, CARL, that builds on the intuition that prior experience in diverse environments equips an agent to estimate risk, which in turn enables relative safety through risk-averse, cautious adaptation. CARL first employs model-based RL to train a probabilistic model to capture uncertainty about transition dynamics and catastrophic states across varied source environments. Then, when exploring a new safety-critical environment with unknown dynamics, the CARL agent plans to avoid actions that could lead to catastrophic states. In experiments on car driving, cartpole balancing, and half-cheetah locomotion, CARL successfully acquires cautious exploration behaviors, yielding higher rewards with fewer failures than strong RL adaptation baselines.

paragraphs: Learning through trial and error becomes hazardous when failures can damage an agent or its surroundings. This paper studies a setting in which an agent first learns in source environments where failures are less consequential, then adapts to a target environment where mistakes carry substantial costs. The challenge is to keep learning despite unfamiliar dynamics while exploring cautiously.

The proposed approach, CARL, uses model-based reinforcement learning across varied source environments. It trains a probabilistic model that represents uncertainty about how actions change the environment and which states are catastrophic. During adaptation, the agent uses that prior experience to assess risk and plans to avoid actions that could lead to catastrophic states.

Experiments involving driving, cartpole balancing, and half-cheetah locomotion show that CARL develops cautious exploration behaviors. It obtains higher rewards with fewer failures than strong adaptation baselines in those experiments. These results support using learned uncertainty to guide relatively safer adaptation; the claim is improved risk management, rather than a guarantee that failures cannot occur.
summary.tldr: CARL uses probabilistic models learned across source environments to adapt cautiously, achieving higher rewards with fewer failures in tested tasks.

title: Cautious Adaptation For Reinforcement Learning in Safety-Critical Settings

abstract: In previous Capsule Neural Networks (CapsNets), routing algorithms often performed clustering processes to assemble the child capsules’ representations into parent capsules. Such routing algorithms were typically implemented with iterative processes and incurred high computing complexity. This paper presents a new capsule structure, which contains a set of optimizable receptors and a transmitter is devised on the capsule’s representation. Specifically, child capsules’ representations are sent to the parent capsules whose receptors match well the transmitters of the child capsules’ representations, avoiding applying computationally complex routing algorithms. To ensure the receptors in a CapsNet work cooperatively, we build a skeleton to organize the receptors in different capsule layers in a CapsNet. The receptor skeleton assigns a share-out objective for each receptor, making the CapsNet perform as a hierarchical agglomerative clustering process. Comprehensive experiments verify that our approach facilitates efficient clustering processes, and CapsNets with our approach significantly outperform CapsNets with previous routing algorithms on image classification, affine transformation generalization, overlapped object recognition, and representation semantic decoupling.

paragraphs: Capsule neural networks assemble representations from child capsules into parent capsules. Earlier approaches often make these assignments through repeated clustering steps, creating substantial computational work. This paper changes the capsule structure so that the assignment can happen through learned matching, addressing the cost of routing while retaining the idea of building larger representations from smaller ones.

Each capsule contains adjustable receptors, and each child representation has a transmitter. A child sends its representation to parents whose receptors match its transmitter well. The authors also introduce a receptor skeleton that coordinates receptors across layers. It gives each receptor an assigned share of the overall objective, organizing the network into a hierarchical clustering process.

Experiments support both efficient clustering and better performance than capsule networks using earlier routing algorithms. The reported improvements cover image classification, generalization to affine transformations, recognition of overlapping objects, and separation of semantic information within representations. Together, these findings suggest that coordinating learned routing components can improve both computational efficiency and the representations produced by capsule networks.
summary.tldr: Learned receptors and a coordinating skeleton replace costly iterative capsule routing and improve results across several visual tasks.

title: A Receptor Skeleton for Capsule Neural Networks

abstract: In the vanishing learning rate regime, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is now relatively well understood. In this work, we propose to study the basic properties of SGD and its variants in the non-vanishing learning rate regime. The focus is on deriving exactly solvable results and discussing their implications. The main contributions of this work are to derive the stationary distribution for discrete-time SGD in a quadratic loss function with and without momentum; in particular, one implication of our result is that the fluctuation caused by discrete-time dynamics takes a distorted shape and is dramatically larger than a continuous-time theory could predict. Examples of applications of the proposed theory considered in this work include the approximation error of variants of SGD, the effect of minibatch noise, the optimal Bayesian inference, the escape rate from a sharp minimum, and the stationary covariance of a few second-order methods including damped Newton’s method, natural gradient descent, and Adam.

paragraphs: Many theoretical descriptions of stochastic gradient descent focus on learning rates that approach zero. This paper instead examines what happens when the learning rate remains finite. Its goal is to obtain exactly solvable results that expose properties of the discrete training dynamics and clarify their consequences.

The main result derives the stationary distribution of discrete-time SGD on a quadratic loss, both with and without momentum. This distribution describes the fluctuations that persist in the analyzed dynamics. One implication is that discrete updates can produce fluctuations with a distorted shape and a much greater size than a continuous-time theory would predict.

The paper discusses applications to approximation errors in SGD variants, minibatch noise, optimal Bayesian inference, and escape rates from sharp minima. It also considers stationary covariance for methods including damped Newton updates, natural gradient descent, and Adam. The quadratic-loss setting is central to the exact stationary-distribution result. Within that setting, the analysis demonstrates why retaining finite-step effects can materially change conclusions about optimization noise, rather than treating those effects as negligible details.
summary.tldr: Exact quadratic-loss analysis shows that finite-step SGD fluctuations can be much larger and differently shaped than continuous-time predictions.

title: Noise and Fluctuation of Finite Learning Rate Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: \emph{Unlabeled sensing} is a recent problem encompassing many data science and engineering applications and typically formulated as solving linear equations whose right-hand side vector has undergone an unknown permutation. It was generalized to the \emph{homomorphic sensing} problem by replacing the unknown permutation with an unknown linear map from a given finite set of linear maps. In this paper we present tighter and simpler conditions for the homomorphic sensing problem to admit a unique solution. We show that this solution is locally stable under noise, while under a sparsity assumption it remains unique under less demanding conditions. Sparsity in the context of unlabeled sensing leads to the problem of \textit{unlabeled compressed sensing}, and a consequence of our general theory is the existence under mild conditions of a unique sparsest solution. On the algorithmic level, we solve unlabeled compressed sensing by an iterative algorithm validated by synthetic data experiments. Finally, under the unifying homomorphic sensing framework we connect unlabeled sensing to other important practical problems.

paragraphs: In unlabeled sensing, linear measurements are available but their ordering has been changed by an unknown permutation. Homomorphic sensing generalizes this situation: the measurements undergo an unknown linear transformation selected from a known finite set. The central question is when the original signal remains uniquely recoverable despite uncertainty about that transformation.

The paper gives simpler and tighter conditions for a unique solution and shows that the solution is locally stable under noise. It also establishes that sparsity allows uniqueness under less demanding conditions. Here sparsity means that the signal has only a limited number of nonzero components, providing additional structure for resolving the measurement ambiguity.

Applying this theory to unlabeled compressed sensing yields, under mild conditions, the existence of a unique sparsest solution. The authors also present an iterative algorithm for that problem and validate it with synthetic experiments. Finally, they use the general framework to connect unlabeled sensing with other practical problems. The results distinguish theoretical recoverability and local noise stability from the separate empirical validation of an algorithm.
summary.tldr: The paper strengthens uniqueness and local noise-stability results for sensing with unknown transformations, including improved conditions for sparse signals.

title: Homomorphic Sensing: Sparsity and Noise

abstract: Transformer is a ubiquitous model for natural language processing and has attracted wide attentions in computer vision. The attention maps are indispensable for a transformer model to encode the dependencies among input tokens. However, they are learned independently in each layer and sometimes fail to capture precise patterns. In this paper, we propose a novel and generic mechanism based on evolving attention to improve the performance of transformers. On one hand, the attention maps in different layers share common knowledge, thus the ones in preceding layers can instruct the attention in succeeding layers through residual connections. On the other hand, low-level and high-level attentions vary in the level of abstraction, so we adopt convolutional layers to model the evolutionary process of attention maps. The proposed evolving attention mechanism achieves significant performance improvement over various state-of-the-art models for multiple tasks, including image classification, natural language understanding and machine translation.

paragraphs: Attention maps describe dependencies among the input tokens processed by a transformer. This paper starts from the observation that learning these maps independently at each layer can sometimes miss precise patterns. It proposes a general mechanism that lets attention develop across layers, using information from earlier maps to help construct later ones.

The design combines two ideas. Residual connections carry attention information forward because maps at different depths share useful knowledge. Convolutional layers model how those maps should change because early and late attention operate at different levels of abstraction. Together, these components allow preceding layers to inform subsequent attention while also accommodating changes in the relationships being represented.

The authors report significant improvements over various state-of-the-art models across image classification, natural language understanding, and machine translation. These results support the usefulness of the evolving-attention mechanism across both vision and language tasks. The architectural contribution is to make the relationship between successive attention maps an explicit part of the model, with both continuity and transformation built into that relationship.
summary.tldr: Residual connections and convolutions let transformer attention maps evolve across layers, improving performance on several vision and language tasks.

title: Evolving Attention with Residual Convolutions

abstract: We study the off-policy evaluation (OPE) problem in an infinite-horizon Markov decision process with continuous states and actions. We recast the $Q$-function estimation into a special form of the nonparametric instrumental variables (NPIV) estimation problem. We first show that under one mild condition the NPIV formulation of $Q$-function estimation is well-posed in the sense of $L^2$-measure of ill-posedness with respect to the data generating distribution, bypassing a strong assumption on the discount factor $\gamma$ imposed in the recent literature for obtaining the $L^2$ convergence rates of various $Q$-function estimators. Thanks to this new well-posed property, we derive the first minimax lower bounds for the convergence rates of nonparametric estimation of $Q$-function and its derivatives in both sup-norm and $L^2$-norm, which are shown to be the same as those for the classical nonparametric regression (Stone, 1982). We then propose a sieve two-stage least squares estimator and establish its rate-optimality in both norms under some mild conditions. Our general results on the well-posedness and the minimax lower bounds are of independent interest to study not only other nonparametric estimators for $Q$-function but also efficient estimation on the value of any target policy in off-policy settings.

The authors recast this task as a special nonparametric instrumental-variables estimation problem, creating a route to analyze its statistical difficulty.

summary.tldr: An instrumental-variables formulation yields conditional well-posedness results and optimal nonparametric rates for off-policy Q-function estimation.

title: On Well-posedness and Minimax Optimal Rates of Nonparametric Q-function Estimation in Off-policy Evaluation

abstract: We demonstrate that co-training (Blum & Mitchell, 1998) can improve the performance of prompt-based learning by using unlabeled data. While prompting has emerged as a promising paradigm for few-shot and zero-shot learning, it is often brittle and requires much larger models compared to the standard supervised setup. We find that co-training makes it possible to improve the original prompt model and at the same time learn a smaller, downstream task-specific model. In the case where we only have partial access to a prompt model (e.g., output probabilities from GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020)) we learn a calibration model over the prompt outputs. When we have full access to the prompt model’s gradients but full finetuning remains prohibitively expensive (e.g., T0 (Sanh et al., 2021)), we learn a set of soft prompt continuous vectors to iteratively update the prompt model. We find that models trained in this manner can significantly improve performance on challenging datasets where there is currently a large gap between prompt-based learning and fully-supervised models.

paragraphs: Prompt-based learning can work with few or no labeled examples, but it can be brittle and require large models. This paper investigates whether unlabeled data can improve that situation through co-training. The proposed process improves the original prompt model while also learning a smaller model specialized for the downstream task.

The adaptation mechanism depends on the access available to the prompt model. When only outputs such as GPT-3 probabilities are accessible, the authors learn a calibration model over those outputs. When gradients are accessible but full fine-tuning is too costly, as in their T0 setting, they instead learn continuous soft-prompt vectors that iteratively update the prompt model’s behavior.

The authors report significant improvements on challenging datasets where prompting initially trails fully supervised learning by a large margin. The findings show how co-training can use unlabeled data under two distinct access constraints. They also give the process two useful outcomes: a stronger prompting system and a smaller task-specific model learned alongside it.
summary.tldr: Co-training with unlabeled data improves prompt-based models while training smaller task-specific models under different levels of model access.

title: Co-training Improves Prompt-based Learning for Large Language Models

abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) in contextual bandits has seen rapid adoption in real-world systems, since it enables offline evaluation of new policies using only historic log data. Unfortunately, when the number of actions is large, existing OPE estimators – most of which are based on inverse propensity score weighting – degrade severely and can suffer from extreme bias and variance. This foils the use of OPE in many applications from recommender systems to language models. To overcome this issue, we propose a new OPE estimator that leverages marginalized importance weights when action embeddings provide structure in the action space. We characterize the bias, variance, and mean squared error of the proposed estimator and analyze the conditions under which the action embedding provides statistical benefits over conventional estimators. In addition to the theoretical analysis, we find that the empirical performance improvement can be substantial, enabling reliable OPE even when existing estimators collapse due to a large number of actions.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new decision policy would perform using historical logs rather than deploying it. In contextual bandits, commonly used estimators rely on inverse propensity weighting. When there are many possible actions, these estimators can suffer severe bias and variance, making offline policy comparisons unreliable.

The proposed estimator uses action embeddings to exploit structure among the available actions. It replaces conventional importance weights with marginalized importance weights. The authors analyze the resulting bias, variance, and mean squared error, and identify conditions under which the embedding provides statistical advantages over conventional estimators. The benefit therefore depends on how the embedding supports the evaluation problem.

Experiments show that the improvement can be substantial, with reliable evaluation in large-action settings where existing estimators break down. The contribution connects a representation of actions to the statistical properties of policy evaluation. This matters for applications with many choices, such as recommendation and language modeling, where collecting logs alone does not ensure that a new policy can be evaluated accurately.
summary.tldr: An embedding-based estimator can make offline policy evaluation more reliable in large action spaces by using marginalized importance weights.

title: Off-Policy Evaluation for Large Action Spaces via Embeddings

abstract: Domain generalization asks for models trained over a set of training environments to perform well in unseen test environments. Recently, a series of algorithms such as Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) has been proposed for domain generalization. However, Rosenfeld et al. (2021) shows that in a simple linear data model, even if non-convexity issues are ignored, IRM and its extensions cannot generalize to unseen environments with less than $d_s+1$ training environments, where $d_s$ is the dimension of the spurious-feature subspace. In this paper, we propose to achieve domain generalization with Invariant-feature Subspace Recovery (ISR). Our first algorithm, ISR-Mean, can identify the subspace spanned by invariant features from the first-order moments of the class-conditional distributions, and achieve provable domain generalization with $d_s+1$ training environments under the data model of Rosenfeld et al. (2021). Our second algorithm, ISR-Cov, further reduces the required number of training environments to $O(1)$ using the information of second-order moments. Notably, unlike IRM, our algorithms bypass non-convexity issues and enjoy global convergence guarantees. Empirically, our ISRs can obtain superior performance compared with IRM on synthetic benchmarks. In addition, on three real-world image and text datasets, we show that both ISRs can be used as simple yet effective post-processing methods to improve the worst-case accuracy of (pre-)trained models against spurious correlations and group shifts.
