The results combine model-specific theoretical guarantees with evidence that recovering invariant structure can improve existing representations in practical datasets.
summary.tldr: Invariant-feature Subspace Recovery uses distribution moments to obtain domain-generalization guarantees and improve reported worst-case accuracy under spurious correlations.

title: Provable Domain Generalization via Invariant-Feature Subspace Recovery

abstract: Unsupervised/self-supervised time series representation learning is a challenging problem because of its complex dynamics and sparse annotations. Existing works mainly adopt the framework of contrastive learning with the time-based augmentation techniques to sample positives and negatives for contrastive training. Nevertheless, they mostly use segment-level augmentation derived from time slicing, which may bring about sampling bias and incorrect optimization with false negatives due to the loss of global context. Besides, they all pay no attention to incorporate the spectral information in feature representation. In this paper, we propose a unified framework, namely Bilinear Temporal-Spectral Fusion (BTSF). Specifically, we firstly utilize the instance-level augmentation with a simple dropout on the entire time series for maximally capturing long-term dependencies. We devise a novel iterative bilinear temporal-spectral fusion to explicitly encode the affinities of abundant time-frequency pairs, and iteratively refines representations in a fusion-and-squeeze manner with Spectrum-to-Time (S2T) and Time-to-Spectrum (T2S) Aggregation modules. We firstly conducts downstream evaluations on three major tasks for time series including classification, forecasting and anomaly detection. Experimental results shows that our BTSF consistently significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.
originalAbstract: Unsupervised/self-supervised time series representation learning is a challenging problem because of its complex dynamics and sparse annotations. Existing works mainly adopt the framework of contrastive learning with the time-based augmentation techniques to sample positives and negatives for contrastive training. Nevertheless, they mostly use segment-level augmentation derived from time slicing, which may bring about sampling bias and incorrect optimization with false negatives due to the loss of global context. Besides, they all pay no attention to incorporate the spectral information in feature representation. In this paper, we propose a unified framework, namely Bilinear Temporal-Spectral Fusion (BTSF). Specifically, we firstly utilize the instance-level augmentation with a simple dropout on the entire time series for maximally capturing long-term dependencies. We devise a novel iterative bilinear temporal-spectral fusion to explicitly encode the affinities of abundant time-frequency pairs, and iteratively refines representations in a fusion-and-squeeze manner with Spectrum-to-Time (S2T) and Time-to-Spectrum (T2S) Aggregation modules. We firstly conducts downstream evaluations on three major tasks for time series including classification, forecasting and anomaly detection. Experimental results shows that our BTSF consistently significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Learning time-series representations without labels is difficult because the data have complex dynamics. The authors identify two weaknesses in existing contrastive approaches: slicing a series into segments can discard global context and create false negative pairs, while spectral information is left out of the learned representation.

Bilinear Temporal-Spectral Fusion, or BTSF, uses dropout over the entire time series to create augmented instances while retaining access to long-term context. It then explicitly models relationships between time and frequency information through an iterative bilinear fusion mechanism. Spectrum-to-Time and Time-to-Spectrum aggregation modules repeatedly exchange information and refine the representation through a fusion-and-squeeze process.

The design combines two responses to the identified weaknesses: whole-series augmentation addresses the loss of context, and temporal-spectral fusion incorporates information from both views of the signal. Evaluation spans classification, forecasting, and anomaly detection, testing the representations across three major downstream uses. The authors report consistent, significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in these experiments, supporting the usefulness of the unified representation-learning framework.
summary.tldr: BTSF combines whole-series augmentation with iterative time–frequency fusion to improve unsupervised representations across classification, forecasting, and anomaly detection.

title: Unsupervised Time-Series Representation Learning with Iterative Bilinear Temporal-Spectral Fusion

abstract: In real-world recommendation problems, especially those with a formidably large item space, users have to gradually learn to estimate the utility of any fresh recommendations from their experience about previously consumed items. This in turn affects their interaction dynamics with the system and can invalidate previous algorithms built on the omniscient user assumption. In this paper, we formalize a model to capture such ”learning users” and design an efficient system-side learning solution, coined Noise-Robust Active Ellipsoid Search (RAES), to confront the challenges brought by the non-stationary feedback from such a learning user. Interestingly, we prove that the regret of RAES deteriorates gracefully as the convergence rate of user learning becomes worse, until reaching linear regret when the user’s learning fails to converge. Experiments on synthetic datasets demonstrate the strength of RAES for such a contemporaneous system-user learning problem. Our study provides a novel perspective on modeling the feedback loop in recommendation problems.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems often act as though users already know how useful each possible item would be. With a very large item space, users may instead learn about their own expected benefits through experience. Their feedback then changes as they learn, creating a moving target for a recommendation system that is also trying to learn.

The paper formalizes this learning-user setting and introduces Noise-Robust Active Ellipsoid Search, or RAES. The algorithm is designed to handle feedback that is nonstationary because the user’s estimates are evolving. This makes the interaction a joint learning problem: the system’s observations depend partly on the user’s current stage of learning.

The authors prove that RAES’s regret, a measure of accumulated recommendation shortfall, worsens gracefully as the user’s learning converges more slowly. If user learning fails to converge, regret reaches linear growth. Synthetic-data experiments demonstrate the method’s strength in this setting. The result links recommendation quality directly to the pace of user learning and highlights why feedback dynamics matter when modeling recommendation interactions.
summary.tldr: RAES learns recommendations from evolving user feedback, with regret guarantees that depend on how quickly the user learns.

title: Learning from a Learning User for Optimal Recommendations

abstract: Model compression is an essential technique for deploying deep neural networks (DNNs) on power and memory-constrained resources. However, existing model-compression methods often rely on human expertise and focus on parameters’ local importance, ignoring the rich topology information within DNNs. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-stage graph embedding technique based on graph neural networks (GNNs) to identify DNN topologies and use reinforcement learning (RL) to find a suitable compression policy. We performed resource-constrained (i.e., FLOPs) channel pruning and compared our approach with state-of-the-art model compression methods. We evaluated our method on various models from typical to mobile-friendly networks, such as ResNet family, VGG-16, MobileNet-v1/v2, and ShuffleNet. Results show that our method can achieve higher compression ratios with a minimal fine-tuning cost yet yields outstanding and competitive performance.

paragraphs: Compressing neural networks helps make them usable on devices with limited memory and power. Many compression methods rely on expert decisions or assess parameters through local importance, leaving network connectivity underused. This paper proposes making the network’s topology an explicit input to the process of deciding how to compress it.

The approach uses a multistage graph embedding technique based on graph neural networks to represent deep network topology. Reinforcement learning then uses this information to find a suitable compression policy. The experiments focus on channel pruning under a floating-point-operation constraint, tying the removal decisions to a defined computational resource budget.

The authors compare against state-of-the-art compression methods across conventional and mobile-oriented architectures, including the ResNet family, VGG-16, MobileNet-v1/v2, and ShuffleNet. Results show higher compression ratios with minimal fine-tuning cost and competitive predictive performance. The findings support using structural information to guide pruning across different network families. The practical contribution is a learned connection between how a network is organized and which compression decisions work well under a computation constraint.
summary.tldr: Graph-based topology representations guide reinforcement learning to select effective channel-pruning policies under computational constraints.

title: Topology-Aware Network Pruning using Multi-stage Graph Embedding and Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Many modern high-performing machine learning models increasingly rely on scaling up models, e.g., transformer networks. Simultaneously, a parallel line of work aims to improve the model performance by augmenting an input instance with other (labeled) instances during inference. Examples of such augmentations include task-specific prompts and similar examples retrieved from the training data by a nonparametric component. Despite a growing literature showcasing the promise of these retrieval-based models, their theoretical underpinnings %for such models remain under-explored. In this paper, we present a formal treatment of retrieval-based models to characterize their performance via a novel statistical perspective. In particular, we study two broad classes of retrieval-based classification approaches: First, we analyze a local learning framework that employs an explicit local empirical risk minimization based on retrieved examples for each input instance. Interestingly, we show that breaking down the underlying learning task into local sub-tasks enables the model to employ a low complexity parametric component to ensure good overall performance. The second class of retrieval-based approaches we explore learns a global model using kernel methods to directly map an input instance and retrieved examples to a prediction, without explicitly solving a local learning task.

paragraphs: Retrieval-based models improve predictions by bringing relevant examples into the decision process. Instead of relying entirely on information stored in model parameters, they can consult labeled instances associated with the current input. This paper develops a statistical account of such classification methods, addressing the gap between their practical promise and the theory explaining their performance.

The first approach explicitly solves a local learning problem for each input. Retrieved examples supply the data for local empirical risk minimization: choosing a predictor that performs well on that nearby collection. The analysis shows that dividing the overall task into local subtasks can allow a relatively simple parametric component to achieve good overall performance.

The second approach uses kernel methods to learn one global predictor that takes both the input and its retrieved examples into account. It does not separately fit a local predictor for every query. Together, the two analyses distinguish retrieval as a way to organize local learning from retrieval as additional information for a global prediction rule.
summary.tldr: A statistical analysis explains how retrieved examples can support classification through either simple local learners or a global kernel-based predictor.

title: A Statistical Perspective on Retrieval-Based Models

abstract: In order to improve reproducibility, deep reinforcement learning (RL) has been adopting better scientific practices such as standardized evaluation metrics and reporting. However, the process of hyperparameter optimization still varies widely across papers, which makes it challenging to compare RL algorithms fairly. In this paper, we show that hyperparameter choices in RL can significantly affect the agent’s final performance and sample efficiency, and that the hyperparameter landscape can strongly depend on the tuning seed which may lead to overfitting. We therefore propose adopting established best practices from AutoML, such as the separation of tuning and testing seeds, as well as principled hyperparameter optimization (HPO) across a broad search space. We support this by comparing multiple state-of-the-art HPO tools on a range of RL algorithms and environments to their hand-tuned counterparts, demonstrating that HPO approaches often have higher performance and lower compute overhead. As a result of our findings, we recommend a set of best practices for the RL community, which should result in stronger empirical results with fewer computational costs, better reproducibility, and thus faster progress. In order to encourage the adoption of these practices, we provide plug-and-play implementations of the tuning algorithms used in this paper at https://github.com/facebookresearch/how-to-autorl.

paragraphs: Comparing reinforcement learning algorithms fairly requires attention to how their settings are chosen. The paper shows that hyperparameters can substantially affect both final performance and sample efficiency. It also finds that which settings look good can depend strongly on the random seed used during tuning, creating a risk of overfitting to that seed.

The authors recommend established automated machine learning practices, including separating tuning seeds from testing seeds and using principled hyperparameter optimization over a broad search space. Separating these stages makes evaluation less dependent on the particular randomness that guided the settings search.

The study compares multiple leading optimization tools with hand-tuned configurations across reinforcement learning algorithms and environments. Automated approaches often achieve better performance with lower computational overhead. Based on these findings, the paper proposes community practices intended to improve reproducibility, strengthen empirical comparisons, and reduce computational costs. It also provides ready-to-use implementations of the tuning methods to make adopting these practices easier.
summary.tldr: Principled hyperparameter optimization and separate tuning and testing seeds can improve reinforcement learning evaluation, with automated tuning often outperforming hand-tuned configurations.

title: Hyperparameters in Reinforcement Learning and How To Tune Them

abstract: Multivariate time series data for real-world applications typically contain a significant amount of missing values. The dominant approach for classification with such missing values is to impute them heuristically with specific values (zero, mean, values of adjacent time-steps) or learnable parameters. However, these simple strategies do not take the data generative process into account, and more importantly, do not effectively capture the uncertainty in prediction due to the multiple possibilities for the missing values. In this paper, we propose a novel probabilistic framework for classification with multivariate time series data with missing values. Our model consists of two parts; a deep generative model for missing value imputation and a classifier. Extending the existing deep generative models to better capture structures of time-series data, our deep generative model part is trained to impute the missing values in multiple plausible ways, effectively modeling the uncertainty of the imputation. The classifier part takes the time series data along with the imputed missing values and classifies signals, and is trained to capture the predictive uncertainty due to the multiple possibilities of imputations. Importantly, we show that naïvely combining the generative model and the classifier could result in trivial solutions where the generative model does not produce meaningful imputations. To resolve this, we present a novel regularization technique that can promote the model to produce useful imputation values that help classification. Through extensive experiments on real-world time series data with missing values, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Missing observations in multivariate time series can admit several plausible values. Filling each gap with a single fixed or learned value can overlook this ambiguity and its effect on classification. This paper develops a probabilistic framework that represents multiple plausible completions and carries the resulting uncertainty into the prediction process.

The model combines a deep generative component with a classifier. The generative component is adapted to capture time-series structure and produce alternative imputations for missing values. The classifier uses the completed signals and is trained to capture uncertainty in its predictions arising from those different possibilities.

The authors show that simply combining these components can produce trivial solutions in which the imputations are not meaningful. They introduce a regularization technique to encourage useful imputations that help classification. Experiments on real-world time series with missing data demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution joins uncertainty-aware completion with classification while addressing a specific failure mode in learning the two components together.
summary.tldr: A regularized generative model and classifier account for multiple plausible imputations when classifying incomplete time series.

title: Probabilistic Imputation for Time-series Classification with Missing Data

abstract: In this paper, we propose an adaptive entropy-regularization framework (ADER) for multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) to learn the adequate amount of exploration of each agent for entropy-based exploration. In order to derive a metric for the proper level of exploration entropy for each agent, we disentangle the soft value function into two types: one for pure return and the other for entropy. By applying multi-agent value factorization to the disentangled value function of pure return, we obtain a metric to determine the relevant level of exploration entropy for each agent, given by the partial derivative of the pure-return value function with respect to (w.r.t.) the policy entropy of each agent. Based on this metric, we propose the ADER algorithm based on maximum entropy RL, which controls the necessary level of exploration across agents over time by learning the proper target entropy for each agent. Experimental results show that the proposed scheme significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art multi-agent RL algorithms.

paragraphs: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, exploration is a decision for every agent, and the useful amount can change during learning. This paper introduces ADER, a framework that learns an exploration target for each agent. It focuses on entropy-based exploration, where greater policy entropy corresponds to a wider spread of possible action choices.

The central step is to separate the soft value function into a component measuring return and another measuring entropy. The authors then apply multi-agent value factorization to the return component. This yields a metric based on how the pure-return value changes with an individual agent’s policy entropy. That sensitivity provides a basis for determining how much exploration is relevant for each agent.

ADER uses this metric within maximum-entropy reinforcement learning to learn individual target entropies over time. The approach therefore connects exploration levels to their relationship with return, rather than treating exploration as a single shared quantity. Experiments report significant improvements over current state-of-the-art multi-agent reinforcement-learning algorithms in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: ADER adapts each agent’s exploration by learning target entropies from how exploration relates to collective return.

title: An Adaptive Entropy-Regularization Framework for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Diffusion-based methods, represented as stochastic differential equations on a continuous-time domain, have recently proven successful as non-adversarial generative models. Training such models relies on denoising score matching, which can be seen as multi-scale denoising autoencoders. Here, we augment the denoising score matching framework to enable representation learning without any supervised signal. GANs and VAEs learn representations by directly transforming latent codes to data samples. In contrast, the introduced diffusion-based representation learning relies on a new formulation of the denoising score matching objective and thus encodes the information needed for denoising. We illustrate how this difference allows for manual control of the level of details encoded in the representation. Using the same approach, we propose to learn an infinite-dimensional latent code that achieves improvements on state-of-the-art models on semi-supervised image classification. We also compare the quality of learned representations of diffusion score matching with other methods like autoencoder and contrastively trained systems through their performances on downstream tasks. Finally, we also ablate with a different SDE formulation for diffusion models and show that the benefits on downstream tasks are still present on changing the underlying differential equation.

paragraphs: Diffusion models learn to generate data through a denoising process. This paper adapts their training objective so that the same framework can learn useful representations without supervised labels. The starting point is denoising score matching, viewed as learning to remove noise at multiple scales.

The proposed formulation encodes information needed for denoising. This differs from the direct latent-code-to-data transformation used by GANs and variational autoencoders. The authors show how the denoising formulation allows manual control over the amount of detail captured in a representation. They also extend the approach to learning an infinite-dimensional latent code.

That extension improves on state-of-the-art models for semi-supervised image classification in the reported evaluation. The paper also assesses representations through downstream tasks, comparing them with autoencoder and contrastive approaches. Finally, changing the stochastic differential equation underlying the diffusion model preserves downstream benefits in an ablation. This supports the usefulness of the representation-learning approach across the tested diffusion formulations.
summary.tldr: A revised diffusion training objective learns unsupervised representations with controllable detail and improves reported semi-supervised classification results.

title: Diffusion Based Representation Learning

abstract: We develop techniques for synthesizing neurosymbolic programs. Such programs mix discrete symbolic processing with continuous neural computation. We relax this mixed discrete/continuous problem and jointly learn all modules with gradient descent, and also incorporate amortized inference, overparameterization, and a differentiable strategy for penalizing lengthy programs. Collectedly this toolbox improves the stability of gradient-guided program search, and suggests ways of learning both how to parse continuous input into discrete abstractions, and how to process those abstractions via symbolic code.

Collectedly this toolbox improves the stability of gradient-guided program search, and suggests ways of learning both how to parse continuous input into discrete abstractions, and how to process those abstractions via symbolic code.

paragraphs: Neurosymbolic programs combine continuous neural computation with discrete symbolic operations. Learning such programs involves deciding both how to interpret continuous input and how symbolic processing should act on the resulting abstractions. This paper develops a collection of techniques for searching over that mixed kind of program.

The authors relax the discrete and continuous optimization problem so that all modules can be learned jointly through gradient descent. Their toolbox also includes amortized inference, overparameterization, and a differentiable penalty for lengthy programs. Making the length penalty differentiable allows the preference for shorter programs to participate in the same gradient-guided learning process.

Taken together, these techniques improve the stability of gradient-guided program search. The stated significance extends to learning the connection between perception and symbolic computation: how continuous inputs can become discrete abstractions, and how code can process those abstractions. The abstract presents these capabilities as directions suggested by the toolbox, while its direct finding is improved stability of the search process.
summary.tldr: A differentiable toolbox improves the stability of searching for programs that combine neural perception with symbolic computation.

title: From Perception to Programs: Regularize, Overparameterize, and Amortize

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have tremendous potential for grounding language, and thus enabling language-conditioned agents (LCAs) to perform diverse tasks specified with text. This has motivated the study of LCAs based on reinforcement learning (RL) with rewards given by rendering images of an environment and evaluating those images with VLMs. If single-task RL is employed, such approaches are limited by the cost and time required to train a policy for each new task. Multi-task RL (MTRL) is a natural alternative, but requires a carefully designed corpus of training tasks and does not always generalize reliably to new tasks. Therefore, this paper introduces a novel decomposition of the problem of building an LCA: first find an environment configuration that has a high VLM score for text describing a task; then use a (pretrained) goal-conditioned policy to reach that configuration. We also explore several enhancements to the speed and quality of VLM-based LCAs, notably, the use of distilled models, and the evaluation of configurations from multiple viewpoints to resolve the ambiguities inherent in a single 2D view. We demonstrate our approach on the Humanoid environment, showing that it results in LCAs that outperform MTRL baselines in zero-shot generalization, without requiring any textual task descriptions or other forms of environment-specific annotation during training.

paragraphs: A language-conditioned agent must connect a textual request to behavior in an environment. One approach scores rendered images with a vision-language model and uses those scores as reinforcement learning rewards. Training a separate policy for every task is costly, while multi-task training requires a suitable task collection and can generalize unreliably.

This paper separates interpreting the request from executing it. First, it searches for an environment configuration whose rendered appearance receives a high score for the task description. Then a pretrained goal-conditioned policy moves the agent toward that configuration. The language model supplies a target, while the policy supplies the ability to reach it.

The authors also explore distilled models and scoring configurations from multiple viewpoints. Multiple views address ambiguities that arise when a configuration is judged through just one two-dimensional image. In the Humanoid environment, the resulting agents outperform multi-task reinforcement learning baselines on zero-shot generalization. Their training requires neither textual task descriptions nor other environment-specific annotations, demonstrating this separation of language interpretation and control in the tested setting.
summary.tldr: The method turns language requests into visually scored target configurations that a pretrained goal-conditioned policy can reach.

title: Bridging Environments and Language with Rendering Functions and Vision-Language Models

abstract: Preference-based Reinforcement Learning (PbRL) circumvents the need for reward engineering by harnessing human preferences as the reward signal. However, current PbRL methods excessively depend on high-quality feedback from domain experts, which results in a lack of robustness. In this paper, we present RIME, a robust PbRL algorithm for effective reward learning from noisy preferences. Our method utilizes a sample selection-based discriminator to dynamically filter out noise and ensure robust training. To counteract the cumulative error stemming from incorrect selection, we suggest a warm start for the reward model, which additionally bridges the performance gap during the transition from pre-training to online training in PbRL. Our experiments on robotic manipulation and locomotion tasks demonstrate that RIME significantly enhances the robustness of the state-of-the-art PbRL method. Code is available at https://github.com/CJReinforce/RIME_ICML2024.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning uses human judgments to learn rewards, reducing the need to hand-design a reward function. Its reliability can suffer when feedback is noisy, especially if a method depends heavily on high-quality expert preferences. RIME addresses this problem by making reward learning more robust to imperfect judgments.

The algorithm uses a sample-selection discriminator that dynamically filters noise from the preference data. However, selection itself can make mistakes, and those mistakes can accumulate. RIME therefore includes a warm start for the reward model to counteract this error buildup. The warm start also helps bridge the performance gap between pre-training and online training.

Experiments on robotic manipulation and locomotion show that RIME significantly improves the robustness of a state-of-the-art preference-based reinforcement-learning method. The contribution couples noise filtering with a response to the filtering process's own errors. This matters because reliable learning requires more than rejecting suspicious feedback: the reward model also needs a sufficiently stable starting point for the transition into online learning.
summary.tldr: RIME combines dynamic preference filtering with a warm-started reward model to improve robustness to noisy human feedback.

title: RIME: Robust Preference-based Reinforcement Learning with Noisy Preferences

abstract: Kahneman & Tversky’s $\textit{prospect theory}$ tells us that humans perceive random variables in a biased but well-defined manner (1992); for example, humans are famously loss-averse. We show that objectives for aligning LLMs with human feedback implicitly incorporate many of these biases—the success of these objectives (e.g., DPO) over cross-entropy minimization can partly be ascribed to them belonging to a family of loss functions that we call $\textit{human-aware losses}$ (HALOs). However, the utility functions these methods attribute to humans still differ from those in the prospect theory literature. Using a Kahneman-Tversky model of human utility, we propose a HALO that directly maximizes the utility of generations instead of maximizing the log-likelihood of preferences, as current methods do. We call this approach KTO, and it matches or exceeds the performance of preference-based methods at scales from 1B to 30B, despite only learning from a binary signal of whether an output is desirable. More broadly, our work suggests that there is no one HALO that is universally superior; the best loss depends on the inductive biases most appropriate for a given setting, an oft-overlooked consideration.

paragraphs: Human judgments reflect systematic biases, including loss aversion. This paper connects such patterns, described by prospect theory, to objectives used for aligning language models with human feedback. The authors argue that part of the success of methods such as DPO comes from their membership in a family they call human-aware losses.

They also identify a mismatch between the utility functions implied by existing alignment methods and those used in prospect theory. Their proposed Kahneman-Tversky Optimization method, KTO, directly maximizes a model of the utility of generated responses. It learns from binary feedback indicating whether an output is desirable, without requiring preference comparisons between outputs.

Across model sizes from one to thirty billion parameters, KTO matches or exceeds the performance of preference-based methods in the reported evaluations. The broader conclusion is conditional: the authors suggest that no single human-aware loss is best everywhere. Choosing an objective involves choosing assumptions about human judgments, and the most useful assumptions can depend on the alignment setting.
summary.tldr: KTO uses a prospect-theory utility objective to align language models from binary desirability feedback, matching or exceeding tested preference-based methods.

title: Model Alignment as Prospect Theoretic Optimization

abstract: Graph self-supervised learning has sparked a research surge in training informative representations without accessing any labeled data. However, our understanding of graph self-supervised learning remains limited, and the inherent relationships between various self-supervised tasks are still unexplored. Our paper aims to provide a fresh understanding of graph self-supervised learning based on task correlations. Specifically, we evaluate the performance of the representations trained by one specific task on other tasks and define correlation values to quantify task correlations. Through this process, we unveil the task correlations between various self-supervised tasks and can measure their expressive capabilities, which are closely related to downstream performance. By analyzing the correlation values between tasks across various datasets, we reveal the complexity of task correlations and the limitations of existing multi-task learning methods. To obtain more capable representations, we propose Graph Task Correlation Modeling (GraphTCM) to illustrate the task correlations and utilize it to enhance graph self-supervised training. The experimental results indicate that our method significantly outperforms existing methods across various downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Graph self-supervised learning trains representations without labeled examples, but different training tasks can encourage different capabilities. This paper studies how those tasks relate to one another. Its starting point is to test whether representations learned for one task also perform well on other self-supervised tasks.

The authors turn these cross-task evaluations into correlation values. These values reveal relationships between tasks and provide a measure of representation capabilities that are closely associated with downstream performance. Examining them across datasets shows that the relationships are complex, helping explain limitations of existing approaches that combine multiple training tasks.

The proposed Graph Task Correlation Modeling method, GraphTCM, explicitly models these relationships and uses them to improve self-supervised training. Experiments report substantial gains over existing methods across multiple downstream tasks. The contribution connects an investigative tool with a training method: measuring how capabilities transfer between tasks provides information that can guide the learning of more useful graph representations, rather than treating task combinations as interchangeable.
summary.tldr: GraphTCM models how graph self-supervised tasks relate and uses those relationships to improve learned representations.

title: Exploring Correlations of Self-Supervised Tasks for Graphs

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in generating high-quality images. Recently, the open-source models represented by Stable Diffusion (SD) are thriving and are accessible for customization, giving rise to a vibrant community of creators and enthusiasts. However, the widespread availability of customized SD models has led to copyright concerns, like unauthorized model distribution and unconsented commercial use. To address it, recent works aim to let SD models output watermarked content for post-hoc forensics. Unfortunately, none of them can achieve the challenging white-box protection, wherein the malicious user can easily remove or replace the watermarking module to fail the subsequent verification. For this, we propose AquaLoRA as the first implementation under this scenario. Briefly, we merge watermark information into the U-Net of Stable Diffusion Models via a watermark LowRank Adaptation (LoRA) module in a two-stage manner. For watermark LoRA module, we devise a scaling matrix to achieve flexible message updates without retraining. To guarantee fidelity, we design Prior Preserving Fine-Tuning (PPFT) to ensure watermark learning with minimal impacts on model distribution, validated by proofs. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments and ablation studies to verify our design. Our code is available at github.com/Georgefwt/AquaLoRA.

paragraphs: Customized Stable Diffusion models raise concerns about unauthorized redistribution and commercial use. Watermarked outputs can support later verification, but a malicious user with access to a model's internals may remove or replace a separate watermarking component. AquaLoRA targets this white-box setting, where protection must account for access to the model itself.

The method incorporates watermark information into Stable Diffusion's U-Net through a two-stage process using a low-rank adaptation module. A scaling matrix allows the watermark message to change without retraining. This gives the design flexibility in what information it embeds while placing watermark information within the image-generation model.

To preserve output fidelity, the authors introduce Prior Preserving Fine-Tuning, designed to keep watermark learning from substantially changing the model's distribution. They provide proofs supporting this preservation objective and evaluate the design through experiments and ablations. The contribution is an approach to watermarking customized models under white-box access, together with mechanisms for updating messages and limiting disruption to image generation.
summary.tldr: AquaLoRA embeds updatable watermark information into Stable Diffusion's U-Net to address white-box protection while preserving generation fidelity.

title: AquaLoRA: Toward White-box Protection for Customized Stable Diffusion Models via Watermark LoRA

abstract: On-device training is essential for user personalisation and privacy. With the pervasiveness of IoT devices and microcontroller units (MCUs), this task becomes more challenging due to the constrained memory and compute resources, and the limited availability of labelled user data. Nonetheless, prior works neglect the data scarcity issue, require excessively long training time ($\textit{e.g.}$ a few hours), or induce substantial accuracy loss ($\geq$10%). In this paper, we propose TinyTrain, an on-device training approach that drastically reduces training time by selectively updating parts of the model and explicitly coping with data scarcity. TinyTrain introduces a task-adaptive sparse-update method that $\textit{dynamically}$ selects the layer/channel to update based on a multi-objective criterion that jointly captures user data, the memory, and the compute capabilities of the target device, leading to high accuracy on unseen tasks with reduced computation and memory footprint. TinyTrain outperforms vanilla fine-tuning of the entire network by 3.6-5.0% in accuracy, while reducing the backward-pass memory and computation cost by up to 1,098$\times$ and 7.68$\times$, respectively. Targeting broadly used real-world edge devices, TinyTrain achieves 9.5$\times$ faster and 3.5$\times$ more energy-efficient training over status-quo approaches, and 2.23$\times$ smaller memory footprint than SOTA methods, while remaining within the 1 MB memory envelope of MCU-grade platforms.

paragraphs: Training directly on a user's device can support personalization and privacy, but small devices have limited memory, computation, and labeled data. TinyTrain addresses these constraints together. It focuses on adapting a neural network efficiently when updating the entire network would consume too many resources or use scarce data poorly.

The method dynamically chooses which layers or channels to update. Its selection criterion considers the user's data alongside the target device's memory and compute capabilities. This makes the sparse update pattern task-adaptive and resource-aware, with the aim of preserving accuracy on unseen tasks while reducing the work required for training.

The authors report accuracy improvements of 3.6–5.0% over full-network fine-tuning, with backward-pass memory and computation reductions of up to 1,098× and 7.68×. On the tested edge devices, training is 9.5× faster and 3.5× more energy-efficient than status-quo approaches. Memory footprint is 2.23× smaller than state-of-the-art methods, while fitting within a 1 MB memory budget. These comparisons support the value of selective adaptation under tight device constraints.
summary.tldr: TinyTrain adapts selected network components to user data and device limits, improving reported accuracy while sharply reducing on-device training costs.

title: TinyTrain: Resource-Aware Task-Adaptive Sparse Training of DNNs at the Data-Scarce Edge

abstract: The difficulty of partial multi-view multi-label learning lies in coupling the consensus of multi-view data with the task relevance of multi-label classification, under the condition where partial views and labels are unavailable. In this paper, we seek to compress cross-view representation to maximize the proportion of shared information to better predict semantic tags. To achieve this, we establish a model consistent with the information bottleneck theory for learning cross-view shared representation, minimizing non-shared information while maintaining feature validity to help increase the purity of task-relevant information. Furthermore, we model multi-label prototype instances in the latent space and learn label correlations in a data-driven manner. Our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on multiple public datasets while exhibiting good compatibility with both partial and complete data. Finally, we experimentally reveal the importance of condensing shared information under the premise of information balancing, in the process of multi-view information encoding and compression.

paragraphs: Multi-view, multi-label learning combines several views of an example to predict multiple semantic tags. The challenge becomes harder when some views and labels are missing. This paper asks how to preserve useful agreement across views while ensuring that the shared representation remains relevant to the labels being predicted.

The method uses an information-bottleneck-based model to compress cross-view representations. It reduces information that is not shared across views while retaining valid features, aiming to increase the proportion of task-relevant information. It also represents multi-label prototype instances in latent space and learns label correlations from data, connecting the shared representation to relationships among the prediction targets.

The authors report better performance than existing state-of-the-art methods on multiple public datasets, with compatibility across both incomplete and complete data. Their experiments also emphasize that condensing shared information requires balancing what information is retained. The contribution therefore combines representation compression and prototype modeling, with evidence that concentrating shared information can improve classification when the process preserves useful predictive content.
summary.tldr: The method combines shared-information compression with latent prototypes to predict multiple labels despite missing views and labels.

title: Partial Multi-View Multi-Label Classification via Semantic Invariance Learning and Prototype Modeling

abstract: The Linearized Laplace Approximation (LLA) has been recently used to perform uncertainty estimation on the predictions of pre-trained deep neural networks (DNNs). However, its widespread application is hindered by significant computational costs, particularly in scenarios with a large number of training points or DNN parameters. Consequently, additional approximations of LLA, such as Kronecker-factored or diagonal approximate GGN matrices, are utilized, potentially compromising the model’s performance. To address these challenges, we propose a new method for approximating LLA using a variational sparse Gaussian Process (GP). Our method is based on the dual RKHS formulation of GPs and retains as the predictive mean the output of the original DNN. Furthermore, it allows for efficient stochastic optimization, which results in sub-linear training time in the size of the training dataset. Specifically, its training cost is independent of the number of training points. We compare our proposed method against accelerated LLA (ELLA), which relies on the Nyström approximation, as well as other LLA variants employing the sample-then-optimize principle. Experimental results, both on regression and classification datasets, show that our method outperforms these already existing efficient variants of LLA, both in terms of the quality of the predictive distribution and in terms of total computational time.

paragraphs: The Linearized Laplace Approximation adds predictive uncertainty estimates to pretrained neural networks, but its computational cost can grow burdensome with dataset size or parameter count. Existing shortcuts introduce additional approximations that may compromise performance. This paper proposes a variational sparse Gaussian-process approach to making the approximation more efficient.

The method uses a dual reproducing-kernel Hilbert-space formulation of Gaussian processes and preserves the original neural network’s output as the predictive mean. It also supports efficient stochastic optimization. The authors report sublinear training time with respect to dataset size and, more specifically, a training cost independent of the number of training points.

Experiments on regression and classification compare the method with accelerated LLA, which uses a Nyström approximation, and other efficient variants based on sample-then-optimize procedures. The proposed approach improves both predictive-distribution quality and total computation time in those comparisons. Its contribution is therefore a more efficient route to uncertainty estimation that retains the pretrained network’s mean prediction while improving the reported uncertainty–computation balance.
summary.tldr: A variational sparse Gaussian-process approximation makes Linearized Laplace uncertainty estimation faster while preserving the original network’s predictive mean.

title: Variational Linearized Laplace Approximation for Bayesian Deep Learning

abstract: In the emergency department (ED), patients undergo triage and multiple laboratory tests before diagnosis. This time-consuming process causes ED crowding which impacts patient mortality, medical errors, staff burnout, etc. This work proposes (time) cost-effective diagnostic assistance that leverages artificial intelligence systems to help ED clinicians make efficient and accurate diagnoses. In collaboration with ED clinicians, we use public patient data to curate MIMIC-ED-Assist, a benchmark for AI systems to suggest laboratory tests that minimize wait time while accurately predicting critical outcomes such as death. With MIMIC-ED-Assist, we develop ED-Copilot which sequentially suggests patient-specific laboratory tests and makes diagnostic predictions. ED-Copilot employs a pre-trained bio-medical language model to encode patient information and uses reinforcement learning to minimize ED wait time and maximize prediction accuracy. On MIMIC-ED-Assist, ED-Copilot improves prediction accuracy over baselines while halving average wait time from four hours to two hours. ED-Copilot can also effectively personalize treatment recommendations based on patient severity, further highlighting its potential as a diagnostic assistant. Since MIMIC-ED-Assist is a retrospective benchmark, ED-Copilot is restricted to recommend only observed tests. We show ED-Copilot achieves competitive performance without this restriction as the maximum allowed time increases. Our code is available at https://github.com/cxcscmu/ED-Copilot.

paragraphs: Emergency department diagnosis often involves triage followed by multiple laboratory tests, creating delays that contribute to crowding. This paper studies diagnostic assistance that considers both predictive accuracy and time cost. Working with clinicians, the authors curate MIMIC-ED-Assist from public patient data to evaluate test recommendations and predictions of critical outcomes, including death.

Their system, ED-Copilot, recommends patient-specific laboratory tests sequentially while making diagnostic predictions. A pretrained biomedical language model encodes patient information, and reinforcement learning balances reducing wait time against improving prediction accuracy. On the benchmark, ED-Copilot improves accuracy over baselines while reducing average wait time from four hours to two. The authors also report recommendations that adapt to patient severity.

These findings come from a retrospective benchmark, whose recorded histories restrict the system to recommending observed tests. That restriction is part of interpreting the reported gains. The authors additionally show competitive performance when the restriction is removed as the maximum allowed time increases. The work demonstrates a benchmark-based approach to coordinating test selection and prediction, with potential as a diagnostic assistant.
summary.tldr: On a retrospective emergency-department benchmark, ED-Copilot improves prediction accuracy while halving average wait time through sequential test recommendations.

title: ED-Copilot: Reduce Emergency Department Wait Time with Language Model Diagnostic Assistance

abstract: In self-supervised contrastive learning, negative pairs are typically constructed using an anchor image and a sample drawn from the entire dataset, excluding the anchor. However, this approach can result in the creation of negative pairs with similar semantics, referred to as "false negatives", leading to their embeddings being falsely pushed apart. To address this issue, we introduce GloFND, an optimization-based approach that automatically learns on the fly the threshold for each anchor data to identify its false negatives during training. In contrast to previous methods for false negative discovery, our approach globally detects false negatives across the entire dataset rather than locally within the mini-batch. Moreover, its per-iteration computation cost remains independent of the dataset size. Experimental results on image and image-text data demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/vibalcam/GloFND.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning commonly forms negative pairs by taking an anchor image and another image from the dataset. Different images can nevertheless share similar meaning. Treating these pairs as negatives pushes their representations apart even though their semantic relationship suggests they should remain close. The paper focuses on identifying these false negatives during training.

GloFND learns a separate detection threshold for each anchor through optimization. The thresholds are learned as training proceeds, making false-negative discovery part of the ongoing learning process. Its detection scope covers the whole dataset, extending beyond methods that identify false negatives only within the current mini-batch.

The method combines this global scope with a per-iteration computational cost that does not depend on dataset size. That pairing matters because it connects broader false-negative discovery with a scalable training step. Experiments on image and image-text data demonstrate the method's effectiveness, supporting adaptive, anchor-specific thresholds as a way to address semantically misleading negative pairs.
summary.tldr: GloFND learns anchor-specific thresholds during training to detect false negatives across a dataset with dataset-size-independent per-iteration cost.

title: Discovering Global False Negatives On the Fly for Self-supervised Contrastive Learning

abstract: We propose, implement, and compare with competitors a new architecture of equivariant neural networks based on geometric (Clifford) algebras: Generalized Lipschitz Group Equivariant Neural Networks (GLGENN). These networks are equivariant to all pseudo-orthogonal transformations, including rotations and reflections, of a vector space with any non-degenerate or degenerate symmetric bilinear form. We propose a weight-sharing parametrization technique that takes into account the fundamental structures and operations of geometric algebras. Due to this technique, GLGENN architecture is parameter-light and has less tendency to overfitting than baseline equivariant models. GLGENN outperforms or matches competitors on several benchmarking equivariant tasks, including estimation of an equivariant function and a convex hull experiment, while using significantly fewer optimizable parameters.

These networks are equivariant to all pseudo-orthogonal transformations, including rotations and reflections, of a vector space with any non-degenerate or degenerate symmetric bilinear form. We propose a weight-sharing parametrization technique that takes into account the fundamental structures and operations of geometric algebras. paragraphs: An equivariant neural network makes its outputs transform consistently with transformations of its inputs. This paper introduces Generalized Lipschitz Group Equivariant Neural Networks, or GLGENN, using geometric Clifford algebras to build that consistency into the architecture. Its supported transformations include rotations and reflections within a broad mathematical setting.

The architecture is equivariant to pseudo-orthogonal transformations for vector spaces equipped with any symmetric bilinear form, including degenerate forms. The authors also introduce a weight-sharing scheme based on the fundamental structures and operations of geometric algebra. Sharing weights in this structured way reduces the number of independently optimized parameters while respecting the transformations the network is designed to handle.

The authors implement GLGENN and compare it with other equivariant models on several benchmarks, including equivariant function estimation and a convex hull experiment. GLGENN matches or exceeds competitors while using substantially fewer trainable parameters. The abstract also reports a reduced tendency to overfit compared with baseline equivariant models. The findings connect algebraically informed parameter sharing with both compactness and competitive task performance.
summary.tldr: GLGENN uses Clifford-algebra-based weight sharing to build broadly equivariant networks that match or outperform competitors with fewer parameters.

title: GLGENN: A Novel Parameter-Light Equivariant Neural Networks Architecture Based on Clifford Geometric Algebras

abstract: Continual learning has attracted increasing research attention in recent years due to its promising experimental results in real-world applications. In this paper, we study the issue of calibration in continual learning which reliably quantifies the uncertainty of model predictions. Conformal prediction (CP) provides a general framework for model calibration, which outputs prediction intervals or sets with a theoretical high coverage guarantee as long as the samples are exchangeable. However, the tasks in continual learning are learned in sequence, which violates the principle that data should be exchangeable. Meanwhile, the model learns the current task with limited or no access to data from previous tasks, which is not conducive to constructing the calibration set. To address these issues, we propose a CP-based method for model uncertainty quantification in continual learning (CPCL), which also reveals the connection between prediction interval length and forgetting. We analyze the oracle prediction interval in continual learning and theoretically prove the asymptotic coverage guarantee of CPCL. Finally, extensive experiments on simulated and real data empirically verify the validity of our proposed method.

Conformal prediction (CP) provides a general framework for model calibration, which outputs prediction intervals or sets with a theoretical high coverage guarantee as long as the samples are exchangeable. However, the tasks in continual learning are learned in sequence, which violates the principle that data should be exchangeable. Meanwhile, the model learns the current task with limited or no access to data from previous tasks, which is not conducive to constructing the calibration set. To address these issues, we propose a CP-based method for model uncertainty quantification in continual learning (CPCL), which also reveals the connection between prediction interval length and forgetting. We analyze the oracle prediction interval in continual learning and theoretically prove the asymptotic coverage guarantee of CPCL. Finally, extensive experiments on simulated and real data empirically verify the validity of our proposed method.

paragraphs: A continually learning model needs to express uncertainty as it moves through a sequence of tasks. Standard conformal prediction offers coverage guarantees when samples are exchangeable, meaning their ordering does not change their joint statistical behavior. Sequential task learning violates that premise, and limited access to earlier task data also makes constructing calibration data difficult.

CPCL is a conformal-prediction-based method designed for this setting. The authors analyze an oracle prediction interval and establish an asymptotic coverage guarantee for their method. This is a large-sample guarantee, preserving an important distinction from an unrestricted claim of exact coverage at every stage of continual learning.

The paper also identifies a connection between prediction-interval length and forgetting, linking uncertainty quantification with the loss of previously learned capabilities. Experiments on simulated and real data empirically support the method's validity. Together, the results address both the reliability of uncertainty estimates and their relationship to a characteristic challenge of continual learning, while adapting calibration to a setting where ordinary exchangeability and ready access to past observations are unavailable.
summary.tldr: CPCL adapts conformal uncertainty estimation to continual learning, proving asymptotic coverage and connecting prediction-interval length with forgetting.

title: Model Uncertainty Quantification by Conformal Prediction in Continual Learning

abstract: Multi-view clustering aims to improve the final performance by taking advantages of complementary and consistent information of all views. In real world, data samples with partially available information are common and the issue regarding the clustering for incomplete multi-view data is inevitably raised. To deal with the partial data with large scales, some fast clustering approaches for incomplete multi-view data have been presented. Despite the significant success, few of these methods pay attention to learning anchors with high quality in a unified framework for incomplete multi-view clustering, while ensuring the scalability for large-scale incomplete datasets. In addition, most existing approaches based on incomplete multi-view clustering ignore to build the relation between anchor graph and similarity matrix in symmetric nonnegative matrix factorization and then directly conduct graph partition based on the anchor graph to reduce the space and time consumption. In this paper, we propose a novel fast incomplete multi-view clustering method for the data with large scales, termed Fast Incomplete Multi-view clustering by flexible anchor Learning (FIML), where graph construction, anchor learning and graph partition are simultaneously integrated into a unified framework for fast incomplete multi-view clustering. To be specific, we learn a shared anchor graph to guarantee the consistency among multiple views and employ a adaptive weight coefficient to balance the impact for each view. The relation between anchor graph and similarity matrix in symmetric nonnegative matrix factorization can also be built, i.e., each entry in the anchor graph can characterize the similarity between the anchor and original data sample. We then adopt an alternative algorithm for solving the formulated problem. Experiments conducted on different datasets confirm the superiority of FIML compared with other clustering methods for incomplete multi-view data.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups samples using several sources of information, some of which may be missing for individual samples. Anchor-based methods make large datasets more manageable by representing relationships through a smaller set of anchors. FIML focuses on learning these anchors well while coordinating them with graph construction and the eventual clustering.

The method jointly learns a shared anchor graph, the anchors themselves, and a graph partition. Sharing the graph supports consistency across views, while adaptive weights balance how much each view contributes. FIML also connects the anchor graph to the similarity matrix used in symmetric nonnegative matrix factorization, giving graph entries an interpretation as similarities between anchors and original samples.

An alternating optimization procedure solves the combined problem. Bringing these stages into one framework allows anchor learning and clustering to be optimized together instead of treating the anchor graph as a fixed intermediate result. Experiments on multiple incomplete multi-view datasets report better clustering performance than comparison methods. The contribution is an integrated approach to scalable clustering when different samples provide different subsets of the available views.
summary.tldr: FIML jointly learns anchors, a shared graph, and clusters to improve scalable clustering when samples have missing views.

title: Fast Incomplete Multi-view Clustering by Flexible Anchor Learning

abstract: There is strong empirical evidence that the stateof-the-art diffusion modeling paradigm leads to models that memorize the training set, especially when the training set is small. Prior methods to mitigate the memorization problem often lead to decrease in image quality. Is it possible to obtain strong and creative generative models, i.e., models that achieve high generation quality and low memorization? Despite the current pessimistic landscape of results, we make significant progress in pushing the trade-off between fidelity and memorization. We first provide theoretical evidence that memorization in diffusion models is only necessary for denoising problems at low noise scales (usually used in generating high-frequency details). Using this theoretical insight, we propose a simple, principled method to train the diffusion models using noisy data at large noise scales. We show that our method significantly reduces memorization without decreasing the image quality, for both text-conditional and unconditional models and for a variety of data availability settings.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can memorize their training images, particularly when data are scarce. Attempts to reduce memorization have often come with worse image quality. This paper asks whether strong visual generation and low memorization can coexist, and uses the noise levels involved in diffusion training to examine where the tension arises.

The authors provide theoretical evidence that memorization is necessary only for denoising problems at low noise levels, which are commonly associated with generating fine visual details. This is a restriction on where necessity arises, rather than a claim that every low-noise problem must produce the same behavior. Motivated by the analysis, they propose training with noisy data at large noise scales.

The reported experiments show substantially reduced memorization without a decrease in image quality. This holds for both text-conditioned and unconditional models across several data-availability settings. The findings improve the observed trade-off between fidelity and memorization and suggest that changing how training uses noisy observations can preserve generation quality while reducing reliance on particular training examples.
summary.tldr: Training diffusion models with noisy data at large noise scales reduces memorization without lowering image quality in the reported experiments.

title: Does Generation Require Memorization? Creative Diffusion Models using Ambient Diffusion

abstract: Recent advances in lightweight time series forecasting models suggest the inherent simplicity of time series forecasting tasks. In this paper, we present CMoS, a super-lightweight time series forecasting model. Instead of learning the embedding of the shapes, CMoS directly models the spatial correlations between different time series chunks. Additionally, we introduce a Correlation Mixing technique that enables the model to capture diverse spatial correlations with minimal parameters, and an optional Periodicity Injection technique to ensure faster convergence. Despite utilizing as low as 1% of the lightweight model DLinear’s parameters count, experimental results demonstrate that CMoS outperforms existing state-of-the-art models across multiple datasets. Furthermore, the learned weights of CMoS exhibit great interpretability, providing practitioners with valuable insights into temporal structures within specific application scenarios.

Instead of learning embeddings that represent the shapes of chunks, CMoS places relationships among chunks at the center of its forecasting model.

The authors introduce Correlation Mixing to capture varied spatial correlations with few parameters. They also offer an optional Periodicity Injection technique to accelerate convergence. These components support the same design goal: making useful temporal structure accessible to a small model without requiring a large representation-learning system. Across multiple datasets, the reported experiments outperform existing state-of-the-art models while using parameter counts as low as 1% of DLinear's. The learned weights are also reported to be interpretable, providing insight into temporal structure in particular applications. Together, the findings suggest that directly modeling chunk relationships can deliver both forecasting accuracy and understandable model behavior with very few parameters.
summary.tldr: CMoS forecasts time series through direct chunk correlations, achieving strong reported results with very few interpretable parameters.

title: CMoS: Rethinking Time Series Prediction Through the Lens of Chunk-wise Spatial Correlations

abstract: Global cooperation on climate change mitigation is essential to limit temperature increases while supporting long-term, equitable economic growth and sustainable development. Achieving such cooperation among diverse regions, each with different incentives, in a dynamic environment shaped by complex geopolitical and economic factors, without a central authority, is a profoundly challenging game-theoretic problem. This article introduces RICE-N, a multi-region integrated assessment model that simulates the global climate, economy, and climate negotiations and agreements. RICE-N uses multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to encourage agents to develop strategic behaviors based on the environmental dynamics and the actions of the others. We present two negotiation protocols: (1) Bilateral Negotiation, an exemplary protocol and (2) Basic Club, inspired from Climate Clubs and the carbon border adjustment mechanism (Nordhaus, 2015; Comissions, 2022). We compare their impact against a no-negotiation baseline with various mitigation strategies, showing that both protocols significantly reduce temperature growth at the cost of a minor drop in production while ensuring a more equitable distribution of the emission reduction costs.

This paper introduces RICE-N, a simulation that connects regional economies, the global climate, and the negotiation of climate agreements. The findings demonstrate how negotiation rules can affect the balance between climate outcomes, economic output, and cost sharing within the modeled system.
summary.tldr: RICE-N simulations show that two climate-negotiation protocols reduce temperature growth and share mitigation costs more equitably, with a minor production trade-off.

title: AI for Global Climate Cooperation: Modeling Global Climate Negotiations, Agreements, and Long-Term Cooperation in RICE-N

abstract: Statistical evaluation aims to estimate the generalization performance of a model using held-out i.i.d. test data sampled from the ground-truth distribution. In supervised learning settings such as classification, performance metrics such as error rate are well-defined, and test error reliably approximates population error given sufficiently large datasets. In contrast, evaluation is more challenging for generative models due to their open-ended nature: it is unclear which metrics are appropriate and whether such metrics can be reliably evaluated from finite samples. In this work, we introduce a theoretical framework for evaluating language models and establish evaluability results for commonly used metrics. We study two categories of metrics: test-based metrics, including integral probability metrics (IPMs), and similarity-based metrics, including Rényi and KL divergences. We show that IPMs with respect to any bounded test class can be evaluated from finite samples up to multiplicative and additive approximation errors. Moreover, when the test class has finite fat-shattering dimension, IPMs can be evaluated with arbitrary precision. In contrast, similarity-based metrics, including Rényi and KL divergences, are not evaluable from finite samples, as their values can be critically determined by rare events. We also analyze the potential and limitations of perplexity as an evaluation method.

paragraphs: This paper asks which measures of a generative model’s quality can actually be estimated reliably from a finite test dataset. Its starting point is the gap between classification, where error rates have a clear interpretation, and open-ended generation, where choosing a meaningful metric does not automatically make that metric statistically measurable.

The authors develop a theoretical framework for language-model evaluation and distinguish two families of metrics. Test-based metrics compare distributions through a collection of tests. For integral probability metrics built from bounded tests, they establish finite-sample evaluation with both multiplicative and additive approximation errors. A further restriction on the complexity of the test collection, finite fat-shattering dimension, permits arbitrary precision.

The result differs for similarity measures such as Rényi and KL divergences: rare events can determine their values, preventing finite-sample evaluability in the framework studied. The paper also examines perplexity’s possibilities and limits. The contribution is a way to separate a metric’s conceptual appeal from whether observed samples can reliably support its numerical value.
summary.tldr: A theoretical framework identifies which generative-model evaluation metrics admit finite-sample guarantees and why rare events obstruct others.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Statistical Evaluability of Generative Models

abstract: Mixup is a widely used data augmentation technique that constructs new training examples by interpolating between existing ones. While simple and effective in domains like vision and language, applying mixup to graph data is non-trivial and there is no independent empirical evidence for its effectiveness. To fill this gap, we conducted an extensive evaluation study following a unified, established evaluation protocol for graph classification. In contrast to prior results, we found that none of the state-of-the-art mixup methods yielded statistically significant improvements over the no-mixup baseline. To obtain further insights, we analyzed the graphs generated from these mixup methods from an interpolation perspective. We found that (i) many mixup methods failed to interpolate well, (ii) high interpolation error led to performance degradation, and (iii) even good interpolation properties did not lead to performance improvements. Our findings question the efficacy of existing graph mixup methods and highlight the need for a more rigorous exploration and evaluation.

paragraphs: Mixup creates additional training examples by interpolating between existing examples. Although the idea has worked in other data domains, applying it to graphs raises questions about what a meaningful interpolation should look like. This paper independently evaluates existing graph mixup methods using a unified, established protocol for graph classification.

Under that protocol, none of the evaluated state-of-the-art methods produces a statistically significant improvement over training without mixup. This differs from previously reported results and makes the shared evaluation procedure central to the contribution. The finding concerns the tested methods and settings; it does not establish that every possible graph augmentation strategy must fail.

The authors also examine the generated graphs as interpolations. Many methods interpolate poorly, and high interpolation error is associated with performance degradation in their analysis. Yet methods with good interpolation properties still do not improve performance. These observations separate two questions that can otherwise be conflated: whether an augmentation meaningfully interpolates and whether those interpolations actually help graph classification.
summary.tldr: A unified evaluation finds no statistically significant gains from tested graph mixup methods, even when their interpolation quality is good.

title: Is Graph Mixup Beneficial? Investigating Interpolation And Empirical Performance of Graph Mixup Methods

abstract: Bayesian experimental design (BED) is a principled framework for data-efficient design of sequential experiments. However, existing BED methods are unable to adapt to dynamic constraints inherent in real-world tasks due to budget limitations, varying costs, or physical constraints that restrict how designs evolve over time. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to BED that enables constrained optimization of experimental designs by combining offline pre-training of an amortized policy and a posterior network with online multi-step lookahead planning using scenario trees. We empirically demonstrate that our method yields substantially more informative design sequences than existing methods across a range of constrained BED tasks, while incurring only a modest additional computational overhead.

paragraphs: Sequential experimental design asks which experiment to perform next to learn efficiently. In practical settings, that choice also depends on remaining budgets, changing costs, and physical restrictions on how experiments can evolve. This paper addresses Bayesian experimental design when those constraints change what sequences of experiments are feasible.

The method combines preparation before deployment with planning during execution. Offline training produces an amortized policy and a posterior network, providing reusable learned components. Online, the system performs multi-step lookahead using scenario trees. Considering possible future developments allows experimental choices to account for constraints across a sequence, rather than treating each choice as an isolated decision.

Across a range of constrained experimental-design tasks, the authors report substantially more informative design sequences than existing methods, with only modest additional computation. The finding concerns the quality of the collected information over a sequence of experiments. It suggests that combining pretrained components with online planning can make constraint-aware design practical without requiring a large computational increase in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: Combining pretrained Bayesian design components with online lookahead produces more informative experimental sequences under changing constraints.

title: Constrained Bayesian Experimental Design via Online Planning

abstract: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) serves as the de facto control mechanism for conditional diffusion, yet high guidance scales notoriously induce oversaturation, texture artifacts, and structural collapse. We attribute this failure to a geometric mismatch: standard CFG performs Euclidean extrapolation in ambient space, inadvertently driving sampling trajectories off the high-density data manifold. To resolve this, we present Manifold-Optimal Guidance (MOG), a framework that reformulates guidance as a local optimal control problem. MOG yields a closed-form, geometry-aware Riemannian update that corrects off-manifold drift without requiring retraining. Leveraging this perspective, we further introduce Auto-MOG, a dynamic energy-balancing schedule that adaptively calibrates guidance strength, effectively eliminating the need for manual hyperparameter tuning. Extensive validation demonstrates that MOG yields superior fidelity and alignment compared to baselines, with virtually no added computational overhead.

This paper attributes those failures to geometry: ordinary guidance extrapolates in the surrounding space and can push sampling trajectories away from the high-density region associated with the data.
